JOHN BUBBLES
Interviewed by George Nierenberg December 1979
Institute of Jazz Studies Jazz Oral History Projects
Beginning of Tape 1 - Side A
This is George Nirenberg interviewing John Bubbles. I'm the interviewer and interviewing John W. Bubbles, is that correct?
That's correct.
B-U-B-B-L-E-S. And this interview is being conducted on December 18th, 1979. This is the first time and only time will tell how long it will be.
To start off, I'd really like to start right at the beginning with you as a child, as a baby, before you perhaps had inclinations at that time to be a performer, perhaps you didn't.

I was born in Louisville, Kentucky, February 19th, 1902, at 1224 Green Street and I lived there for a while and my mother wanted me to meet my uncle who wanted to see me, so they took me to Smyrna where my uncle lived for him to see me where I stayed for quite a little while. Then my father got a job working for the Nashville Saddlery Company in Nashville, Tennessee and my

mother moved to Nashville from Louisville where I went to school first in Nashville when I was 5 years old. I went to school and after I went to school when I become 7 years old, that's when I went on the stage in an open air theatre at 15th and Joe Johnson Street -- I was looking at the show from the front, I was out in the front, watching the show as a kid at the age of 7 and I thought I would go back after I'd seen the show and see the people to see if I could get a job singing in the show because I was thinking I heard could outsing anybody/sing on the stage.

So I went back and asked them and they told me I'd have to come back -- who told you you could sing? I said I didn't -- I told myself. "All right, you go ahead and get us some music and bring it back, you have rehearsal tomorrow." So I did, brought the music back on singing a song called, "I'm So Glad My Mama Don't Know Where I Am." "Where I'm at" is the way you phrased it, you know.
And they liked my singing, they gave me a job, 25 cents a week and bring all the people that wanted to see the show. And I started with that.
And after I did that --

One question. That first experience of performing on stage, you must have some feelings about what happened when you got up there, how people responded. What was it about it that you liked? You weren't dancing then.
No, just singing.
What inspired you to sing? Was your mother a singer? Was your father a singer?

No, I just made myself. Just me, I was a singer. I was the only entertainer at that time, you could tell -- after all, being 7 years old. I never heard my mother sing, but she sang and I guess my father sang, too. But they didn't do no profession. I'm the first professional out of the family. So they enjoyed my singing, they enjoyed me and the public received me very well.
You were just a little child, then.
That's right.
What feelings were you going
through on the stage there all alone singing?

No feeling, I was just like anybody else that would be on the stage singing. I didn't have no feeling to go out there, no excitement, just singing. Like Shirley Temple would sing. How would she do, she wasn't excited, you know. I was what you call a born actor, born performer.
Was the audience all black when you sang?
I presume they were. I didn't look to that. I guess they were all black, colored neighborhood.
I take it you were a success.

Oh, yeah, yeah. From that I that I thought I had to go to school. In fact I was in school, because if I was 7 years old I was in school. So my mother thought they'd move me to Indianapolis. So I went to Indianapolis and I got to be 9 years old. That's when I went on Amateur Night at the Washington Theatre in Indianapolis, Indiana.
But there was something
inside you that made you want to continue to perform.

Something about Indianapolis, my mother wanted to go there, too, same as Nashville. See, being born in the country to go to the city, then a city on top of a city, Indianapolis was more popular than Nashville. So she wanted to go to Indianapolis so she took me to Indianapolis, Indiana. That's where we started the foundation, transferred me from the Hadley Street School which is in Nashville to the School No. 24 in Indianapolis where I stayed from the age of 7 to 9 -- I went on Amateur Night and after going on Amateur Night at 9, won the first prize for eight straight Fridays, eight straight weeks.
What is Amateur Night?
Who's the best -- like -- what Channel was he on.
There was no television --

No, no, no -- this was amateurs you know, with Ray Bolger -- not Ray Bolger but what's his name, I can't think of his name. However, Amateur Night -- you can translate that later. But the point I want to make for you, I went on Amateur Night for
(Ed.-Ted Mack's Amateur Hour)
eight weeks, winning the first prize every Friday night.
As a singer.

Yeh. So much as that the people couldn't get no contestants in there unless they took me out. If they know I'm going to be on the program they won't contest. So they took me out so what could I do then but sell candy, sodas and stuff in the theatre, you know, to earn money that I wanted to make -- you understand? And the manager of the theatre had me go to the film company and bring back the films and distribute the play bills that they had for what's coming, that would help earn some money. Then I worked for the Indianapolis Star getting customers to take the paper, winning the contest, bicycle contest -- you wint a bicycle if you won the contest, and so forth, I did that.
Did you win a bicycle?
Yeah, 'cause I got a lot of customers. Then I was about 9 years old or 10 -- maybe about 12 or 13 years old, I went to Kinger's Packing House, a meat company, you know to work there,

stamping meat. I worked there for, oh, maybe a year. Then I once saw a Billy goat and I wanted my father to get me a Billy goat, but he didn't want me to have a goat, he wanted me to have a pony. So while he was working for the Nashville Saddlery Company, he made a set of harness for a pony; but I never got the pony; but I saw a goat, so I got a Billy goat and he made a harness to fit the Billy goat and I made myself a wagon and they let me put the goat in the shed, the coal shed. That's where I kept the goat with the wagon and all.
Anyway, that went on for about three years.
Did it have a special meaning to you, the Billy goat?

Oh, I wanted a goat because the goat was popular. I had friends that had goats, you know, and I got a goat. Then I wanted to do the last day of school performances of the show they have on, I wanted my father to make me a carrier-van and have a Billy goat and do Indian and cowboy stories, which I put on at the school, you know. And that was my popularity and I wanted to have that movement

in the school. Then I wanted to be at the head of the class in singing. I wanted to be at the head of the class in drawing, manual training, all this, / I wanted to be at the head of the class, so I worked hard at that and worked hard at that. So finally -- we were coming home from school and all the kids had to pass by a white school on North Street and at this white school all the kids was throwing rocks at the colored kids. Well, I didn't understand why. So one day I told my mother about this. And she said, did you tell the teacher? And I said, yes, I told the teacher. What did the teacher say? Nothing.

So I was going to school the next day, so I told the teacher -- and that day my mother wanted me to come home early because she wanted me to take her to the doctor. So she says okay. The next day I'm going to school, the teacher lets me out early before any other kids get out -- she lets me out. So I'm going to find out what makes these kids throw the rocks. So I got behind a tree, looking at these kids and I saw who was throwing the rocks first. I didn't say nothing. But that day I saw it, but the

next day I prepared for it. So I set up a rock quarry -- 10 rocks in a pile here and there, and zig-zag here and there, where I would have to pick up the rocks and have a battle with rocks, okay? What should happen, the next day I waited to see who was going to throw the first rocks, and the white kids were throwing the rocks. So I thought they were just bad because the colored kids just run, they didn't want to start no rock throwing and they didn't know there was anybody in the crowd -- there was nobody in that crowd that they were throwing rocks at. I was by myself behind a tree. So I'm the one started throwing rocks back at the kids. But I did it all by myself. I throwed all the rocks I had in my hand, I throw them and then go to the pile and throw them, go to another pile and throw them, till I run the kids past the school that they came out of. And all the kids joined me helping me to throw rocks at the kids. I had more rocks coming from the colored kids than white ones -- do you understand me? Therefore, they seemed to be satisfied, they stopped throwing rocks after that day.

The next day my mother says to me, 'The kids still throwing rocks?' 'No, they stopped.' I didn't tell her what stopped it. Because she would have had a fit if she knew what I did. I didn't tell her. So after this thing happens I go peacefully and quietly until finally the boy that had a Billy goat, he was doing a lot of stealing, so they wanted to blame it on me. Therefore, my mother wants to get rid of my goat, 'cause he had a goat.

So I was at the packing house at the time she saw a candleman wanted to buy the goat because the goat had very pretty colors -- brown, white and black, spotted albino, very nice goat. So she sold my goat.

Then I wanted to go to a park in Indianapolis where they have lawn swings and they have chain swings, but they didn't allow colored people to walk children to swing on the swings, chain swings, you know. But you could swing on the lawn swings, you know, old lawn swings with backs to them that four people could sit in. Well, I thought I'd tell my mother to let me go to the park. She says, you can go to the park but you get back by the time I get from

the store. I said, okay.
So as I boy I never knew my name was going
to be JB.
What was your name?
Just Bubber -- B-U-B-B-E-R.
John Bubber?
B-U-B-B-E-R.

That was your middle name --
and your last name?

Sublette. But the boy that
they took with me to the park, his name was JB. He
was younger than me and we go get in the swings, the
chain swings. But I wasn't thinking of creating
nothing, just get in the swing. I don't know what
possessed me or plodded me to get in the swing, but
I got in the swing and I'm swinging and I want to go
over, you know. I want to go over. So he's there
swinging, swinging and I was swinging and oh, I stand
up in time to get off. So a couple of kids come over
and say, 'Get out of that swing.' Nobody answered him
then. So a little while later about four or five more
kids come when the other kids were there. 'Okay, get

out of the swing." So the boy, JB, got out of the swing but I stayed in the swing and about four or five more boys came over. Must have been about fifty boys around the swing to tell me to get out of the swing. I look over here on the one side, there was a park guard and a matron. I looked over on the other side there's two or three colored people over there so they can see what's happening.

So they hollered again, "Get out of that swing." I said, "When the cat dies," which means when the swing gets down to where it dies of its own momentum I would get out. So I let the swing calm down, calm down, calm down, calm down, and it finally gets down to where I can step out when the swing is not swinging. As soon as I stepped on the ground the boys attacked me. Get the point? When they attacked me, I'd been seeing so many pictures in life that I knew more about how to get out of a gang than they did, you know. So I ducked the guy that hit at me this way, the one guy kicked at me, I went in the crowd, got under the legs and came out right behind them, you know. And I run from there over to a push

merry-go-round and I got over there and the park guard and the matron never said a word, so I figured I would -- I was now mad because they wouldn't say nothing and the guys could do what they wanted to do and there was about fifty of them over there by the tree. So I thought I would wait to see what happened about this happening, and the tears started rolling down my cheeks and I had deck overalls on, the pants, and down the side of the pants I had a knife that I play mumble-peg with, you know. So I get this knife out of the side and I opened up the knife, and while they were laughing and celebrating at what they had just done, and I go to this crowd of boys, and I ain't thinking about nothing but going to this crowd of boys -- first come, first served.

So I guess about eight or nine of the boys run and one fella stood there. He's the one fella that got cut. So when I cut him, that was all. Soon as I saw the blood, that was all, and I turned and I run. They ran me all the way up to my house, I was right across from the park, they run me in there. I forgot I had a basement, I run past the basement, the

basement where they put the coal in, I run past that and run over to the fence that leads from the undertaker's yard over to another yard. So I get up on the fence to go over and I had thrown rocks to keep them back while JB was running and he was the one that was in front of me and I'm protecting him by throwing rocks at them, you know. So what should happen is when I get to the house and passed the -- I don't think about the transom where you put coal in, I passed the transom and go to the fence because I got to keep going because the guys are crowding me. So I get to the fence, so I figure I got to get over the fence -- I get up on the fence then one guy's down here to catch me as I go over the fence and one guy's coming over here. So I finally get down over the fence on this side instead of going back and it's an alleyway going out to the street. And between the alleyway there was a piano box, upright piano box sitting there. So I ran up to this piano box -- seeing pictures of that give me the thought -- and I get behind the piano box. The guys passed me like a freight train -- bang! (Unintelligible). And what happened

after that some people next door saw me get behind this box and they hollered, 'Hey, come over here,' after the boys passed. I jumped over the fence at some white people's house, they had known me, had me in their living room, they locked the door, I sat on a settee and I took the knife that I had and hid it in the pillows on the settee. They called the police, police came -- all the boys are gone now. So they got the police wagon out there, a Ford, what you call an open-top Ford, you know, four-seater. So they put me in the Ford, take me down to the station and I'm under arrest, naturally;but first they take me to the hospital where this boy was to recognize if I'm the fella. 'That's him,' says the boy. So the boy was being held by a policeman over there that's already in the hospital and the police got me so when he wants to get loose, I want to get loose 'cause we want to get together. It's all right with me. But he don't get away, I don't get away. They already know that's me because they've all recognized me -- that's me. Okay, I don't mind that's me.

So I go on with them to the Detention Home. They take me to the Detention Home, okay? I get to the Detention Home, they've got to notify my mother. But somebody notified my mother, the lady that had me in the house. She notified my mother and told her what had happened, told her the whole story. My mother come down to the Detention Home to get me and I had a reputation in that town. I mean a reputation. About the Indianapolis Star, about the Five and Ten Cents Store, Kinger's Packing House, all (inaudible).
How old were you then?
Then? 12, 12 years old I think it was, 12 or 13.
However, the only way they could get me out of the Detention Home was to take me out of town and out of town I went. They put me into Louisville.
With your family, your whole family left?
Yeh, Yeh, they got to leave, they got to follow me.
Did you have any brothers and sisters?
Sisters, no brothers, I had two sisters.
Older or younger?
One older sister, one younger sister.
So now you're off to Kentucky.
Yeh.
With your mother and your father and your two sisters.
Yeh.
Because that was the only way they could keep you out of the Detention Home.
That's the only way they could get me out.
So that's where I went to work for a bicycle company along Marcus Street, called the Van Dyke Bicycle Company, making bicycles.
Had you stopped performing?
Look, I had to do something between that time. I can't just pick up a job.
But you were still singing.
Yeh, but I wasn't singing between times, this is what happened to that.
What kind of music were you singing?
Any kind of song, all kinds.
For example, what songs?
"Darktown Strutters Ball," "When You and I Were Young, Maggie," "Beautiful Doll," "Midnight Choo-Choo Leaves for Alabam'," and, oh, I can't make head nor tails of all the different songs I sang.
Where did you learn all of thos?
From the Five and Ten Cents store.
On the radio, the phonograph?
Five and Ten Cents store.
Was it on the radio or --
No, they're sheet music.
Sheet music.
Yeh, they played it in the Five and Ten Cents store. I buy the music of it and I go to

the Five and Ten Cents store and my partner will play it there. But then I had met him then, but the point of it I'd learn the pieces -- get what I mean -- just learn the words, later I learned the music, you know.
What was it about the songs that interested you?

The different lyrics that interested you -- what was in the song. See, a song like "Mammy O'Mine," "Beautiful Doll" and "When the Midnight Choo-Choo Leaves for Alabam," all the -- today all the songs I heard, oh, so many years ago, it ain't even funny. The point of it is that I finally got to a place where I wanted to really entertain.
Louisville, Kentucky.
This was after I met my partner. See, that's where I met a partner.
In Kentucky?
In Louisville.
Was J --
JB, that's the kid I went to school with.
So you never teamed up with him and tried to do singing?
No, I didn't go to school with Buck, Buck went to another school.
So now you're 12 years old and you're in Louisville, Kentucky.
That's right. That's when I bumped into my partner.
How did you happen to bump into him?

In a bowling alley, setting up pins. Grody's (phonetic spelling) Bowling Alley, setting up pins, pin boys. Different leagues played bowl, you know. That's how we came about. We started to entertain the soldiers.
You were bowling there?
No, no, we just set up pins.
You were both setting up pins together?
Yeah.
So you were both working there.
There are about four or five alleys, you know, my alley was next to his, one of them things, you know.
How did you find out that -- did he play the piano and sing, too?

No, the idea was, we had gotten to the point -- I met him in the bowling alley, then I learned afterwards he had a bicycle in the shop where I was working. Then getting his bike out of the shop when he didn't have money to get it was one of the partnerships that stuck. Then he would take me to show he could play piano, he took me to the barrooms, you know, where he'd been going before and playing piano. He took me there to where he played piano and I'd sing, then we got a hit playing at different bars for the soldiers at that time -- 1918.
He was playing a piano at 12 years old in bars?
He was playing piano, yeah, who could tell, who cares how old he is as long as he plays piano. Nobody cares.
What kind of music did he
play?

Every kind, any kind you can think of -- all notes, he played classics, too, man. Sextet from "Lucia di Lammermoor" and all classics, man, he could play classics. I taught him how to play ragtime -- classics and ragtime. But that's what he did. But my point there, what I'm trying to bring to your attention is that when we set up pins in the bowling alley, he lived on the east side of Kentucky and I lived on the west side, like, you know, on the west side and we were busy as cats on a tin roof in these different bars. Then we just began to advertise for the Indiana Truck Company at state fairs.
How did you do that?

Entertain -- singing. He played piano and I sang. That's the type of entertainment -- singing and playing the piano. You must realize I could sing, man. You must realize I could sing. Do you think Al Jolson could outsing me? In a pig's eye. No, man, I just can't get over how - so sad in my mind for me not to take vocal lessons to reserve my voice -- preserve my voice, do you know what
I mean? I don't know why, but he was that just kind of a fella, I guess.

Anyway, getting back to where we entertained for the Indian Trucks, there was a fella called Humboldt Collins -- he was the manager of the Indiana Truck Company -- we used to advertise his trucks and he used to take us around to different parties, places to play for him, which was magnificent. Then we'd play the (inaudible) in the Waterson motel in Kentucky, the biggest hotels that were there, you know. We played in the Five and Ten Cents Store. We'd sell sheet music, advertising the sheet music. He played the piano and I'd sing maybe a song or so. And the people wouldn't have it unless they'd hear the song and then they'd buy and use it. If you didn't know nothing about music, you can always buy a song anyway. Just to hear me sing it, the entertainment going on, which was then very good, very good.
Could you read music?
No and he couldn't either. Nobody could read -- now, we don't need to read to learn to sing the lyrics.
You'd hear it then somewhere else --
No, Buck played it, Buck played it, he didn't read no music, he played.

He'd hear it -- you'd whistle it to him, he heard it, you know what I mean. All that he didn't know already. Oh, he was a genius. He give Art Tatum a few bars. Fats Waller, he give these fellas a few bars of music. Earl Hines. He used to hang out with Louis Armstrong, you know. He got so he played trumpet like Louis Armstrong. He could play piano well, you know. Now, you heard him play.
Yeh.

So he could play piano so well -- he stood up to play, you know. However, we did this. I found when we were playing in the different bars and I would listen to him play and I'm thinking of how an act would be under that name. That's when I formed the act of Buck and Bubbles.
End of Side A - Tape 1
Beginning of Side B - Tape 1
... 21 years old?
No, we hadn't gotten to your being in the Detention Home.
Oh, you forgot that, huh?
I don't think you told me. You told me you were in a Detention Home.
I told ya how my mother got me out! Didn't I tell you that?
Right.
By going to -- taking me out of there -- to Louisville, didn't I tell you that?
Mh-hm.
Well, then, what point are you making?
Well, what was the --

Getting me out of the Detention Home and being able to participate in the Amateur Night thing, that put me in the line of professional. I got to go farther than where I am. And where can I go? It's just like here, where can you go after you play the Orpheum Theatre. Got to go to San Francisco, 'cause

how many theatres can you play? You see what I'm trying to say? Well, in Louisville and in Indianapolis the field is much smaller than what it is in New York or Chicago in the entertainment world. Therefore, I got to go. If my mother don't get me out of the Detention Home, I'd still be in Indianapolis and the reason why they let me out is because I'm going to create more difficulty with the prejudice going on, I'm going to be a helluva Negro, man. That's common sense tell you that. I was worse than Luther King, but I'm violent, he ain't. That's the difference. Do you understand? 'Cause I could kill ya in a minute, that was my point then and I wasn't thinking of death, wasn't thinking of death. You understand me? If you hurt me or you do something wrong to me, shame on you, shame on you. Well, when I went in that crowd of fifty fellas, man, you know I had a whole lot of nerve to go in a crowd of fifty boys with me, I'm only 12 or 13 years old. But I din't give a rap. I just went on. But see what it debted me for doing that? Now, I didn't know I was going to do this now. Don't forget that, I didn't know this. I don't build this up for

trouble. I'm building this up to tear down the situation that's causing trouble. I'm going to try to stop throwing the rocks. I'm trying to stop that kids can't play on the swing. I don't know these things are detrimental. Only feel they are things that should not be.
Who told me to do it? Nobody. Nobody told me I could do this either.

So when I did this, I'm thinking all the time -- thank the Judge for making that decision. I'm thanking the Judge today, because he knew that I've got to be 20 or 21 years old or somebody is going to die, sure 'nuff. Gotta. And prejudice goes by age and if this was only a kid, what will I do with a man that's 21 or a man who's 35. I'm going to have to shoot him. You understand? I'm not like a guy selling dope in the theatre or selling dope in the schools. I'm the same kind of guy that's selling violence in the school. I'm the same kind of a guy, only I ain't got dope, I've got malice. And I didn't carry nowhere. I'd have ended it all right there. I'd have ended it all right there. You understand? But later on in life

it did happen that -- by travelling I learned quite a bit and I needed to learn. So getting away from Indianapolis, going to Louisville, there was a show came to town in Louisville, a big show came to town, understand? I'd say a carnival came to Louisville, carnival. And I wanted to join this carnival and we did an audition for the carnival, Buck and I, but Buck was too small. He ain't big enough for his age.
Did Buck have his own piano?
No, there was a piano everywhere we go. There was a piano everywhere. The barrooms had a piano, the Ten Cents store had a piano. Everywhere we went -- at parties they had pianos.
This Buck, were his parents in Louisville?
Yeh.
Your parents were in Louisville with you at that point, too.
Yeh. Yeah.
How did they feel about you sort of starting to be in show business?
How did they feel?
Yeh.

I was one of the boys that the parents wanted to be what he wanted to be. All except one thing, I didn't want to be a doctor. My father wanted me to be a doctor. But I didn't want to be a doctor because I couldn't stand the idea of people dying. To me I couldn't see that as I see it today, as I see what that doctor situation is today, too. If I had been a doctor I'd have taken care of everything. Same as I dance, I'd take everything and dance, I'd take everything in a situation, don't care what it was. I'm sorry I didn't get to go to school in one incident but one thing gives me another one, in another incident.

Clarence Muse put it in the Clarence Muse biography about him being a lawyer, studied to be a lawyer. But the field was so small for the Negros as lawyers that he thought he'd be an entertainer. So he put the lawyer down.
The same thing applied to me when I got my partner. When they wouldn't let my partner go with the
show -- the carnival -- I went with the carnival for maybe two or three months, maybe a little longer. And I went traveling with the carnival --
Who wouldn't let your partner go with the circus --

The owner of the show, that's who wouldn't, the owner of the show. His mother wouldn't mind him go anywhere with me, but the owner of the show, just like if you had a show, you wouldn't take Dave because it was against the law if you take him. That's the same principle.
He was too small.
Yeh, underage.
He was how many years younger than you?
Four.
You were 12, he was 8 then.
Yeh -- he was 9 really. I was 13.
What kind of a carnival was it?
Variety shows, like they had
different ferris wheels and the Whip, merry-go-round and everything you could think of for a carnival. It was like a circus, almost like a small circus.
Was it all black?
No, no. No, no, all white. Only black thing they had in it was the show, was the colored show.
But you were part of the colored show.

I wasn't part of nothing, I hadn't gotten in the show yet. But they had a show like the side-show in the circus. This is what they had. I went with this show. But before I went with this show, Ringling Brothers wanted me to go with them, when I was 13. And my mother asked me if I wanted to go, I said / no, I don't want to leave my mama. I wouldn't go.
How did they see you?
They heard about me, they didn't see me, they heard about me, man. I was the knownest entertainer in Louisville. Why, sure.
You were only 12 years old.
I don't care how old I was.
How old was Shirley Temple? How old was Shirley Temple, was she 12? Go ahead, answer that.
She was younger than 12.

Daggone right she was, but she was white, you understand that? Why? Why -- George, you can question me for years on different things but if you don't use the thought of the difference between white and black and Carter's Administration of Human Rights, then you're way behind, you're way behind. He's got as much right preaching human rights as I have knocking you in the head with a brick. You understand what I'm saying? Somebody has to start it. Luther King was about the greatest one to start it. If you can't take conceptions from him, who will you take it from? Not from Carter. I don't know what to say about that, but the only thing I can say is that you've got to take it into consideration that the world of yesterday is not the world of today. And the world of today is not the world of tomorrow, because tomorrow is still coming. It's getting worse and worse, things are getting worse and worse.
We'll get back to where I was. When the circus

wanted me and I wouldn't go, this carnival that was in Louisville, when I went to Indianapolis I said -- I went there with a fella after we got the act together -- we got the act together -- see the name of Buck and Bubbles together, then we played at the state fair and all --
I'd like to go back just a second -- this carnival that you were part of, now you became part of the black show, what was the carnival called?
Superior Shows.
Superior Shows. Who were some of the performers that were in that carnival with you? Do you remember any of them?
Oh, I'd have to fish back to think about them. There was about eight or nine different ones. They had a fella in there that put me in the cabaret, his name was Kid Fox, and, oh, I can't think of --
What did this carnival consist of, the part that you -- the black show?
Singing and dancing --
What kind of dancing?
Clog dancing -- buck dancing, I guess you called it then, too.
No tap dancing?
No.
Was there any other kind of dancing?
No.
And was it white people doing this kind of dancing?
Colored.
Were they good?
Yeh. We had a fella called -- I can't think of his name -- you're going back over 50 odd years, man. I'm almost 75 years back now or more.
You have an extraordinary memory.
I don't know about that. What you left off was the part that made it so interesting for me traveling!--
Well, you seemed to be

Why? Why --you've got the question of why and I told you why. About the Detention Home situation, how much I appreciate the Judge making the decision he made because he knew later on in life I was going to do more harm than what I did. And that's only the beginning -- and at my age, what am I going to do with somebody that hangs out with me that's older than me, that hangs out with me. See what I mean? So I give the Judge credit for using the judgment he used by letting my mother take me out of the school, take me out of town to get me out of the Detention Home. I thought that was beautiful. He doesn't know what a favor he did for me. You understand? Because I was traveling ever since. Ever since. Now, I go with this carnival -- not the circus now -- I went with the carnival. So I went with the carnival for about -- I'd been playing partners and everything, Buck and I playing the barrooms ane everything, I told you that; and this guy Humbolt Collins used to take us around and he had a

way of introducing us that was superior. Superior. He would go to your house or any friend's house who were white, ring the bell and his entrance was, "let us niggers in and if you don't want us niggers here we'll leave." They liked him so well that they over- looked that we were colored. They received him and Buck and I as though we were one of them. If we entertained, we were four times greater.
Who was this person that was introducing you?
Humbolt Collins.
And he was your manager?

No, he was just a fella that had the Indiana Trucks I told ya. He took it upon himself to take us around to different parties. He wanted them to hear us entertain. You understand? And through him was a great movement because his saying nigger didn't mean nothing, 'cause we knew he was white, we knew he was white. What he was saying didn't mean nothing. You understand? What meant something was him telling this other white fella who he had that the word when he used it wasn't as harmful to us as it would be

to George and Jim. You get my point? Therefore, they received us knowing that we know who we are without them saying who we were. And they don't have to bring up the term at all, 'cause he's already introduced us as being one of us -- us -- he used the term, it was us.
Well, we got along fine, until finally I got into this carnival, and I was with the carnival about two or three months --
Let me just go back a second. What type of white people were you performing for, what kind of parties? Were they wealthy whites?
Private parties, private. I don't know how wealthy, how wealthy could they be, how would I know. How would I know? You help me out.
By the kind of homes that they lived in.

Nice homes, nice dress. Everybody ain't welcome because they got-(inaudible). I didn't worry about that. They were people that I wanted to get to know Buck and Bubbles. I wanted to get them to know us in the same spirit that this man knows us.
What was in it for him? Was he acting on it?

No, no. The same interest you take in an act, same thing, ain't no different. But the point is Nazzaro was an agent and a manager, but you're not an agent. The point I'm trying to bring out to you just the interest you took in what you're doing is the interest he took in what he was doing. If we can help him in what he was doing, selling cars, advertising -- well, he had a good idea. I enjoyed his friendship and everything and we were successful to his managerials, okay?

And after being with the carnival maybe two or three months -- there was a fella in there they called Kid Fox, he was an Indian. He wanted to see me get a better break than this carnival, 'cause I was much too good for the carnival because the man that run the carnival, he was a nice guy, nice guy, but he'd give you peanuts instead of chocolates. If you take the peanuts, didn't know no more than the peanuts, you don't know no more than the peanuts. You don't know what the chocolates tasted like.

And this Indian fella, he come to be a friend of mine, he took me to a cabaret in --when the carnival got to Detroit. He took me to this cabaret to do an audition. He'd get me there and let them see me sing. That's all he wanted to do. He did and that put me in the cabaret division. Now, not the carnival now, cabaret division. 'Cause I go in the cabaret, man, I tore the cabaret down. I used to make so much money in the cabaret, people throwing money and all. However, I played two cabarets at once, one right across the street from the other. Because I was an entertainer. Shirley Temple didn't have nothing on me. And don't you think that -- what's his name, can't think of his -- Buck was as good on the piano as Louis Armstrong on the trumpet, and you can see how good that must have been. Of course you ain't heard half the things he could play.

But anyway, when I got this job in this cabaret called the Palm Pavilion in Detroit, Michigan, Grashet Avenue, I got another job across the street from the Palm Pavilion called the Royal Garden. I used to entertain in the Royal Garden and go back and
entertain in the Palm Pavilion between shows, you know. One show and then the other.
So you left the carnival at this point, then, and you started performing in cabarets?

Not yet, I got to get through with the cabaret. I'm going to finish the carnival, in Detroit I'm going to finish because I got set on the ground floor, the guy wants to give me a contract, so I'm going to finish the carnival and go with the cabaret. So I did, till I was 15 years old.
I take it Buck was back in Louisville at this point.
Yeh, but he's writing me to come home cause he got a job for us.
Could you describe visually what -- not only visually but what would happen in the cabaret, what was the show like, what kind of things would happen in there?
Well, they had the entertainers there, versatile entertainers. They'd sing, they'd dance -- same as when you go in the theatre now, there's

no difference, there ain't no difference. The same entertainment that you carry on now. They ain't changed that style of entertainment in the world yet. Singing and dancing, they got that all going on. Or do you think they changed?
I didn't live back then so I don't know what it was like.
No, but it's the same thing. Same thing going on now.
Well, was it all black, first of all, this cabaret that you were in?
Yeh, the guests was black and yeh, black musicians, black entertainment, black audience, okay?
Only for black communities. And the kind of music that you sang and the kind of dancing --
It wasn't that kind of a place you could come if you were black or white. It didn't make no difference. It wasn't prejudiced. But the majority of people that patronized the place were colored.

When I get the contract and everything for the cabaret, I put the carnival down. I get the letter from my partner to come home. I'm with the carnival and I put it down and go to Detroit. While I'm in Detroit -- a guy was cheating in a game so I want to leave the cabaret now. Instead of not playing I just as soon leave the cabaret. Get what I'm saying or do you? Not that I could quit gambling and be sufficient, but to leave the cabaret, I'd be better off. That's my point.

So I go join my mother and my older sister who was with another show which is -- what was the name of that show? I forgot the name of that show they were with. Anyway, I went to join them and then I figured I'd go from here, I'd go back to Louisville because Buck wanted me to come back. So I go back to Louisville and the job he had was ushering in the gallery in the B.F. Kay-May Anderson Theatre in Louisville, Kentucky which was quite surprising. I would have never went back for no job like that. But to please him I took the job.
We were only ushering in the theatre about

two weeks when an act appeared out of vaudeville, an act came and he was too sick to appear, so the manager called us down from the gallery to want to know if we wanted to go on in this act's place. I told him yes, because this manager had seen us at these parties. He knew what we could do. His name is George Carter.

However, he say, you go home and getyourself together and come on back for the next show. So okay, we did. We went on home and got dressed, got our clothes, come back for the next show but didn't know he was going to have a tutor for us. He had a tutor there for us to help us dress and put us on the stage, colored fellow, who was an entertainer, comedian, and we had to put on gloves, burnt cork -- our natural color you wouldn't see, we covered that with burnt cork, like Al Jolson, understand?
Was this the first time you did this?
This was the first time that we did it. We were the first Negro act that ever played in this theatre, too. We were the first Negro

act that ever played in this theatre. There had never been a colored act in that theatre before we got there. And we were such a hit, they kept us a second week. We had a beautiful act, beautiful act. Buck had a baby grand piano, center stage, Eton, Buster Brown collars, butterfly ties, black felt hats, white gloves, patent leather shoes, spats. He walks out on the stage to the piano with an introduction. He gets to the piano, he makes arpeggio on the piano and he starts playing the song that I sing off-stage:
"And now we are aged and gray, Maggie Our trials are nearly done, Let us sing of the days that are gone, Maggie Since you and I were young."

And I walk on the stage and nobody could tell whether I was black or white because the voice -- I had a great voice -- get my point? If we made a reputation with my voice, man, you know I had a voice, don't you? Understand?
So we opened up such a hit, they kept us there for two weeks and such a hit, the manager was so pleased that he said there was a big company coming in next week --no vaudeville now----- big company,
called the Kiss Me Company and I'm going to have you all to do an audition for him and maybe he'll take you with the show.
Can you just step back just a little bit and just tell me what happened after you came out on stage and they realized you were black and what happened --

They don't realize we're black -- how can they realize it? How are you going to tell? How are you going to tell? I got burnt cork on, how are you going to tell I'm black. He's got on gloves, I've got on gloves. What color are we? I just told you burnt cork.
I see what you mean. So now you're out there and what did you do? What's the act? Once you get out on the stage, what was the act that you did?
Singing and playing the piano.
You mentined that when Buck came out there was an introduction. Who gave the introduction?
The orchestra.
I see.
Oh, come on, George, you've got to be kidding.
I didn't know if somebody came out and introduced you or if there was a --

No, not like that, you go on like a vaudeville movement. They don't go out to introduce vaudeville acts. They used to have cards that would go on to do that. You go to your cabaret in Las Vegas, they don't do that. They have cards to show who's coming next. And they would just play the introduction of the music that you're going to use, the music to get you on, instead of being alone on the stage in silence, you know, so you walk on and play. Okay?
How many numbers did you do?
Four.
Do you remember the tunes?
I did 'Back Home in Indiana,' 'International Rag,' 'Shine' and the blues. Well, you never heard of them back there anyway. We did -- these

are daisies, I can't explain them to you -- the results of it. Because you didn't know. If you saw me in the attire that I wore you could understand that my talent surpassed the attire, the costume that I wore. When I was by myself I had on pants with a blouse over your knee and spats and butterfly tied collar. Of you should have saw me. But the point I want to bring to your attention is that when we make a success the show comes to town. The manager introduced us to the manager of the show and told him about us and we did an audition for him and we did an audition for him the first chance he got he wanted to know if we wanted to go to New York. We told him yeah. "Get your mother and so forth and I'll draw up the papers and you get your mother and all to sign and I'll take you to New York." Okay.
That was pretty quick.

That's what you got to work with man -- what have you got to work with? What have you got to work with? What are you going to do with Frank Sinatra, man, let him go out through your fingers? Why I used Frank Sinatra, because you know who Frank
Yeh.
Are you ready?
I'm ready.
So I gotta get Buck out of school.
You're saying about talent --

I've got to get Buck -- what are you saying. Do you remember what you said? The man is going to take us to New York, that's what I told you, that's the last thing I said to you, he's going to take us to New York and he said get your mother to sign the papers and so and so, I'll take you to New York. How did it go so fast, that's what you said. Now I'm back into where I left off at by saying to you I had to get Buck out of school. You just seemed like a self-assured kind of kid. You pretty much knew what

Born that way I guess. Born like that, man. Been that way since I was born. Only thing I didn't know is the difference between a man and his wife. Didn't know that difference. If I did know that difference he wouldn't have taken my father when he did. Okay?

Oh, God, tell you that later. I want to get to this point where I just said I got to get Buck out of school. So I go to Buck's school to see his principal.

Where were we?
... about the bicycle and it didn't cost him nothing' cause I didn't grab it, let it go against me and ever after we did all right.

I was down at tobacco Hodgets --

Tobacco in a Hodgets, in like a keg, that's a Hodgets and you roll this on a flat car, wagon and they put sticks up to keep from rolling off and you drive it to where it's got to go and they take it off.

That's okay.

You were a hard worker then.

Well, it was a hard try anyway. My enthusiasm was at the peak, at its peak. I kept myself busy at all times, trying to get this and that. If I wasn't doing one thing I was doing another. I went to shining shoes, and if I wasn't shining shoes I was hoving bubbles, I hoved butts, I'd sell rags and things back then and coal, I kept myself busy all the time. I used to have to get up in the morning to go to the restaurant to get the fire rolling

in the kitchen of the restaurant, then I'd wash the dishes and go to school and come back after school to take over the job waiting on table, I served the dinners and things like that and oh, I had a job. I had a life really, I had a real life. I can't get over that. I don't want to get over that. I just want to remember that as long as I live. I'm glad I heared her, she had to bear me. That's the main thing. Because I'd be worried about how she would get along and thank God I was able to take care of her until she passed away. God rest her soul. And my oldest sister, I am glad I was able to take her children and raise them and now my little younger sister, she got so many children , by the grandchildren she time she used to seeing her wants to find out what she'd been doing. She's so busy all the time. All the time busy. Going to see this one here,
this one here. Some is in Colorado, some is in Virginia, some is in New York. She got scattered all over. It's terrific when you think about it.
Well, you've got a lot of family that's around today.

That's their family, not mine. I ain't got but one sister that's in my family. Her family is a different family from mine. Because when you leave Baptism or the Baptist religinn and don't go to the Christian Science or go into Science of Mind or something like that, you're out of my jurisdiction and I'm not for the belief that they have. I believe in Jehovah all right. But I don't believe under the method that they take it, uh-uh. I don't think I have to go and tell about the reason about the Bible, if you ain't learned it, shame on you. What am I supposed to do now, I ain't supposed to do that. They think that's what they're supposed to do. Not me.
Are you a very

I think so. Not a fanatic, though. Not a fanatic about it, no. I read the Bible a while, pretty good, because I -- do you know about the Bible? Do you know where right and wrong began? No? I wonder why. I wonder why, George. You don't take time out to think about where right and wrong began. So many people want to do right and so many people want to do wrong. You should try to find out where it began. I did. It's my business to find out where it began.
When did you find that out?
Reading, studying.
When did you find that out?
Oh, a long time ago. Long time ago.
What was it about that question that made you want to investigate? The answer to it.

Because there was so much that was wrong that they try to make right and there's so much that's right that they try to make wrong. That's why. You find so many people think they're right when they're wrong. So many peoples' wrong think they're right. You find that, don't ya? Okay. I want to find out where it began. Which gave the controversy on -- give the opposite of the Lord and the Devil. They gave the opposite. So the Devil was wrong and the Lord was right. But the Devil wanted everything to go his way, but God wanted to go the way he wanted to go, where he wanted it. So the conflict of those two things makes you want to know who was right and who was wrong. Word of God went out over that. The Devil had to leave where he was, leave where he was in Heaven, he was an Archangel. So he had to leave there, but he left on his own volition. Didn't nobody kick him out. It's his desire put him out. The foundation went out from under him, and he found himself falling and the serpent was

behind him which found him a tail, I guess. Did you ever know why man was born? Why God made man? Oh, you do know why God made man. I guess you know why he made woman but you don't know why he made man. God made man to look after the garden.
Did you ever consider devoting yourself to the Church?
Yeah, but they beat me to it. I was just ready to go, when he beat me to it.
Who's that?
Bill Bailey.
Well, why would Bill Bailey having devoted himself to the church have any effect on you?
Because I didn't want to be one out of many. He was a dancer and I didn't want to be in the line of what he was doing.
About what age was this?
About, oh, I'd say, must have been 40 years old, about 40 years old.
You certainly have the voice to become a Gospel singer.
Yeah.
Did you ever consider that?

No. I only considered being a minister. If I had been a minister I could have considered that, which is something. But I hear these guys like -- these different ministers -- Billy Graham and Falwell and another one -- Leroy something. I hear all these guys and there are so many people trying to get so much money off of it, that's what I don't like about it. You can't do it for nothing, you got to get paid for something. But that's the idea. Now I don't want to do it.
I want to go further up a little bit to the point where, I'd like to go to where you're in Germany. Right?
What part?
Let's go back to the part -- when you had pneumonia and Buck went off, Nazarro brought another Bubbles in, I forget exactly --
Willie Bryant.
Willie Bryant

Yeah, because they came -- I wasn't in the hospital, I was at home. After they did the show they come by my house to see me and they told me the story about them staging the holdup and said they were robbed. They told me about that.
You mean one of the --
No, the two fellas, look, Willie Bryant and Buck was telling me the story of how they played like they were robbed you know to keep Nazarro from taking all

the money from them. See? And I knew they were together but that was the thing -- I didn't find anybody to work with me. I didn't want to look for nobody to work with me when he got sent away, I was going to do it by myself.
You mean after that you never went back with Buck?

No, no, what do you mean. I got well -- a long time -- when I was 33. Look, I was 33 years old. I was 33 when I was sick -- in 1933 when I had pneumonia, that made me 31 and Buck and I were together for 40 years and he just passed in 1955.
Well, the fact that Buck went with another performer, did that have any effect on you?
No -- what effect would it have on me? It was only temporarily they were doing it. It was not a definite. How can they do a definite act?
Were they successful together?

Just that much. What could they be successful, it's like 'loan me your overcoat, it's raining,' it's the same difference. There was no effect on me. The idea was that pneumonia had me and they just had to make a few dollars, this boy was laying off and Buck was laying off so they get together and do an act.
When Buck was incarcerated --
She wanted to know if I wanted to look for anybody to work with me, I said, no, I did it by myself. I'd work by myself. Now, where do you want to go now? Where do you want to pick me up?
I said it was amazing that you could have somebody on your back for so many years -- Nazarro.
I heard you. I know what you're going to say. See, Nazarro is Jewish but the point I'm trying to bring out to

it, you see, the Jewish people are very clannish, they stick together, you know. If you told a Jewish friend over there how rotten I was, he'd take your word for it, you understand? More so than he would take somebody else's word saying I was good and the other person was a different nationality. But the person who's Jewish and said to the other Jew. He says, you know this guy, he's terrible. Don't trust him. That's all he needs to say. Now get the Jew that says he don't know what he's talking about, get the Jew that says that. That's what the William Morris did. They figured that this guy was wrong all along. So we're gonna give this guy a break, we'll give him a chance. I'm going to cut the act from $750 to $350, they're going to give me a contract in Chicago and going to pay our transportation and everything, a couple of hundred dollars in our pockets, sure they're gonna take that. I told them the reason and all and they knew I should have gone from Nazarro long ago. They
knew that. Some people trying to get us to break up that act from him long ago. I wouldn't break it up.
Why were people trying to break the act up?

Because they wasn't no good. They saw the guy was taking advantage, that's what they saw. We never got what we deserved. No, uh-uh. We never put -- somebody be put that was worthwhile. We could have went in (whats'name. Look I got my voice cultivated. We could have went in Ripley's Believe It Or Not column. Look how many things we went in. We went in everything you could think of in the entertainment world. Ain't nothing you could think of we didn't go in. Believe me when I tell you. Everything. Go ahead, you think of something. I don't care what you think of. You can't think of nothin' in the entertaining world that Buck and Bubbles hadn't been in. We played with everything worthwhile to be played to be played with. Every

theater in the City of Los Angeles, every theater in the City of Frisco, in London, every theater in Scotland and Glasgow, Edinburgh and every theatre in San Francisco, every theater in Philadelphia, Atlantic City, every cabaret you could think of that's worthwhile. You name it. Just think that over a while. You can't name no theater or no cafe that Buck and Bubbles haven't played in. Now that's a whole lot. What big show have Buck and Bubbles not played in, from the little show to the big show, we've been in all of them. In fact we had a show of our own called Hot Chops and a fella, his name was -- what was his name -- aw, Lord, I can't think of the fella's name that wrote a song for Buck and I called Adison Carey. He wrote a song called Buck and Bubbles. I don't remember how the song goes now, but I wrote a song called "Bubbles." "Who am I to blame If Bubbles is the name It's not a mystery Bubbles may burst in the air Them bubbles may never get anywhere It isn't in a name that one should be ashamed. . ."
I can't think of the words to that song. That's the song I wrote for "Bubbles." Then I wrote another song called "Somebody's Going To Make You Fall in Love," that's another one.
The "Bubbles" song was on your album, wasn't it?
No. "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles" on the album. Okay? Give me something else.
You did perform at Radio City?
Yeah, the first negroes to play there.
The first negroes?

Yes, the first ones. And they tore down the Steel Pier and we played at Steel Pier, too. But they don't advertise that Buck and Bubbles were the negroes that played the Steel Pier, but they got everybody else's name up there like Lou Holtz and Milton Berle -- many of the acts that played there

but they didn't name Buck and Bubbles. We stand out like a sore thumb in the world of entertainment. We stand out like a sore thumb, believe me. You run it down, you'll find out. This girl, you know, when you get back to New York, you know, she was in the office. Run her down and see what she found out. Miss Johnson. Run her down. How do you think she's successful. What do you think is making her success -- John Bubbles 'cause I'm the only one living in those ages, you know. And through what she got from me, me being the last one alive amongst all the yesterday performers, that's how she's able to get by. They had her on the program more than once to do an interview. She's doing a great job. She got to the place where she wanted everything or nothing, they didn't want to do nothing. You know what I mean? She wanted to pay for nothing. Get it all free. I gave all I wanted, all I could give her, free. I give her costumes and material to make a -- what's the name? I give her a suit, shoes, cane.
Where you going to pick it up from?

Well, we're going to jump around a little bit now. We just want to fill in a few holes, okay? We'll do this from time to time. We're with you when you're in Germany now. You're there stranded. You received a ticket from the producers of this film that you were supposed to be in to come to Germany.
Yeah.

I don't get to realize nothing. Take it the way it goes. No, that was too much to do. They send me a one-way ticket, it's easy

to get the ticket going back if I'm going to work for them. But they sent the one-way ticket. I don't know. I'm not worried about not paying me. I'm just worried about getting over there, that's all. But I didn't know there wasn't going to be no job. That's the way it was. I didn't know there wasn't going to be no job for me. He said to Lee Bouveau that "you've got to pay for that hotel he's in and you've got to pay for his living while he's here. So Lee Bouveau got another place for me to live that he had to pay for. He had to pay for it but I don't think he paid for it, I think the
agency paid for it because they okayed me to leave there to go to Kaiserslautern.
But you wouldn't work for Lee Bouveau.
No.
But you stayed there for four years.
Yeah.
Couldn't he have just given you a ticket home, Mr. Bouveau?
He didn't.
Did you ask him?
No.

I figured another day, another time way down the road some place, maybe 40 years from now I'll do something that I get a chance to do what I want to do in keeping with what I can do.
What do you feel that is?
Well, I have to wait until it gets here. Can get here now because I'm in this condition, can't do nothin'.
Ideally though, what would you like to be doing and performing?
What I'd like to do now? Nothing. It's all right. Nothin' is good, too, as long as you've done enough. I

think I've done enough, you know. I would lay down now and be peaceful. Then I could do a little of this and a little of that and it would be all right. But a whole lot of this and that, no good. I'm not able.

Yeah, everywhere. Everywhere I could get a job. Between '41?
Between '47 and '61.

'47 and '61. Yeah, I was in New York. I performed at this club on Broadway, this was 46th Street and Broadway, a little club, a combination, a little revue, about four people and a band, 5-piece band.

Sonny Grear from
Duke Ellington's band. They had a bass player from another band. They had a girl singer and a girl dancer -- Mae Barnes was the girl.

No, they did it by themselves, danced by themselves.
What was their style?
Well --

About three weeks, that's all.

Yeah.

Mh-hm.

Look what you're saying now. Buck died in 1955, I told ya, if I come back in '53, what did you say?

Yeah. That's why I said, look what you said. Then I got back in '57 then, didn't I? Was it 1957?
So then you were in Europe for eight years. If you left in '49 and got back in '57, you were there for eight years.

It's not that important if you don't remember his name. The important thing is how your life changed without Buck.

Well, life didn't change, the situations changed. Life stayed the same, you know. But the situation to do things was different. See I had to rehearse my own music where he used to rehearse. I had to depend on myself instead of depending on him as a person I want to talk to on the stage. Had to talk to myself before I went on and after I come off. So I had nothing to go to but myself.

Naw, they figured it, if they saw Buck and Bubbles, they can miss Buck. Because I was busy from the time I hit the stage until I went off but you couldn't tell who was supposed to be with me. If there was a lull and for some reason he wasn't there, it would be different. But it wasn't, which was something to think about.

Oh, and I'd like to tell you about -- or did I tell you about it. I wanted to tell you about some of the things you hadn't heard about and I thought it would be just right for you to hear really, especially when we played the 500 Club, Buck and I in Atlantic City in the year of 1932 and we also played the Steel Pier in 1924 and the Steel Pier was on the boardwalk, you know that.
What is it about -- in particular about these performances that you recall?
These are stand-out places in Atlantic City.
Was there anything special that you remember about those particular performances that you did there?

Well, the places were outstanding. Steel Pier was outstanding, you know. Being on the Boardwalk in Atlantic City is outstanding where it was done and the year it was done in. And then we go to the Standard Theater in Philadelphia in 1924, had the privilege of playing with Jack Johnson on the program doing exhibition boxing. I guess you remember Jack Johnson, dontcha?
Mh-hm.
Our first heavyweight championship by a champion fighter, rather. Then on the program there at the Standard Theater, Ethel Waters on the bill and

Sandy Burns is the comedian, Marshall "Garbage" Rogers comedian, at the Standard Theater. Then we had the Berry Brothers. We had Ada Brown and Sam Russell who was a comedian, George Wilshire was a straight man and we had the Lucky Seven Trio, was a dancing trio. We played the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia and we played at the southwest Phillie, we played the Pearl and in West Philadelphia we played the Lancaster Theater called The William Penn on Lancaster Avenue in 1925 and it was an all-white show.
What kind of entertainment were the whites doing?
They were versatile, singing -- that's about all they could do, sing and dance.
Were there any particular white performers that you
remember?

All of them. By name I remember them. Such as Ray Samuels, Tom Patricola, he's a dancer. Then you got a woman who plays the piano called Frances White, she was a piano player. We had Frank and Mel Brittons' band. Had Henry Sampson's band -- we played with so many different people it ain't even funny when I think about it. I'd like to tell you when we went to Frisco to play on the bill with Anna Marie Alberghetti at Fairmount Hotel where we stayed for about two weeks.
This is you alone now.
Yeah.
What year was this?
Well, what was happening with tap dancing in those days?
Dancing was still
Was it as popular?
Yeah. It was popular then, mh-hm.
In the '50's?
Yeah. Yeah. And I want to get away from --I forgot to tell you about being with -- I told you about Judy Garland in the Met in the rounds --
Well, we haven't really gotten into that in specific terms. Can you tell me about that?

Judy Garland at the Met with Alan King -- we played the Metropolitan Theater in New York, we played the Baltimore. We opened in Baltimore to break in the situation. Then we come into New York at the Metropolitan, then we went to Chicago and after we got to Chicago we played the Opera House there and we come to Los Angeles. We played the Civic Auditorium here with Judy
Garland at the Met --
What was it like to work with Judy Garland?
It was lovely working with Judy, she was a nice person. I enjoyed working with her and her children, too.
Which children?
Joey, Elisa Minnelli and her other daughter called -- Joey is the son and Norma is her other daughter's name. Norma, she's a singer.
What did you do in that show?
I danced, I did my act and I did a number with Judy Garland called -- what's the name of that song? "Me and My Shadow," is it? Yeah, "Me and My Shadow" I think we did.
How did you do it?
"It's 12 o'clock, we climbed the stairs --"

That's just a part, a thought of the song. I would sing the verse of the song, sing the song" "Me and my shadow holding down the avenue" And I'd go off in the wing and get her and we come on together walking doing"Me and My Shadow." And we'd dance it -- we just walked, "Me and My Shadow" you know. She was my shadow and she was following me, understand? And we'd do that which was after I had done my act. I did my act before that, which consists of singing and dancing which you know.
What would you sing? That time you were going solo so you're act must have changed considerably.
It didn't change so much. I just did a solo of the song. I think I did "Rhythm For Sale" and I did -- oh, I forgot the songs I did. "Nobody Knows" and I did --
Is that "Nobody Knows The Trouble I See?"
No.
What is that song?

"Oh, many the times I feel so lonesome But nobody knows and nobody cares I've grown so tired of being all by my lonesome I want somebody to love, cuddle and snug As cozy as a little bug in a rug Oh, many the times I feel like spooning But nobody knows and nobody cares I guess I'll put in a little ad that I want some lovin' oh so bad But nobody knows and nobody seems to care"
Then I sing that and I sing "Shine."

"What is thereabout me that makes me feel well dressed The same old clothes, shoes and hat The same old things rearranged And it's very plain to see just how it happened to be I put some polish on my scrappies I made a shoestring into a tie I cut the corners off the end of my coat so they wouldn't fly I got my shirt from a silver lining I made my cane from an old oak tree And that is just the reason why The folks all nicknamed me Just because my hair is curly And because my teeth are pearly Just because I always wear a smile And suits to dress up in the latest style Gee, I'm glad I'm living I take troubles all with a smile Because my color is shady A wee bit different maybe That's why they call me Shine."
Can you remember any of the other tunes that you did while you were performing with that?
No, I don't know of any others. That's all the songs I sang -- "Shine" and --
What was she doing?
She's off-stage, I've got the stage to myself.
I mean what was she doing during --
She was getting dressed.
I mean, what was her performance, do you remember anything she did?
"When the Moon Comes Over the Mountain." And that other one she did -- what's that other one she did? I know all of her songs, I can't think of one of them right now. Can you imagine that?
Well, we can go on because I would imagine -- this is a touring show.
Mh-hm.
It started on Broadway and just toured around the country.
Yeah.
Alan King was also in it. He did comedy.
Right.
It had some chorus girls in it and chorus boys, too.

No. I was the only one.

Yeah.

Joe Glaser, Associated Booking.
How did you feel about him?
Okay.

Oh, Lord, the difference was night and day, different as night and day. So much difference, he's a polished man compared to him. You know? He was a pleasure to work for and a pleasure to work with in my book.
Were you married at this point?
Oh, yeah.

Yeah -- no, no where are we?
Judy at the Met which was '61.
'61, I'm married this time.
Your second wife -- your third wife?
Second wife, '61? I must be married to the first wife. The second one, I was way down the road. I done broke off with Nazarro when I got the second wife.
So '61 you were married to -- were you married for the third time?
Yeah.
When was that?
When I got married.
For the third time, when was that?
Your third wife.
What happened? You mean you changed every 10 years.

No, I just changed when things weren't right. That's all. I don't know what was the hardest. For them to get used to me in my life or me get used to them in their life. That's the hard part. However, the first wife died. Then I got the second wife and the second wife came along in 1945.
How did your first wife die?
From pneumonia, I guess. I was in the hospital when she died.
What were you doing in the hospital?
Stroke.
At what age was that?
I was 60 -- I had the stroke in '67 and I was 65.
That's when
That's when my first wife died.
Are you still married?
No. No. No.
Your second wife -- why did your first marriage break up?

Well, because -- I wanted to get a home for my mother and a place that we would have and I wanted to put the home in my mother's name and she didn't want it in my mother's name so I didn't get the home. She wanted it in her name and I didn't want it in her name. And she liked to go and carry on, I guess. Her way of living her way of life and I didn't like that. So I wanted to get a divorce. So I did.
And your second wife, how did you meet her?
I met her at the Negro Actors Guild and she got into a little

difficulty with the Guild after, which I told you about and that's when I got the offer to go to Germany to do the film. Right after that she got into difficulty. But I stayed there to keep the apartment when she got free to come back so she'd have a place to come to. For me to start looking for a place -- she would never get out, but I wanted to make it as short as possible. So I kept the place, when she got out then I had this letter come to me concerning the show I had on Broadway, it's a little club. Then if I was over in Germany, I could make money and could do a lot with this little review and I didn't want to take the responsibility of having these people on my answer getting overseas and back.
So he told me if I come I could do a picture and that's when I told you about the picture situation.
However, she says she didn't want me to go. I said I ain't going to be gone but 10 days. So she busted out, started crying,

you'd think I was going to fall off a roof somewhere. But I didn't know she could see further than I could. She saw I wouldn't get back, I didn't see that. Not for lack of money now. But she saw I weren't coming back. That's the kind of thought she must have had, 'cause I didn't get back. When I come back it would be another idea.

I found somebody else I liked when I came back and I spent all the time trying to get them to come to America and I finally got them to America and then when I got them to America was hanging out with some friends and she wanted to come in at 12 o'clock at night and go out with Tom, Dick or Harry wherever they wanted to go. I didn't know she was the kind of person she was until after I got her away from England. She was from England. I got her from England to Germany and I found out she wasn't the kind of person -- and she wanted to divorce me. So I says, go ahead.
This was your
second wife or your third wife?
Third wife.
And that was your last --
Yes, last affair.
When did that end?
It ended 1964, '65.
Was she white?
Mh-hm, yeah.
This is the first --
First white wife, yeah, yes and she was so mixed blooded that I didn't know what she was going to do. Anyway, she was Mexican, English/Mexican descent.

She's a dancer.

I met her in England because I'd gone from Germany to England to do theshow "Memories of Jolson" and she was rehearsing for the show and I think it was the piano player who was colored who was a friend of hers, as a

Well, she wants to quit the show. I said, you don't know what you are if you're going to quit.
