So let this be the time that you're going to learn something. So she stayed with the show.
So she stayed with the show and that would be all the provinces of London and I want her to become an (Actor's) Equity member because I became an Equity member so that

I could get the fullness of the show. See?
The guy can't shove you around if you're a
member of Equity. So I become a member, I got
her to become a member and we were two members
of the show.

Now, this guy, the piano
player, he was a friend of hers and because she
decided seemingly that she didn't want to go
some place with him or go somewhere, I don't
know where he wanted to go, but he seemed to
want to tell the press about her, because he
was backstage when the press came by for some
kind of information concerning the show and
he told them about her. And she used to brown
down on the show, you know, so therefore nobody
got to find the newspaper man but this piano
player. He was giving all this information to
the newspaper about her and he's the only one
who knew all about her, understand? He's colored,
understand? Take the newspaperman was white,
but the girl was white, so what happened is that
it come out in the newspaper about her being the

only white person in the show. When it came out in the newspaper then they wanted to put her out of the show. Then I brought -- No, you can't put her out. I'm only learning to like her now. Don't her out because she's my wife, 'cause I ain't married to her. Don't put her out because she's my sweetheart because she ain't my sweetheart. Son't put her out of the show 'cause Al Jolson backed up and got in the show so why can't she brown down and be in this show. That was my argument.
Browning down, what does that mean?
Change your color from white to brown.
After this initial experience with her when was it that you realized that she was someone you were very interested in?
At this point, at this point I become interested in her when

they put her out of the show, that's when I became interested and I didn't want her put out of the show so I was going to quit if they put her out. I'm going to quit. Understand? So they don't put her out of the show. She's an Equity member now, too. Don't forget that. Listen, they couldn't fire her whether they wanted to fire her -- they had to pay her fare back to London and they had to pay her just like they pay all the rest of the actors that they paid and the only ones that could get paid was the ones that were Equity members and I was an Equity member, she was an Equity member. The rest of them weren't Equity. They were AVA, you know?
What was the show like, was it a variety show?
No, the show had a cast of people doing a show called -- I forgot what that show consisted of -- it was not a variety show, no. "Members of Jolson" was the title of the show and we were all doing

entertaining parts -- I've forgotten what the story was. Anyway, when the show closes, like here in this town when the show closes, and she stays here until the show goes back to London. Then we go back to London and I put the case in court and I won the case and the Judge said, "Now, you go back to America and tell them what England did." "Okay, thank you." And I come back. I didn't come back to America then. From there I went to Germany and I took her back to Germany. I'm going to get her a job in Germany.
She was good, I take it.

Mh-hm. And I got her a job in Germany and I taught her to dance different from the way she was dancing. She was a good dancer in what she was doing. Beautiful girl. Beautiful girl. Did you hear what I said? Beautiful girl.
However, when I showed her some dancing -- we did some shows, we went to Italy and all. I had a unit of my own over there
and I brought the unit throughout -- certain places -- I went to Italy, I went to France with this revue I had and I got commendations from the Special Service.
You had put this show together yourself.
Yeah, uh-huh.
It was basically a variety show?
Yeah, the show I put together was, yeah.
What did it consist of?
It consisted of dancing, singing, that's all.
This woman that you subsequently married, what kind of dancing did she do?
What do you call it -- what do you call that dance -- it's like a jazz dance plus kicks, that's about the size of it, kicks and jazz dancing, that's what
she did and did a tap to go with it. She did a kick, tap, dance. It was a good review, very good. I thought so. We got a lot of praise with it.
Then we got to places where the managers of the hotels would get stuck on her and they can't see what she's doing with the show.
Was the show all black except for her?
No, no, mixed show. Integrated.
Why didn't some people understand why she --
Don't ask me, they thought she should -- say that again.
Why did people not understand?
Because they thought she could do better without the show, by herself. Suppose you come along and you thought she could make a good wife for you, would

you want her to be with a show? Would you want her to be in a show? Well the guy didn't want her to be in no show. How you going to want her to be with the show, then leave her alone, 'cause you can't bother, leave her alone. She doesn't want to be with you, she wanted to be with the show. You gotta talk her out of being in the show, you know that. You kiddin'? You've gotta be kiddin'.
Did you receive any flak because you were with a white woman?

No, I didn't receive nothin', didn't receive nothin'. Didn't have no difficulties at all. None whatsoever. None whatsoever, okay? Didn't expect any, didn't find any. I didn't set up for none and I didn't find any. So it all turned out just like I wanted it to turn out and she made the first decision. I got the other half of the ticket that she come over here on. I got the other half, she had to have

a round-trip ticket to leave and I got the other half,'cause I bought the ticket from here and send it there, so she come back with the other half. When she came here, we were here I guess about two months and the woman that we met over there had an Indian sweetheart and we met her in Germany and she was a good friend of ours. She saw me on Broadway and left her number and never got on the phone yet, I'd been longing to see her for a long time. She's a dancer, too. Had a dancing school and sold her school in order to go traveling with this Indian. He's a heck of a dancer, too. This Indian fella could dance, oh, he could dance. Hands interpretation -- oh, he was terrific. I took him in my car in Germany, I had a car in Germany and of course I had to pay for it every week. I had a wad of money -- when it come every month and it was due, I had a wad of money to the bank 'cause there wasn't enough money in the bank to cover it.
However, I got the car by
myself, no co-signers, you know. But I used to drive them to the place where we had the opening and bring them back, you know. The Indian --
You ultimately got married to this woman back in the States.
In the States, yeah.
And that marriage lasted for --

I came back in '57 -- I think we got the divorce in '59. I was at Lake Tahoe when she come to get the divorce. She wanted me to give her a divorce and I said you've got to come here because I can't get off. So she come there and I was hoping to God some place was open when she got there so I could get the lawyer to sign the thing. So we did, we finally got it. Do you think she's been glad? She's been glad, I've seen her since then. I was at the Riviera with Eddie Fisher when I saw her

again and when I come to Las Vegas to do a show I brought her to Las Vegas. When she arrived I bought a car for her when she arrived, I bought a Chrysler for her when she arrived in America and I called up every day, every day I called Germany, talked to her long distance from The Sands where I had come to work Peter Linda Hays (spelling). I called up every day and found out what was happening, how she was doin'. I had to sell my car before she left over there to come over here. She sold it when she got over here.

The woman that I was telling you about that we met over there and was a friend, this Indian's sweetheart, she was telling me what makes this girl so unsettled. She says you're not married, maybe if you'd marry she'd be more -- she ain't got nothing to depend on. "She can depend on me." "But you're not married to her," that's one point.
See, there was only two white

women that lived in the building where we were living at, which was the Lenox Terrace in New York and she liked to come in at 12 o'clock, we got a colored doorman, I'm on the ground floor and there's another colored fella in the apartment house that has an apartment that's married to a white woman and he's on the 5th floor, I think it was. He was a dancer also, a dancing teacher. And she wanted to come in at 12 o'clock and I thought it was bad for her to come in at 12 o'clock at night to be a lady. So I says, "I want to (inaudible) haven't I?" "No, that don't go." Then she wants to go, somebody take her to a show 'cause I was busy with the bar and I didn't have the time to take her to the show and watch after the bar and all that, so I let her go to the show. I let her go to the school where she wanted to learn how to cut stones, she liked to cut stones. So she had a hobby, that was it.
So that was one of our movements of separation and I helped her do that, I

said "Go ahead." I didn't put no protest against it. I asked you last, do you think she's happy? Do you think she's happy? She done married again following this divorce. But she came back in order to try to entice me to look over the divorce part, but I didn't. I was at Harris at the time. She was stopping across the street from Harris at the Wagon Wheel Hotel, I think that was it. And I'm over at Harris. And she gets to stay there, she wants me to come over to have breakfast. I went over to have breakfast and there she was decked out in her negligee of "no consent" and I said to myself "not me." And I went looking for a lawyer to get the papers straight. We did, got the divorce and that was it. So later I saw her again when I was with Eddie Fisher at the Sahara, I think it was and I don't think I was -- I had just come from the hospital in Chicago where I had been under a doctor's care and she says -- asked

how I felt and everything, I said I'm doing all right. "How are you?" When a friend of mine passed away here in Los Angeles she came to see this friend from Las Vegas, but I got her a job with Eleanor Powell in Eleanor Powell's show when she came to Las Vegas 'cause I took her there on a show I was doing in Las Vegas. I took her from New York to Las Vegas 'cause I wanted to do this show, open the show called the Carver House, colored on the west side of town, a colored club, colored casino 'cause negroes wasn't allowed in the casino on the east side, you know, in Las Vegas. So I take her out there and while we're out there I get her the job working with Eleanor Powell in I think it was The Dunes. Then I found her colors then really. Understand? Really what she was, I didn't know that. You see, in those clubs you go there and you spend and you got some dough, the guy that's on the

floor, like the floor manager of the club, he goes around to see who's who, who's got what and who want's what. So he picks out the girl in the show for you or for him, you know. Like an old talent's been coming to the club, I've got a new one for you and the woman in charge of the girls backstage tell her, "Get Miss so-and-so, have her come to such and such a table after her show." As the girl goes to the table, the fella knows she's coming. When she gets there she's well known to show me there. The girl don't know that he knows she's going to be there, but the girl that brought her out there to the man knows all about it. So the guy that this one puts her next to he's gambling and get about four or five $5 chips or maybe $10 chips or maybe $20 chips and he puts them in front of her so she can gamble. She don't gamble. He tell her, put it in your pocket. So this go on for a while, you know. Now, he wants a recess, he wants to eat something. He don't need this gambling money, he's just there killing time.

He's shilling now, with this girl he's shilling. So he says, "Go on, go ahead and gamble." She said, "I don't gamble." So he says, "You feel like eatin' somethin', let's have somethin' to eat." So he leaves the table, takes her to the dining room to eat and they sit down to eat and he starts to ask her, what makes her be there, why is she there, who is she with -- so-an-so, they just go over the things and she tells him.

Now, she's got already about $300 he done give her at the table, understand? He'd give her $500 like nothin' or $1000 like nothin'. He give her this $300 and she thinks she's got somethin'. Much more than she's going to get for the week. Give her $300, she takes the $300, she don't want to give it back to him. So she goes to eat with him.

Now he wants to show her his room where he's livin'. She can't say no, I can't go with her because she ain't got nobody. She goes with him to his room, she don't want to give him back the money, so she's hooked. Under-

stand? This only happened once to my knowledge. That I could read, I could read awful fast, you know. What did I do? Don't fit me. This don't fit me at all. First outing I can get, thank goodness. Now this is my wife! This is my wife, understand? This ain't no woman, this is my wife! And this is what she's got to be doin'. I done got her the job with Eleanor Powell so she'd be doing something while she was there in Vegas.

Well, anyway I can break out would be good. Her way would be better than mine 'cause I ain't got no one, but she's got one, yes, she found one. It's understandable that if you found somebody better than me or you can get along better with them than me, go ahead. Same thing is given to me. I can do the same thing. So she found a person, okay? So we got divorced.
But when I saw her again at the whats'name), she got married again, guy goes buys her a car and going to do everything, so-and-

so. That's then, I'm going to New York, then I come to California. When I'm in California I'm here and I got the stroke. My friend is over on 35th Street somewhere. Girlfriend I know, dancer, was in the show with "Memories of Jolson." This girl was in the show "Memories of Jolson," which give me more key points on who was in that show -- God rest her soul, she passed away. And this girl -- my ex-wife come to see this girl, 'cause she was her friend, but the same guy choose the white girl to be my companion on the stage rather than the colored girl to be my companion, because she was more attractive. She was more sought after. That's why I chose her, you know.

Like they put on pictures today, they get the most ugliest negro woman and find the most handsome negro man to match them up -- ugliest team in the world. Sad as McKinley's funeral. Understand what I'm saying? That's the way they do. They had a thing on the program last night about that. Two negros,

one is the president, one is the treasurer of a club they're trying to set up now concerning why these producers all pick on the wrong people for the pictures and don't give the negros no work. They've got that going on now.

But to get back to this girl. When she comes here to visit this girl that was sick, I'd been talking to her on the phone, she's a good friend of mine anyway, I talk to her on the phone 'most every week. I don't know my ex-wife is over there now. But the phone rings. I pick up the phone. When she says hello, I says hello. She says, "How are you?" I says, "I'm all right, how are you. Watcha doin' in town?" "Where are you?" She says I'm over to so-and-so's house. "You are? How long are you going to be here?" I'll visit. I said, "I'll be coming over to have coffee sometime." "Okay." Hung up. That's the end of that.
Well, this girl is sick, this girl gets so sick, I talk about I'll get her to get relief on her property tax. I get her fixed

up to get some help from Homemakers Chore. This is the girl that's sick. She finally has to go to the hospital. She goes to the hospital. Well, I began to (wolf) my ex-wife. I don't care. But during the course of time, I find out from this girl what her phone number was, what her address was and everything in Las Vegas. Found out she was married and found out she had a child, found out they're divorced. All this I found out from this poor girl, God rest her soul, she's dead. I ain't heard from the ex-wife yet. So I let it slide. I'm not worried about that nohow. She'll see me way down the road somewhere, you know? Beautiful girl, lovely, but just ain't got no managerial rights. You got more sense in your little toe than she has in her whole body. No brains. I can't give her none, because my color is wrong for her. But I can see what she don't know and I was trying to save her. I wasn't doin' her no harm. I took her out of nothin' into somethin'. She was a nothin' in Germany. In England, too.
We stayed Adelaide Hall's house in London. They had an apartment house. We stayed with them.

Oh, to tell you about it is terrific. In the episode of that marriage and that friendship death and the divorce and the separation. Now, brother, I had so many plays, so many moves in life -- so many.

Well, see, we had a party -- that show we were with, that first show we were with with Harry Steppie in "Dancing Around" that's the girl in that show I fell in love with, was white, but my mother don't know I'm marrying a white girl and I don't know why 'cause she thinks that things are just as bad for white and black.
This is back when? You're referring to the first girl that you --
Can we get to -- I understand that this was supposed to be the truest romance that you had in your life.
Mh-hm.
Can you tell me the story from the beginning of that -- tell me that whole story.
The only story of that is, after I met the girl in the show --
What show was this?
"Dancing Around."
And you were with Buck at this time?
Yeah.
What role were you two playing?
We were doing an act.
It was a variety show.
No, it was a show. No, they had a comedian, chorus girls, straight man in the show, the comedians would do jokes and they'd do sketches, like that, you know.
Who were some of the comedians?
Harry Steppie was the only comedian they had in the show, Harry Steppie, he was the comedian.
Any other dancers?
No. All the girls were dancers. All the girls were dancers and they had one boy, what's his name, Alan Walker was a dancer.
Was it an all white show?
Yeah.
Except for you and Buck.
That's right.
And you basically just did your routine.
Mh-hm.
Now this chorus line, this woman was a member of the
chorus line.
Mh-hm.
How did you meet her?
In the show.
Did she come up to you or did you come up to her?
No, no, no. We were in the hall, you know, rehearsing and after rehearsal I met her, you know.
Who said what first?

Who said what first? She said what first, 'I like your dancing. I like your dancing.' 'You do, I'm glad you do,' says I. 'You don't do any tap dancing, do you?' says I. She says, 'No.' I said, 'You dance all right otherwise. You do a good dance, too. In fact I'm going to say you're a good dancer.' I don't think about no marriage, just am I trying to interfere with some boy's girl. This is what I'm watching. I don't worry about

whether she's married or not. If she ain't married she ain't nobody's girl. As young as she was -- she was young, too. See I'm 19 years old now, understand? She's about 18. Now I'm 77 and she's 76. Just send her a birthday card the other day, you know. And her husband come to me to ask me about her being only a friend of the man she's going to marry. The friend of the man that this girl is going to marry came to me -- he's the guy that's going to marry her, he's a friend of the guy, and he's going to find out for his friend how she was. Was she a good girl, was she a nice girl, so-an-so-and-so. Well, I don't know what he's got up his sleeve, so I thought I'd direct him to the office, to meet me at the office. That's where Nazarro was.

... and nobody knows you have any brains, and you go through all these things. (Unaudible) on that thing, biology, like Clarence (Muse) was talking about if they were sure he didn't have any brains, they wouldn't give him the job. The same thing happens when you got brains, you can't show your brains and get no job. You talking about the negro sufferin', I don't think the negro has suffered as hard as the Jewish people have suffered. They had as much trouble to go through as we did, or more. But I don't think they had the education that the negro had to go through his. You see what I mean, that's the big difference. If the negro didn't have no education it wouldn't be hard. But he had the

They're going to put him again for another run for the President, you know that. He's going to run again. You know that, don't ya. And he's going to win this time, ain't that funny? Why? This is Tape No. 23, Interview with John Bubbles. We put in the (inaudible) at this point because Mr. Bubbles got carried away.
You must remind yourself sometimes of Nazarro's prejudiced. He's been that way all along but he never told about it. You can read that all over his actions.
And when I had him meet me in Nazarro's office to let him find out from Nazarro about this girl he wants me to tell him about.
Was this particular fellow black or white?
White. When Nazarro got through with him, I guess he could go through the floor-board, 'cause Nazarro called her everything but a child of God because he was marrying her

'cause she was like a negro. But this fella doesn't know that's why he's describing this girl that he is, he doesn't know that's why Nazarro is doing that. He just thinks that's just a natural way for him to be describing this girl. But I know why he's describing her like that. She ain't nothin' like he said in my book. She's just too fine and don't like him. And he thinks she should like him other than liking me. You don't like me 'cause I'm as good as this guy is. She like me 'cause I have much more to offer than this guy, especially as a human being. He may have some money, but money didn't excite her.

So anyway, he gets the information. Now I take him down to the bar and I says to the man, done told him what she is, everything, -- a child of God that she's so-and-so-and-so. So I take him down to the bar to have a drink or so and I just told the fella at the bar, I said, 'You know if I had the money ain't nobody would get that girl. Because she's too good for anybody I know. I depend on the white people for my livin' and I know they don't want me to have no white girl and that's why I won't marry her, that's exactly why,' I'm telling him. My mother's told me also about it. So I'm letting him know that's why we're not married and that's why we're not as close as we would have been because I can't get too close because if I get too close I'm going to get hurt in my profession. They're not going to give me no bookings, I know that. I saw that happen. So I know it backwards.
(Inaudible)
George Kirby, it happened to him. I had to tell him to leave the white woman and he might get some work. He

finally did and he got some work, then he went back to the girl again and then he got messing up with the dope, then they got him because the white girl gave him away. She stooled on him. But the girl that he was with before, he bought her a home in Chicago. She got a home in Chicago and she put up her home and put up a bond for him, the white girl in Chicago did.

But the other one he had in Las Vegas, she was just using him and no case of whether they found her guilty of nothin', she wasn't even mentioned, no trial for her or nothin' when they prosecuted him. He's probably out on bond by now, I guess or for parole or somethin'.

Anyway, so what should happen is he understands that this girl is too good for this fella he's looking out for. He's looking out for a friend of his who is going to be the one the girl is going to marry, he's talking about.
Well, he got that far. But I
don't know he's the guy that's going to marry her, I don't know he's the guy. This is the guy that's going to marry her that I'm talking to.

So the next day I called up the girl to tell her about this guy that came and she wanted me to describe, was he so-and-so, yes. "Yeah?" "Yeah." She says, "He was, huh?" Now she don't tell me that's the guy she's going to marry. I described the man who was there, she know who he is and that's the guy she's marrying.
I sent her a card before and I wrote her a letter the other day. I said, Did this fella ask you, her father for her, she had no answer to that. I never told her --

Now we all meet, all three of us meet. He doesn't know no more about me than I know abut him. He doesn't know about her and I no more than he's just seen us. And we're close friends, you know, from way back. We've been through that show together and real good
and oldest friends, I guess, in show business, it was at our age that we started together, you know. But just to show you how things happen.

Well, she's going to write me another letter as soon as she gets back from The Poconos. She's up in The Poconos for the summer. She's going to write me another letter after she gets her birthday card. I didn't send no Christmas card 'cause it's near Christmas on her birthday. So, she was the one that got me first. But I couldn't get her, following my mother's advice. But now my mother's dead is why I married this girl. I'm going to see how right my mother is. I'm going to marry this girl. My mother was right, but I picked the wrong girl, that's all. She finally got this girl that I'm talking about out of Easy Street because she's sorry. I know she's sorry because she's not a mother now, don't ever expect to be a mother and she saw me coming along and see what I'd done with myself after she got married
to this guy. Then I did sail on my own, by myself, you know and they were going to come and see me in West End but they couldn't make it, to see me Black Broadway. They'll be coming this next time.
Well, can you explain to me a little bit about that courting period between you and she? How that went and how you sort of flirted with one another, etc., when you were both on the show?
What can I say?
Well, you described a little last night about the way you courted one another with your hat, etc.
Yeah, with the notes and the hat and so forth, yeah.
Tell me a little bit about that?
That's about the size of that. Other than -- I didn't tell you the part --
We didn't

Okay, when they give this party for the club, Buck and Bubbles were the only males allowed in the club at the party. So we go to this party, so I instruct Buck before we get to the party not to dance with any of the girls, just take care of the victrola and I was to do whatever the next thing to do is, to serve the food and serve the drinks, but don't dance. Okay.

We're in the party, we bring a five-pound silver cake plate for the club and one of the woman's husband -- one of the girl's husband brought us down to their room in this hotel, and this was in Canada. And when he left us there he cried, when he went out he cried before he left us, you understand?
Why did he cry?
Don't ask me, man, how could I know that? I couldn't know that. I wondered the same thing you wondered,
why did he cry? I don't know why he cried.
Was he sad to leave you at this party with all the girls?

What he was sad about, I don't know. What he was crying about, I don't know, George. And I looked at the idea I says, everything is all right -- his name was -- m-m-m, I know that man backwards. However, he goes out of the room, leaves us there. If you want me, I'm upstairs, that's what he left word. If you need me, call me upstairs. Okay. He goes.

Now this boy was a dancer, he was the guy -- he didn't think much of negroes in the first place. He made you think he did, but he don't. Anyway he got the fellas in the lobby to tell them about the party going on and about Buck and I being there. So a couple of the guys, and they may have had a drink or maybe didn't have no drink or maybe smoking a reefer, who knows. They come to the door and knock on the door. Buck and I is in the room

where the victrola is. The girls is out in the room where the table for the food is all on. Buck and I are in the room where the victrola was and I am waiting to hear who's coming to the door and they found out it's a couple of strangers of the town that come to the door to knock on the room where there are no men allowed. They already know who's in the room, but the girls don't know they know this. So the President of the club goes to the door to see who it was. They wanted to come. She says, "You can't come in." "Why can't we come in?" "No men are allowed." He says "Buck and Bubbles are in there," he comes out with. She wanted to know how he knew who was in there. So he calls them, "nigger lovers" and he hits the girl. And I have moved from the room where Buck was into the other room where they were answering the door where the girls all are. And I'm going to see who this guy is at the door, after she gets hit. And the girls are there trying to get her up and fix her, and I'm trying to go to the door, and

one girl has got this arm and one girl has got that arm, they won't let me go to the door. I finally get away from the girls. I think they had an iron there, a smoothing iron, that the girls press things with. I think there was an iron there somewhere that I took this iron and I was going to hit this guy with the iron from where I was sitting. But anyway I didn't throw the iron, I got up and went to the door and just went all over the girls standing there holding the door and grabbed this fella. Now up the hallway, there's a guy waiting to help this guy that come down here. Well, I saw him up there, so he don't know I'm looking at him. He thinks I'm just here busy with this guy -- I'm busy looking at him, too, you know. So I hold this guy -- he comes down there to help this other fella. When he comes I took this fella I had and just swung around, fell down with this fella in front of this other guy and this guy fell on the both of us, you know.

So this guy don't know that I'm set on these things to do. He's set on going through the motions I was going through, you know. He was caught in the middle of his trap. Okay. So the girls got to get me up and get me in the house and let the guys get away from the door.

So now we're going to whip this guy that's in the show because he's the one that told the fellas. So the next day we plan on getting him. I let Buck take care of him because Buck was for him. Eddie is the guy's name. Eddie is the guy that brought his wife in, Eddie Scarf, S-C-A-R-F.
Why were there no men left --
It was for all women.
Then why did they have --
Don't ask me that, man. How would I know? They just wanted to have
a stag party for the women, that's all.
Why did they have Buck and Bubbles then?

Don't ask me -- that's the best of what they thought of Buck and Bubbles. Could have been a setup, who knows, 18 girls in negligees, it must have been a setup, man. Did you hear me tell Buck to don't dance with nobody? It must have been a setup, trying to get Buck and Bubbles in bad with the public. Plus they're an agency. Don't you understand. They couldn't take me no where they went, man, I was hip on all corners.
Why did you go to the party then?

I went to the party because I know what to do. That's why. I wind up all right. Nothin' happened to me. Listen, I cover the fence of the white woman, I cover the fence of all things. What did I do? I didn't grab none of the girls. I didn't humiliate none of the girls. Understand?
But it was one of the husbands that dropped you off.

Yeah, he knew what kind of a guy I was. Understand? He's only crying because I must be put up to a test or somethin', man. He would hate to see these two guys go down the drain. That's about what he's crying about. Understand? I hate to see these two guys, because they are good guys, man. He don't want to see us go down the drain. Understand? That's what he's crying about. But I don't know that. But when all the things crop up maybe I'll put two and two together. That's simple as pie. When a guy is gonna come down and tell all these girls, gonna get in and bust it, and know who's in there and everything, cuss them out. They were white. Why would he want to do it to hurt them.
So after you beat these two guys off --
I don't beat nobody up, didn't beat a soul. I didn't beat a soul.
You pinned them down.
I just stopped them from doing what they wanted to do. They didn't get in, they didn't hurt nobody -- hit that girl, they wouldn't have gotten away with that if I could have helped it.
And then what happened, you went back into the party after that?

I was still in the party, the party was still going on. They're outside the room, man. We're in the other room. Just shut the door and the party still stays. We didn't close the party on that account, God bless. All we did was just play the victrola and all like nothing happened. But I'm thinking about -- we're going out and what shall we do. Keep a cool head. We kept a cool head.
The next day we got the feeling we'll look for this Alan, Alan Walker, he was the guy we want to find because he was

setting these guys up and then Eddie Scarf talked us out of it and I'll never forget that. So imagine going through that? Now this girl, this girl now, this same girl I've been telling you about, she was in the party. She was the one who wanted to dance ballroom with me, I told her I don't do no ballroom dancing. I'm a tap dancer, not a ballroom dancer, don't know how to dance. And Buck don't know how to dance either. So neither one of us knew how to dance. Do you understand? So what, is she going to make us dance? So imagine taking one of the girls to dance with her? Can you imagine -- I guess you can imagine it, dancing with the girls, or any girl, you know -- smelling like a rose garden. That's what they smelled like. Got all kinds of perfume and everything and beautiful outfits they had on. Wouldyou do it, huh? You wouldn't want to kiss one of them, would ya? Thank you. Thank you. Any ordinary man would. Any ordinary man would. You understand? If he's human. And

look at the age now. Look at the age you've got -- more gullible now at that age than you would be at manhood, you know what I mean? Got to get caught. Got to get caught. What do you think Buck and Bubbles climbed from, huh? Climbed from being able to evade. We evaded all the possibilities of doing -- well, I won't go into that. Let you have that.

Once they asked for me -- Mae West, she asked for me at the Olympic Gardens when I went there to see Gorilla fight. She had her maid with her, sent the maid over to tell me that she wanted to see me. You tell her you better get Gorilla Jones for her. So they got Gorilla Jones, she went and got Gorilla Jones. So they made a date. But Gorilla Jones don't know they made a date. He don't know I know she sent for him. All he knows is that they come for him, but she done bid for

me first.
Well, I was back in Gruman's

chauffeur to have her secretary to come in and

sat in the back seat. When I got in, she had
her legs crossed up to here. You understand?
Above her --

Above her knee,
yeah, understand? She had her legs crossed above
her knee. When I got in the car there ain't no
way to miss seeing her legs. She sent the
secretary to tell me if I wanted to do a picture
-- she wanted to learn to dance, that's it. She
wanted me to teach her a few steps, that was it.
When I get in the car, she wanted to know if I

wanted to go in this picture she had. I says, I don't know, but if you want to ride around until I do my act and come out, I can let you know. She says, "Here's my card, when you get a chance, you can give me a ring." Did you call her? Did you call her? I didn't call her. I didn't call her. But the next day I went down to the Dunbar Hotel where Gorilla Jones was livin' --

Yeah, he's black. He is a prize fighter. I went down to the hotel where he was livin', the Dunbar, to see him and he was getting dressed to meet her. About six months later I see him in Chicago at 47th and South Parkway, walking like the Crazy Kats, with his hands behind his

I says, "What's the matter?" He says that so-and-so-and-so, you know they run me out of town burned up my car. I said, "They did, don't talk about it. No, You can't put that in no newspaper, man, 'cause that's your own fault. She ain't done nothin', it was you. Just forget that, you're the one. Don't talk about her. 'Cause it was you, don't put her name in the paper about nothin' because if you didn't have no better sense than you did, Shame on ya." "You're going to lose my friendship if you do, 'cause I know you shouldn't do it."
That man has gotten through thanking me yet for not putting her name in the paper, talking about that incident. Then I saw him in Seattle, Washington, a little later. Gorilla Jones.
They ran him
That's right.
That's right -- not just see, but in the room, in the hotel room, must have been, I think (inaudible).
Do you think that was a setup as well?
No, that was no setup. That was an incident that happened on account of bad judgment. He had bad judgment, you see.
What was Mae West's intention?

Aw, "Come up to see me sometime." So what should happen, I see him in Seattle. He knows we're coming. He left word at the desk that Buck and Bubbles were coming in -- tell them where I am. And he was across the street in a pool hall, he's racking balls in a pool hall across from the hotel. When I went and saw that man in that pool hall, man, he went up to me and put his arms around me. I'm

wondering what for because I hadn't learned nothing that happened since then. He was so glad that I stopped him from doing what he did. He told me what happened. Told me that his mother got a home and how nice she had been to him. I don't need to say no more concerning how glad he is that he took my advice. That's what he got from my advice.
Now, she is now touring some parts of California and some parts of the United States with him on his life story.
Who is?
Mae West.
On his life story?
Yeah.
What do you mean on his life story?
She's supposed to be writing his life story or somethin'.
I see, and he didn't write any bad publicity about her in the
newspaper --

Aw, did I need to say that? I told you his mother got a home from what I did. What he didn't do but what he wanted to do or she wouldn't have got that. She wouldn't be writing his life story. She's doing a picture since I heard about that. So they must back off of that tour. But however, I threw away more things, man.
You just said it would be different.
To write his life story, which she could have done in the beginning, you know.

Can you get back -- I want to get back just a little bit -- you started to tell me a little bit about the way you and this other girl that you had considered getting married to but your mother advised you not to. "We used to play with each other " in terms of the way you courted one another. Tell the story about the --
We courted about the notes and the hat.
Tell me about that.
That's all I have to tell you.
Can you tell me about that?
Yeah, after I'd come down to do my act, I would put my note in my hat because I bumped my hat down because I wanted to make a change to a strutting outfit.
This was in the show. What was the name of the show?
"Dancing Around."
Where she was a member of the chorus line.
Yeah.
Okay. What would you write in the note?
How cute she was, how lovely she was, how nice she was and how

wonderful it was that I had a chance to meet such a person and with all hopes -- the note varied from time to time on different things I would say to her concerning herself, her family and her brothers and our meeting each other, and she was -- she used to go, I used to take her uptown to nightspots like when the speakeasies were going on.
Were there any problems because she was white and you were black?
No, no problems.
What kind of notes would she write to you and put in your hat?

Same kind of notes, to answer me back, the same thing I said, how nice I was, how glad she was to know me. She's the first one who told me I was going to be a star. I didn't know this. Hadn't the slightest idea. All these things she saw I didn't see. I didn't see where she saw it. This
man she was going to marry, I didn't see that. I thought I was going to be the man, but I wasn't.
But you would have been the man if it wasn't for your mother.
I guess I would have.
Did your mother meet her, by the way?

I think my mother did. See, I had a picture of her -- I think my mother met her. But I had a picture of her that was the last word. However, my mother met her and my mother liked her but my mother couldn't see me marrying her then, that's all, she couldn't see that. But I couldn't see me not marrying her. But I didn't, only on account of that mess she gave me about her father. I'm sorry that I didn't marry her. I would have married her instead of the other girl. See, I picked the wrong way 'cause I got a prostitute when I married the other girl.
The message that she gave you from her father was what?

I had to ask her father to marry her. That's the message. I don't want to ask her father because I don't think her father would have said so. So I don't ask him. But I used that for the grounds that we don't get married.

You'd be surprised how many different organizations you have to belong to to get in this business and be on the ground floor. Do you know that? You've got to belong to AGVA, AFTRA, SAG, NAG and Equity. American Guild of Variety Artists, American Federation for Theater and Radio, Negro Actors Guild, Actors Equity -- all these things you have to belong to in order to get a welfare contingent out of this situation.

Now, I didn't get to tell you about doing a show with Ted Lewis. Did I tell you about the Ted Lewis show? I was his shadow. He used to have a boy called Charlie Witty and Charlie Witty and him got into some kind of difficulty and he thought he'd take me to substitute for Charlie Witty so I went along with him to Frisco for a two-week contract at the Club Bimbo and I worked with him, doing

"Me and My Shadow." Somebody one night hollered from the balcony, "Which one is the shadow?" Now Ted Lewis is white and I'm black. But someone hollered out, "Which one is the shadow?" So we must have been doing pretty good with it.
You did that same routine with Judy Garland.
Yeah. And that was in Frisco and after we leave the Bimbo club which was booked by Associated Booking office.
Mr. Bubbles, now I'd like you to tell me a little about your teaching Fred Astaire.

Yeah, Fred Astaire wanted to learn a few steps going along with the dancing he does and I told him I had to see my manager because I didn't know what to charge or what to do, because I thought he was just a friend of mine so he saw my manager and my manager charged him $400 a lesson, $400 an hour, you know.
How much of
that did you get? $400 an hour.
I got the money. How far along was Fred Astaire in his career at this time?
Way up, way up in his career. He passed all the slow down points.
Where did you teach him?

I taught him a few good steps he could use. I think he was satisfied. And while I was teaching him, I got a chance to show the things to Marilyn Miller who was a friend of his that he brought along as a guest and I noticed in her dancing she was more apt to catch a step than he was, so I wanted to show it to her, so he'd get more for his money that he was going to get because he was slowing up to me for what I had to show him, because it would take him longer to get it, 'cause I had some intricate steps at that time.
So she learned it and she took off to show it to him, wherever he wanted to go to do it, you know. So they did.
Do you know what he did these steps that you taught him in?
No, in his dancing when he got around to it, I guess.
I told you about coming from overseas, 'bout Lou Irwin bringing me back from Germany to do the part of Bill Robinson and the first (inaudible) of the 20th Century.
You never told me that.

I'm just telling you now. And he brought me back. I was number one on the list for the Bill Robinson Story, I was doing it for 20th Century Fox and he got me a five-week contract with Peter Lynn Hayes and Mary Healy at the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas in the event that I don't pull through with this audition to become the part in the play -- the picture.

So I took the contract, he brought me back and I went with Peter Lind Hayes at the Sands and the had a strike on 20th Century Fox so I didn't get to do the picture. So I stayed with Peter Lynn Hayes at the Sands for the run he had there and then he took me to New York on the Godfrey Hour. So I was with him for two years -- 1957, stayed with him until 1961, then I went with Judy Garland in 1961 at the Met. Then I come back to the -- when I was with Anna Marie Alberghetti to Canada and then I went to Chicago with Anna Marie Alberghetti at the Palmer House for a five-weeks' engagement. And then I went to California from there to do the Frisco show. Then do Ted Lewis' show in Frisco. And after the Frisco show to go overseas with Bob Hope with his Christmas Show, which I made three trips over there with him, first negro on the show. And in the meantime I do the show for Dean Martin, do his show. I become a member of Friars' Club of California at that time, too.
I'm a Friars' Club member, too, now.
Well, can you tell me a little bit about how you got involved with Dean Martin, Bob Hope, Steve Allen, Perry Como -- how you got involved in that whole world of television.
By being good in the other part of show business.
Had you been involved with them before prior to this?
No, no. No, they go looking for talent and you can find it if you look around. They're looking for talent, George.
Well, who set it up?

It gave me an opportunity, the setup. If I played -- go down and play the Hollywood Palace and you see me, that's how you found out that I was the one, but they set me up for Bob Hope while I was overseas. I told you Mrs. whatsname set me up for that, 'cause she played my (inaudible) for

West Command. She did my whole act for him. That' set me up for Bob Hope whenever he heard it, or whenever somebody told him about me. She'd be looking for me. They saw me in the vaudeville theaters, I've been on the stage long enough. I created enough understanding in the business. I don't have to get with nobody. They see me, I'm perfectly figured. They can see me on the stage. That's where the people get all the people for shows or something, they go all around in different theaters where they're playing or find out who's playing where and go catch it, and they caught me playing. And I guess George would have done the same thing.
Well what did you do on the Bob Hope show -- first of all, what was your relationship with Bob Hope like?
Great. Great. First gag I told him, he didn't laugh.
Do you remember what that gag was?
Sure. The gag

was I asked Bob Hope if he believe in integra-tion. And his answer was to be yes. I say his answer was to be that. If he said no, I wouldn't be able to do the gag. So when he said yes, I did the gag on our first show that we did overseas following him not doing the dance that we had rehearsed together during a return for a bow on the stage he didn't do the dance, he just went down front and said, "There he is, John Bubbles. We've been trying for six weeks or six months to get John Bubbles and we finally got him." I said, "Yeah, knowing he hadn't been trying. I just said, "Yeah."

But I'm mad now because he don't do his dance that we rehearsed together. So I said, "Hey, Bob, do you believe in integration?" With all these soldiers integrated he's got to say yes. So he says, "Yes." So I says, "Well, kiss me." And that did it. That did it. You can imagine that, can't you? So that was my first gag with him. Well, coming back, he was ever so glad. I went over once with Anna Marie
Alberghetti and we did this show with Bob Hope overseas, which was very good --
How many shows did you do with him?
Three.
And you went to Vietnam.
Vietnam, Istanbul, Tripoli, Manila, Bangkok.
Were there any other black performers?

Thailand. No, I'm the only one. I'm the only one -- now don't forget you're interviewing me for what I did, not the black performers, just what I did. It will stand out where I was, what I did, when you spread it out. Because there weren't no other negroes in the show. They had no other negroes -- I'm the first negro who went over with him. There were no other negroes in the show that you ever heard of, have you? I never heard of any with his show.
What about Steve Allen, when did you start performing with him? Were you also the first black to be performing with him?
I'm not the first, no, uh-uh.
What did you do with him, you were just on his talk show?
On his talk show, yeah. I did my act with him which consists of my singing and dancing and I did an interview on his show just recently regarding George Gershwin's Porgy and Bess.
What sort of fellow was he?
Who?
In relationship to you -- Steve Allen.
Nice, nice guy.
I have another source that you did an American Musical Theater show.
Mh-hm.
Sissle and Blake and Hank Jones were also on the show.
Yeah.
Can you tell me about that and what it was about.

It was just me and they were musicians in the show, but just me I would do my two or three different songs and tell a gag of some kind. What kind of gag I told then I don't really know. But I did a gag and I did songs and I danced. That was my pattern of entertainment.
I also understand you did a lot of talk shows and you developed a relationship with Johnnie Carson.

Mh-hm, yup. There weren't a lot of talk shows out. I did a lot of shows but that show with Johnnie Carson, that show was one of the most outstanding talk shows. Peter Lynn Hayes was a talk show, so was Arthur Godfrey. Merv Griffin was a talk

show, too. I've been on all the talk shows. I've played them all and my repartee with Steve Allen was about as good as could be expected and I enjoyed being with him, working with him. He was the nicest guy to work with. So was Jack Paar and so was Merv Griffin. They were all nice guys to work with and also Jerry Lewis, Dean Martin. m-m-m -- when you come to think about it, they were all right.
How you fixed, George?
And I know that your first album, although I can't quite understand why you did it so late in your career --

When I could get it done. When I could get it done. People don't go along making albums because they're very expensive. So what can I do? I gotta wait until somebody comes along, the label that comes along to make it. That's what happened.
Were you able to record some of the songs that you had

No. Just did the songs they had for me to do. While I was making those I found one between times that I wanted to do and make, you know. But I didn't start off making 'em, I started off with what they had there, the platform that would sell for me, the amount of songs I was going to do and the name of the songs and everything -- like "Someone to Watch Over Me," was one of the songs they had. They had another song, I forget the name of that song. It's too bad my memory is so bad. I can't remember.
I take it that this period in your career was not that exciting. Were you performing live during this time as well?
Yeah.
Who were you performing with, where were you performing?
When?
The time of
the '60s, prior to your stroke.

Yeah. I just told you who I worked with, just told you. I told you Anna Marie Alberghetti, I told you with Katrina Valente I performed before my stroke. I told you about being in Germany, told you about with Perry Como. I told you about -- this is prior to the stroke. With Ted Lewis, that's prior to the stroke, with Judy at the Met was prior to the stroke.
Can you describe the circumstances of your career immediately preceding your stroke and what the effect of the stroke was?
No career. That's the end of that. Stop right there. Stop right there. What am I going to do? Go ahead, help me out. You help me. If you could help me, very good.
Can you describe the circumstances of how --
I wasn't able
to dance, I wasn't able to walk.
I understand that, but I'm talking about when the stroke happened, where were you?
I was in bed, I was asleep, okay?
Had you just been performing?

No, I was at the Americana Hotel in New York, understand. That's where I was living when I was working with Judy Garland at the Palace and it was on a Sunday night when we finished the show, all right. On a Monday I was all right -- Tuesday -- when I went to bed Monday night, no pain, no nothin'. I woke up Tuesday morning, couldn't pick up my left hand, compree'? That's when I had the stroke -- I didn't find out -- the doctor, he didn't tell me what it was. No falling down on the street, no taking to the hospital, because I went to the hospital on my own. I walked in the hospital, had to come out

in a wheelchair, okay? I walked in there and I come out in a wheelchair. Now mess with that one. Go ahead. Disgraceful. Disgraceful. Can't do anything about it. Can't do a thing about it, what can you do?
So you were performing right up to that last minute.
Yeah. My last show was on a Saturday -- Sunday night. Monday and Tuesday I didn't do nothin', Wednesday I was in the hospital.
What year was this?
So what were your feelings at that point, I mean, you were a popular dancer especially, there went your profession.
No, I don't know that. I don't know that. I don't know that at all. How did I know it? I don't either. My arm didn't stop my profession. I didn't care

about my arm. I didn't figure that's going to stop me. When this leg was spastic, that's when I couldn't dance and that's when I was thinking about, will it ever get right. But I wouldn't -- there goes my career, that's how that happens, that's all. But I found out I couldn't dance so that was the end of that.
When did that leg become spastic, at the same time?
Oh, about a few days after I was in the hospital, a few days after I was in the hospital, you know? It happened in the hospital.
There was nothing that they could do?

Seemingly -- they didn't do nothin', seemingly. I needed more therapy than what they were giving me and I was telling the girl, the girl knew I needed more therapy, but she helped me get out of there because I wasn't getting the treatment I needed and I was so glad she helped me get out, I didn't
know what to do, but I got out. So what did you do in between that period when you initially were ill to now? What were you doing? Did you continue to get involved --
Nothin', nothin', nothin', just what you see me doing now, nothin'. Did that for 12 years, nothin'. You understand? Nothin'.
Okay, the last few minutes we have on this tape we might as well go back to Harlan Dickson of Doyle and Dickson.
And Brothers. What about them? Harlan and Darlan is brothers. The Dickson brothers. What about them -- at the Palace Theater. Back in 1925, '24.
They were clog dancers.
Yeah.
Was this the first time you'd seen that type dancing?
First time I'd met them, yeah. uh-hm. That's the time of whatsname back in those days, Will Mahoney and also Pat Rooney.
That was your first introduction to tap dancing.
What? No, Bill Robinson was my first to tap dancing.
Bill Robinson was the first tap dancing you ever saw?
Not saw, no. Bill Robinson was going on before that, before I saw Doyle and Dickson.
Did you know Bill Robinson well?
Yeah, pretty well.
Did you two ever dance on the same stage?
No. He danced on the same stage. I was a singer on the same stage. We appeared on the same stage, but we
didn't dance on the same stage. He did the dancing and I did the singing, Buck did the playing. We never come into conflict dancing.
Where was this?
That happened at the -- I think it was Providence, Rhode Island. Providence, Rhode Island.
What sort of fellow was he?
Nice fellow, course he was a nice guy. Just about like you are, you're a nice guy. He was a nice guy, too. Yeah.
Good dancer though, too.
Yeah, good dancer, good showman, too. You can't take that away from him. He was all.
Well, shall we close with a song?
What song are
How about "Rhythm for Sale."

I can't do that. Can't do that. No, close with my song, man. You want to close with a song, I give you my song to close. Okay. I'll let you use my song to close it. Just don't try to sell it, that's all. Okay?

"Never wanted a favor Never asked for a loan I've got my little bag of troubles Still they're all my own And any time I feel lonely Feel I'm far, far away I just get down on my knees And heaven hears me say Don't ever try to go too far Don't try to be more than what you are You'll get there better way by far Than always belittlin' me Don't say you-all when you should say you Don't say George if you don't know who The same thing for one is always good for two When you're always belittlin' me I never knew of all the things that you've done To feel that one was me And underneath the setting sun I never dreamed you could be so cruel

Don't make believe you really care
Don't leave me groping in despair
You'll never ever get nowhere
When you're always belittlin' me."
That's for you, George. That one's for you,
George.

George, put this on the tail-end. I'm so glad you came, and I hope you're happy before you leave, I hope you have a nice trip back and until I see you, keep well. I'll try to see you in May or maybe before, I think I can get there in April, I'm not sure. It all depends upon what George thinks about what we send him.
How do you feel about blacks on Broadway? How do you feel about this appearance on the stage for you?
In what way?
Well, it's been a while.
I've been on the stage before.
But it's been a while since you --

It makes no difference, I want to be able to walk when I get back this time. I want to get some more therapy, if I can. I want to be able to walk. I don't want somebody holding me, a cane and all that jive, you know?
I'm sure you will.

I'm going to try. I was sure I was going to get well before now, but I wasn't. I've been in this thing for 12 years now. I don't miss nothin'. I don't miss the stage, I just miss the money that I don't get from the stage. That's the thing. That makes everything coming, you don't know where you're going. You know what I mean? All the bills come in, you don't know where you're going.
But you've been very nice company. You've been very nice to have. You and Karen both. And I hate for you to have to go back. But I know that's where you live, so I
wish you a nice, happy return, safe return, and good health all the way, and until I see you just don't forget to keep well and may God bless you and be with you both. And thanks for everything.
If there's anything I can do for you, George, don't forget to call on me.

Sure we'd like to go to New York. Yes, I'll get my mother and all to get an okay to sign the contracts. Okay. Thank you. So I'm now on my way to the Principal of the school where Buck goes which is called The Clay Street School and I see the Principal and I tell him like it relly was. I says, my name is John W. Sublette from School No. 17 and I would like to get Ford Lee Washington out of school because he has such marvelous hands on the piana, there ain't nothing he's going to learn in this school that's going to do him as much good as his talent in the field and we have a chance now to go to New York, the only opportunity we have to get to New York before we have a chance to go into show business like we should. And I could appreciate no end if I could get him out for that purpose, 'cause he ain't going to learn much in school, much more, what's he going to do with it after he learns it? Says I to he. 'Cause things were critical for

an education let alone talent, what you can't get with education you can get with talent, but you've got to have superb talent to get anywhere and you have to have a college education same as what's-his-name, Paul Robeson or Frederick Douglass or Booker T. (Washington). You have to have a certain education to get anywhere. But, however, the Principal said, who's going to take care of Madd Washington? I says, I will take care of him. He said, you go home and get a paper from his mother to make sure you're his guardian and I'll let him out. And that was as easy as pie.

So I go to Buck's mother and I get the guardian papers for Buck which she signs and everything and we get him out of school and I get my mother and all to get to the manager and everything and get the contract signed. They're going to pay my mother $35 a week and all expenses for me -- gonna give $35 a week to each mother. It was like a godsend to me, but not knowing what I know after getting to New

York. However, I take Buck's clothes and put them in my trunk so we'll only have one trunk with both sets of clothes. We go to to the railroad station to catch the train with roller skates. We catch the train and go to New York with the man and they got a man in New York to meet us -- I can't think of his name but the man that's going to manage us after we get to New York is Irwin Rosen, that's his name and he was in a band but nobody knew but him about it, I didn't know it. However, they don't get no bookings for us, they don't get no place for us to work. Finally got one job for us to work, first job we got after about almost a month there and we got a job in Staten Island at the St. George Theater in Staten Island -- was a good hit over there, good hit. Now only singing and playing piana and I'm singing out world this/-- you believe me, you believe me I'm singing. I could sing a while. However, we do that engagement, three days I think it was -- three or four days

at the most.
So we go back to New York, hang around for a while and it would come the end of the week, we'd go down to get the money in the office to pay our rent and the man says -- he has the office open and a vestibule, where people sit in the vestibule and wait while you go into the office to talk to the manager who he had looking after us. So we go into the office to talk to the man to get the money to pay the bill and he wants to know if we think money grows on trees. So I says, no, I don't think that. What do you think the money's going to? Now we're paying I think it was $35 a week for a room -- I think that's what it was then or $2 a day, something like that anyway. However, he pitches such a fall about the money and the pople out in the office could hear him talking and they wasn't people that we knew anything about, so I didn't say nothing, I let him go ahead and talk. When he got through talking, he called me over to the desk from where I was sitting to pick up

the money. When I walked over to the desk he pulled out a roll of money, enough to choke a horse. When he counted out the little measley money he was going to give Buck and I to pay the expenses I shook my head and said no, and the tears rolled down my cheeks and I walked out of the office with 25 cents in my pocket, over 300 miles from home and I walked out of his office and said, "never mind" and I took Buck and we walked out. We only lived around the corner from the office. We lived on 41st Street and the office was on 42nd. We were between 7th and 8th and he was between 7th and 8th on 42nd and we were between 7th and 8th on 41st.
It was just you and Buck living together.
Yeh.
You had your own apartment --
No apartment, we had a room there, we had a room. How you
get an apartment at $35 a week? We you get that at? You ought to be ashamed of yourself thinking like that. There ain't nothing been handed out since I've been born.

So we go to the house, open up the trunk, take out our roller skates -- but I didn't tell you, this fella when we got to New York -- forgot to tell you that the man took us the next day down to Leo Feist, the biggest music publisher in New York City. He took us to Leo Feist on 7th Avenue between 47th and 46th -- 48th I think, on 7th Avenue. He took us there to let them hear who it is it was that they brought back to New York. They had a lot of entertainers there, singing songs, learning songs and so forth, that's a regular place to learn songs, Leo Feist, biggest music publisher in New York. Okay? So we must have sang for about two hours, played piano for about two hours. When we finished we met the manager of this music publishers and all, and he told us he was taking us back to 41st Street to tell us don't go back there no more

unless he tells us, unless he takes us. Okay.
This is the beginning. Kids are not allowed around New York. Understand? September 1919. Would you believe that I walked out of this man's office, about three months later after he said that, I done play Staten Island, come to his office to get the money, he raised his hand, walked out of the office and for the first time about three months later I walked back -- get your roller skates -- put our skates on, I said, Buck, put your skates on good, man because you're going to skate a while. So we put them on and we went up to 7th Avenue and they got the third rail in the middles, so we're not used to the third rail, boy we got to get used to it today cause we got to jump the third rail. That means three rails I got to cross on roller skates.
So we go up to 7th Avenue and 41st Street and we go to Broadway. We catch a car going up Broadway. I grabbed the car and grabbed his hand, like a chain and we'd hang

onto the car, we get up to 47th Street, between 47th and -- now, we're going to Leo Feist that's what I told you before -- we're going up there for the first time since we were first there to tell them what has happened -- the manager of the music publishers and tell him what had happened.

Okay, we're skating around on 7th Avenue on Broadway between 47th and 48th, on Broadway skating, catching cars going up and catch them coming down. We got about 500 people watching us skate -- get the point? So much the police had to holler, 'Get out of there!' He thought we was a couple of niggers that were just going to run cause he said get out of there? We just jumped across the tracks, spread eagle and coasted right under the policeman's legs, right by his feet, stopped right in front of him. Now that was in front of the Strand Theater. So you know we weren't scared to obey his orders, plus here we are. So the people come up stating, 'Where do you teach that?' 'Do you

teach skating?" No, no, no. "What do you do?" "I entertain." So we put our skates on our shoulder and walked from 47th Street, and between 47th and 48th on Broadway around to between 47th and 48th on 7th Avenue, which is only half a block, it's about half a block when you measure it 'cause it runs into a point, you know, 47th runs into a point to 49th Street and Broadway. Get what I mean? Get what I'm sayin'?

However, we go around there and I get Mr. Sally Cohen is the man's name who runs the place, Sally Cohen. Never forget him as long as I live. And I called him to tell him what happened. He said just a minute. Now he's heard us enough, over two hours singing, playing piano. So he knows about this agent, he knows about him. So he called him up to tell him to come over, he ought to hear somebody, he had somebody he wanted him to hear. So he comes over. Now he doesn't tell on the phone my story but he waits to get him over here to tell him
what has happened. Well, when he tells him what has happened when he's over there. The man says, don't worry about it. He heard us now, heard us sing, he wants us to go on in his act.

How good could we have been, George? How good could we have been if there's a man who's been too good for the stage, they had to cancel him out for being too good for the program, he's a understanding, does an acrobatic act, he's going to bring us on into his act. Now how good could we have been if he was going to put us on in his act. He thought of a trick that he does, he was going to miss it and make it his excuse to get us on. Get what I mean? Set it up. Perfect. Okay.

When we go to his office to agree to go on the stage with him at the Columbia Theater and pick up the money to pay the landlady because I didn't take it from this man. They were going to give us the money and I walked out of the office. But this guy, Nazarro was going to give us the money to take
care of the rent. So he gave us a check. I said, what could we do with a check, makes it out to the name of the people where we're staying over there, give it to her. Okay. that's straightened.
Then we were going to go on the stage with him on a Sunday concert at the Columbia Theater at 47th Street and Broadway on a Sunday, which we did.

So it comes down for us to get ready to go on the stage to do the concert, Sunday concert at this Columbia Theater, I heard the manager and Nazarro talking about he don't want no niggers in the theater, didn't want no niggers on the stage. I heard him talk about that. But they don't know I hear 'em. I'm off stage and hear this. And he tells him he's going to bring us on in his act -- no, he didn't want us in the theater -- on the stage. So, when they comes to arguing the point, I'm going to tell Buck when they finish arguing -- Nazarro says to the manager, you go back out in front

and manage the theater and I will take care of my act. And I start up the stairs to tell Buck about it. Something says, don't tell him. Then I go on back and wait for the time for us to go on and Mr. Trick had introduced Buck and Bubbles, two boys that he met at Carnegie Hall and asked him would he give them a job in the theater, so he thought he'd bring us along. One plays the flute in 14 feet of rice pudding. Are the gentlemen there? Their names are Buck and Bubbles.

So we walk on the stage in vagabond dress, yella shoes, brown pants, blue coat, brown cap and gray cap. And we walk on, the audience had a big "Oh," and we start off. The first song we did was "Rhythm For Sale." After "Rhythm For Sale" I did another song, can't think of the name of it. However, he says, "Bubbles, I'd like for you to tell the audience about the letter that you got from your mother." Now I had never told Buck about what had happened before we went on concerning

the manager not wanting to send us on the stage. I didn't tell Buck that. But I had the feeling inside yet of what had happened. So when the manager goes out and wants me to tell the audience the story about the letter I received from my mother, I used the song, "Mammy O' Mine," recited the verse which is a verse that goes -- you can tell from what I have witnessed concerning the manager not wanting us on the stage, you can tell about how my feeling was by the song that I'm going to tell you now, the verse of the song says,

"I read your letter, Oh, Mammy O' Mine I feel much better, Mammy O' Mine But still I'm kind of homesick, too No one can cure me, but you Mammy O' Mine, below that ole Dixon line I'm longing to kiss you, I miss you all of the time I read the letters you write and I kiss your picture each night For they remind me of days of long ago Oh, Lawdy, how I'd like to be with you When I'm alone, my thoughts go wandering home And I start thinking of you and feeling so blue I could cry Now I know why, Daddy used to say, the Good Lord he blessed us

But when he gave us you, Mammy, Mammy
you're the bestus, Angel divine
Wonderful Mammy of my-wah-wine --
Ta-la-da-da-del-deda-dee -- "
Tears were rolling down my cheeks, standing
ovation. Held up the show and you know how I
felt because I was really -- that song really
hit the spot because I was thinking of my mother
concerning what has happened to me already 'bout
the man not wanting us to be on the stage, you
know. You can understand that.
So I finished the song, the
audience stood up, they applauded, they yelled
and raved. Well, the act is over.
Well, the act is over. The
manager comes down the aisle after the show was
