Buck said, don't leave me. You know I ain't
gonna leave you, but I ought to go on home now but there wasn't enough money. I didn't go, stuck it out. Now, Buck is only 13 years old, I'm 17.

About two weeks later I played the Aubodon Theater, 168th Street and Broadway. Now, there my voice cracked at the Abodon Theater and I thought I should take up dancing, I hadn't danced a leg yet, to compensate for my voice I'd do a dance, that's what I thought.

About three months after we played the Columbia Theater we played the Palace and no negro played that Palace, man, for months and months, they told me we wouldn't get in there. We played it. In less time -- they were still getting in the Palace when we played it. However, we played the Palace. First Negro act held over a second week in the Palace Theater. We went on the stage with such people like Ray Samuels, Clayton Jackson and (Jimmy) Durante, (Fred) Warings Pennsylvanians,

Tom Patricola, the dancer, Jack Donahue. Look, we had a big bill, eight acts and after the first week we had to be placed on No. 2, next to closing, about the third act. They had to put us on next to closing because nobody wanted to follow us. We turned out to be the next to closing act from that point on.
Then we got on the Orpheum circuit.
You weren't going black-faced any more?
No. Only in Louisville.
Only in Louisville.
That's all.
You said you performed along with Nat Nazarro's act.
Yeah.
How did the two acts combine?
Great, because
only thing he did was acrobatics. He was an understander, he had a top mounter. He thought a one-man trick and missed the trick, that's when he introduced us.
Could you describe his act?

Yeah, acrobatics. He's an underlander. He juggled a kid around he'd do a flag up, he'd do a -- the kid would do a back somersalt, back flips and they'd do handstands. It was an acrobatic act. You know what acrobats are?
And how would Buck and Bubbles play into that?

No, we didn't play into that. The idea was he'd do that part and then he'd miss the trick, the one-hand trick, which is his last trick. He missed the last trick, understand? With the one hand? And when he missed the trick he'd pull a gag to him by his boy -- "every time I stay out late you come home drunk. One of these days

you'll be out drinking and I'll come home drunk." This gag. He missed this trick. "Ladies and gentlemen, I had to be at Carnegie Hall the other night, two gentlemen asked me if I'd insist them running their recital in vaudeville so I thought I'd run them along. Are the gentlemen there? I think one of them plays a flute in four feet deep of rice pudding. Buck and Bubbles? Bring them on." Here we come. I told you how we're dressed. Okay. On. That's how we got on the act. Now we do our song and dance and we burned it.

So we go on the Orpheum circuit on bills with Frances White and Walker -- Walker-- can't think of his first name. And there are quite a few acts on the bill. However, However, we played the Orpheum circuit to California, we got into California and we got an audition to do for the Pathe' Studio, we got an audition for Pathe' Studio and we got a chance to make some Hugh Wiley shorts.
You were
pretty young then, weren't you?

I'm 19 by now. Hugh Wiley shorts, Dimmie & Wildcat and I made eight of them. Then the manager wanted to show that he could direct a picture better for us than we could do under anybody else's direction. Which was a sad situation, so I gotta vouch for him that we could do better with some other director than we can with him than with any other director. We had to vouch for him to become our director. Buck and Bubbles are so strong with their talent that what we say concerning being directed would be taken up by the studio to the extent of changing the director for the picture and get him a job since we can do better. We got him the job and that guy liked to have killed us. He'd liked to have killed us. He had us working from 8 o'clock in the morning until 5 o'clock in the evening, plus 8 o'clock the next morning, all night. That's what he did. That's what he did.
The people used to like Buck

and me so well that the guys used to holler at me coming onto Midway on the free fareway, you know, coming onto the studio lot. "Hey, Bubbles, how ya doin'?" "Okay." "Come here. I guess you want some money." I didn't say a word about no money. I says, "Oh, I ain't worried about that. "Your check is ready." She goes gets two checks, one for Buck and Bubbles, one for Nat Nazarro. So she gives me both checks. That's how I found out Nazarro was getting two salaries. Then instead of me (inaudible) to get Nazarro, I thought he was going to be all right after that -- no, he got worse. Then he wanted to make it so the mistake was in the office --
Nat Nazarro was directing you in those Pathe' motion pictures?
Yeah, mh-hm.
But you in turn had a lot more power than he did because you were the one who chose the director.

That's right. But he really, not like him to get that way -- let him -- God rest his soul. However, getting back where I was trying to explain to you concerning the two checks. That showed me he was stealing. I didn't know that. Instead of me discarding him from that point on I went on like nothing had happened, but I figured I'd fix it so he wouldn't be -- I would be so reliable, not thinking of nothing but him. Not myself now. Thinking about him. If I'm under allowed, he can't do nothing, but I'm hurting myself. I ain't thinking about that. I ain't thinking about hurting myself, I'm just thinking about hurting him. But I'm hurting myself. So I would get drunk so he couldn't depend on me. Get my point? It got to a place where he thought liquor would rule me. So he would keep the studio going all night, get a flask and bring it in to give me a drink with the flask to keep me awake. Half the time I was
asleep, my eyes half-closed. Cameras going with my eyes closed. They'd wake me up to drink. Makes me look like I took dope or something, you know.

I let that slide. Oh, man, what I went through, I can't tell you because it will come out. However, he died with two sets of books, one for him and one for the government. They got him. They find the books. That fixed him up. He was dead three days before they found out he was dead.
So I am now thinking about how I'm going to do. And I don't think about getting none of my material that he's got in the office of where I played and what I've been in. I don't think about that.
Wasn't this at the beginning of your relationship when you began to realize what was happening with the money?
No, how could I know that. I done played the Palace Theater,

I played the Columbia Theater, I went off to California, I'm just coming to California. How much time have I had to find out? That's the first time I saw two checks for the act of Buck and Bubbles. How could I do that? Go ahead, you tell me. Have you been following the story? You missed it.
I just have not --
You did what? What? Now, you didn't follow the story.
(Inaudible) in terms of how many years you'd been with him at that point when you first went out to California.
I what?
How many years you'd been together by the time you went out to California.
What are you talking about -- oh, I see what you -- your point is how many years we'd been together --
Two years and you already were successful to go out to Hollywood at that point, had established a big enough reputation to --

It would have been bigger than what it was if the manager hadn't been so selfish in his own way. He didn't want us to get a name because he thought we'd leave him, that's why he was like that. But I had a thought, I just had a thought of making a name. I had to fight like a dog to get that name up in lights, man. That was some trouble, I mean that was trouble. Anyway, getting back to the point of doing the shorts and finding the checks and all, he got worse instead of getting better. I didn't think he was going to get worse. I thought he'd try to settle up. No, it was mine to realize he had made a thief out of himself before some people really appreciate his every effort set forth in our behalf, you know. I

didn't pay nothing. What I said -- here's a sad story like every time I think of it I'd almost cry, to think I was robbed of my goodness, same as Buck would have been robbed of his talent. If he had stayed in school with book learning to do what with, get what? Sad. However, from the Pathe' studio we come back to New York. We came back to New York and come back on the Pantages circuit, from New York to California on the Pantages circuit. Now we have already now played the Paramount Theater with Bing Crosby when he first got there, with Frank Sinatra when he first got there, were on the bill with these guys at the Paramount. I was in high society, wasn't I?
Were you the only black act?
Yeah, there ain't no two black acts on no bill. One time in California there was two colored acts on the same bill.

I was wondering what happened. We went to Oliver, that's what I was talking about. We passed that, now, went to Riverside, where I grew up in Riverside. Burns and Allen, where do you go from there, I thought was going to be another question. But it wasn't, I was just going to feel my way and I might as well go into Germany and start doing special shows then that way. If we can't go do chronological as we're going. And I'm trying to find out what to follow them with, what we talked about before, you said that you asked me about the colored acts on the same bill, didn't you, and I brought that out and when I told you about the places I played with Bing Crosby, Frank Sinatra at the Paramount and Bing Crosby at the Paramount and the Globe with Tony DiMarco and Sallie -- now we're we going from that Riverside Theater --
How old were you then, about this time, so I get the context
About 21.

You'd already been to Hollywood, you'd done some Pathe' films, right? You'd been with Nat Nazarro for two years now with Buck. You were both traveling together and you're back in New York after Hollywood. After Hollywood did you go directly back to New York?
Yeah. That's headquarters.
New York was the headquarters.
Yeh, that's where all the theatrical profession is, in New York.
You weren't tap dancing at this point, or were you?
No -- when? 21? Yeah.

20 years old, between 19 and 20.
Well, you talked something before of having seen clog dancing and buck dancing --
Yeah, that was the carnival.
Did that always remain back in your mind as something you were interested in?

No, no. I only started about dancing when I was concerned after I lost my voice. My voice cracked at the Orpheum Theater. That's when I thought about doing something else basides try to sing. I'd add another talent that's why I took up dancing.
Well, dancing was getting big -- tap-dancing was very big then, wasn't it?
No, it wasn't big, how do you mean it was big?
Weren't there a lot of people doing it?
No, not to my knowledge, the only person doing dancing was Bill Robinson, all the rest of them was like preliminary things, no main events.
In other words, tap-dances weren't the main act?

No. Fred Astaire was going then, you know, and Ray Bolger and Tom Patricola and James Bodden and Jack Donahue and the Misconi Brothers. They were dancing then, but the idea was that I just put the dancing in my mind from my voice cracking and I thought I'd start dancing by myself.
These original Pathe' films that you made though, they were just you and Buck singing and playing the piano.
With a company, with a company, all colored, too, cast.
Do you

remember the names of any of these films? Yeah. Name of the film "Black Narcissus," "In And Out," "Honest Crooks" and I think of the one with ostrich, had an ostrich in one, can't think of that. But the place where you get your (inaudible) they got them, you got your film, they got those things, you know.
So now here you are, you're 20 years old, you start tap-dancing, picking it up. You figure that your voice is cracking?

That's where I actually go from Riverside, leaving Frank Sinatra and go back to -- let's see, where do we go from there. 1920, 1921 -- I've forgotten what year that was, 1921. I'm going to California now on the Pantages circuit. I left the Pantages circuit -- was that then -- I can take that later -- I can take Paul Small next and Finkelhoff, they were agents for a show called "Curtain Time," "Laugh Time" and "Show

Time." These are different shows that they put on that we were in with them where we had Connie Boswell, Jack Haley. We had George Jessel and this colored act called Miller Brothers and Lois, that's a dance act --
Tap dance?

They danced on a pedestal, you know, same thing. However, those shows at the Curran Theater in San Francisco, they would have like the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles -- the Pantages Theater -- no it didn't get to the Pantages Theater at that.

We did that then we come back to New York -- after coming to California, then we went back to New York again. At this time when we go to New York we do the other circuit, the Loews circuit -- The Loews circuit then we'd go to the Poli circuit.
Who was booking you at that time?
Nazarro, through the other offices, you know. Maybe we
had two or three offices booking us, you know.
Were you accompanying their act at that time --
No, no, we were doing by ourselves, we're working by ourselves now.

Oh, there's another scene that I forgot to give you and that scene is when we were at the Pathe' studio I decided I wanted to break the contract, I wanted to get out from under the contract. After I found these different things happening with Nazarro, I wanted to get out of that contract, you know.
What did the contract obligate you to do? What were you obligated to do?
Everything.
Other films, you mean?
No, no, no. To get out of the contract with the management -- that's what we're talking about, the management

now. So what I did was -- oh, there's another thing now -- I should think to vitalize this, to take this to a more systematic situation is we leave the Riverside Theater -- you got that. That other part comes in another place I see -- We go back to New York. During this time I think is when Chuck and Chuckles came to New York - 1921 -- you passed 192 -- Pathe' studio was in 1922, wasn't it, or was it '21 -- '22, wasn't it?
I'm not sure.
I think it was '22. Pathe' studio, wasn't it or was it '21, 22 wasn't it?
When was the first time that you started tap-dancing?
When I was 18.
Can you tell me about that?
I got to get you
You don't have to get us down there. You can just start talking about when you really started tap dancing, what influenced you initially, why did you decide to start tap dancing.
I told ya.
Right. Can you tell me a little bit more about that?

I told you that my voice cracked at the Audubon Theater, I thought I should do another talent instead of the one I am losing. That's when I think I'm losing my voice. You understand? That's how I decided to do another talent, to dance. That's what interested me in dancing, my voice cracking, you see? Then I started dancing -- okay? Then they had a player club uptown called the Comedy Club where all the fellas used to hang out, entertainers used to hang out in this club and meet at this club, waiting for bookings or places to work or play.

That's where they'd meet to hang out and they had a little dancing session down there that goes on. People learn how to dance and everything down there, you know. So you can come down there and practice or rehearse, if that's what you want to learn or steal what you want to steal -- one of those things, you know. So I went to this club to see what was happening and they didn't want me to dance, I started dancing, and they didn't think I was good enough. So they routed me out. So then I went to California.
This club was up in Harlem?
Yeah.
Was this also called the Hoofers's Club?
Comedy Club. What was the Hoofers's Club -- I'm trying to think what the Hoofers's Club was.
It sounds very similar. There's a pool hall in the front.
In the back room was a dancing hall. They'd let dancers go there --
No, this was downstairs in the basement. It don't make no difference. Either one is the same, Hoofers Club or the Comedy Club.

However, I go into California on the Fantages circuit I think it was at that time in the year of 1921 and since they wrote me out of this Comedy Club or Hoofers Club, whatever you want to call it, I went to California and thought I'd learn dancing while I was away. So I did. I studied it while I was away, day and night. When I came back I stayed up all night to learn the one step. I was dancing until about 6 o'clock in the morning. And the restaurant was open, I got through with the step. I had to cry because I was so overjoyed that I had gotten the step that I wanted called "double-over-the-top"and I go around to this restaurant at 41st and 8th Avenue to get some coffee and donuts after I
finished, this was in the morning. I had to take my shoes off at night to keep the sound from going through the floor, you know, to learn this dancing, the step, you know?
Why did you take your shoes off?

Because I made too much noise tapping with shoes on, too much noise. If you are downstairs and I'm upstairs and I was dancing over you, what happens? Then if you're next door what happens at 3 o'clock in the morning, 4 o'clock in the morning, what happens then? Just like that dog over there, that's in the daytime, too. What are you going to do at 4 o'clock in the morning with a sound going out like that.

So that's what I did, took my shoes off and danced stocking feet until I got the step, and I got it and I got so happy about it I cried and I went down to the corner to get some coffee and stuff and went back up to Harlem the next day to see what they had against

me this time. So everybody would dance, dance -- come around to be time for me I could go out and dance, so I danced, and I did this step, that was it. That one step stopped everything, the one I stayed up all night for, that made me the master of the dancing at the club, for the Hoofers Club. Everybody talked about me then. "You ought to see that step. You ought to see so-and-so and so."
So I got the dancing down and I wanted to do some other kind of thing, I wanted to mix my style up, do negro dancing and white dancing together.
Who was in the Hoofers Club then? Who were some of the people that were --
Baby Laurence, you had a fella called Port Chops, you had what's his name, oh, Dickie Wells, Dickie Wheaton, Corn Bread, Buster Johnson, Ford Marcelin Jones and Buster Bowie, Preacher --
Were these
people all local (inaudible)? (cross talk)
Yeh. Corn Bread --
Were they also performing on the stage anywhere?
Yeah, when they'd get a job, yeah.
Was Bill Robinson a member?

No, this is underclass people. This man, he's on Broadway. Bill Robinson is on Broadway. We were just getting together here. The idea is, because I'd been on Broadway, too. But the point is this is not for those people. This is unprofessional. The people is not so far advanced in the business. That's what this is. Like an amateur night thing. You don't take Bill Robinson and Ray Bolger and Fred Astaire and put them down in the basement where I learned to dance, do ya? They don't belong there, they're not/am I in that category at all;
So what can I tell ya now? That you had to do something to get into the club, the last time you were there they had made --

No, you're learning -- you're learning, you're going to the club to learn. That's what this thing stands for. It's like a pool hall where you learn to play pool. This is where you go to learn to dance or rehearse or whatever you want to do at this place. You understand? Now a professional person don't go in this place for that purpose. No, no, you don't do that, so we don't look for those kind of people in there.
I had heard that some people were considered the kings of the Hoofers Club, the best people there. People that all the kids used to emulate.
Who told you about that?
Chops, I mentioned it to him.
Told you what?
There were kings in the Hoofers Club, like the Tip, Tap & Toe.

No, no -- Tip, Tap & Toe there -- no, no, no, no. This was before Chuck and Checkers came to New York, so how could he tell you about something he heard -- he only heard about this, but it wasn't what he thought it was. Now more than what you think they are now, same difference. He's far now from what he was. He ain't up to par for what he came here. However, this ain't a place where those kind of dancers -- they don't need to go to that club. You don't go there for that. You're finished dancing when you're out on the -- how can I explain it to you? How can I explain it to you?
I think I understand.
No, I don't think you do, that's why I say, how can I explain it?
It was a place to train. What was it, a bar above it, pool hall above it -- it was in the basement of a building, right?

There was nothing above it. Just an empty store above it. I think there was a barber shop above it -- barber shop. But it's a place where you go to learn, it's almost like a hall, it's a place -- they let us use it because there wasn't anybody in it and we used it to practice dancing and anything else we wanted to practice in there, you know.
What was that step that you were trying to get that night?
"Double-over-the-top."
You stayed up all night just to --
All night, yeh, just to get that step.
It took you
one night to get it.

I got it one night by luck. I'd been practicing all along. I'd do it in the daytime, but I couldn't get it finished in the daytime, so I'd go through the night. But I didn't stop doing it until I got it and it went to the next morning.
So you were really a late starter when it came to tap dancing.

Yeah, I'm the last one. I'm the last one that's considered, you know what I mean? There were a lot of dancers, but no one had reached the penacle like Bill Robinson, Fred Astaire and all them, understand? They're still trying to get there. But I'm working on mine until perfection. I've had consideration in the -- what is that paper -- Ebony -- another one called -- it's a woman's magazine, I can't think of the name of it.
Were there people that were influencing you at that time that you were trying to emulate in dancing?
No, myself, man. Emulate who?
I don't know.
I don't either. Who emulate --
Did Bill Robinson have any influence on you?

No -- no, no. I'm in a different category altogether, man. 'Cause Bill Robinson don't sing and none of the dancers sing and I'm a singer. So I'm in a different category. So they ain't doing nothing that I want to do. I want to do something myself, okay? That's why my dancing was so different because I made it up myself. Then I want to make it different to make a routine of dancing and mix it with negro dancing and white dancing. So when you saw me you didn't know who I was in dancing. I was a Fred Astaire, I was a Ray Bolger, I was Jack Donahue, I was a Tom Patricola, I was about everybody when you saw me for the different things I did, but I

didn't have their style. I had my style. See the difference in what I'm trying to say? So that took precedent and then I wanted to sing and dance and dance and play, play an instrument while I danced. I wanted to do that, too. I did that a while with a ukelele. When I was going to California because they didn't like the way I was dancing, so they mixed me out as being considered a dancer in their category. So I went to California at which time I learned more about dancing and by learning more about dancing, I want to come back to New York after finishing the engagement in California -- I come back to NewYork with still the idea of dancing and I learned the dancing sufficient enough to go back to the Comedy Club to be recognized. So from that we go to Canada at the Chez Maurice.
Buck wasn't dancing then, too, was he?
Buck, about all
he could do is sing. He danced a little bit not much, just a little bit, enough to a tap step No. 8.
What kind of dancing was he doing?
Same kind, tap dancing. He'd do no tap dancing, same -- no different style.

You got Chez Maurice? Make this sufficient enough to get out of the contract.

headline act on the bill and I had to find what other acts were on the bill before that and what kind of billing they got and all and see what Buck and Bubbles would be rated.

No, no, this was -- how you mean the first year?
This is when you were about 24 --

Filing suit.
So I found a lawyer in New York and presented my case to him

and he filed the action against Nazarro for neglectment of management and the suit was filed at $150,000; and we had the trial and the Judge as more or less in favor for Buck and Bubbles, because Nazarro tried to prove that he taught Buck how to play the piano, so much that I didn't know how to do nothing and neither one of us knew how to do anything, he did everything. So the lawyer found out about the phones situation and he went and got a brand new phone book and that's how he won the case. He come to court the next day with a new brief case with this brand new phone book in it. When he got before the Judge and presented his case to the Judge, plus the number in the phone book -- what it was the two phones showed up that this guy was conspiring in some way -- or his secretary was conspiring, that he lost the case. But the Judge told my lawyer, why don't you settle it for four or five thousand dollars. He made this statement to the lawyer. And my lawyer said, I want to go back during recess and talk it over and we'll pick up after.
The lawyer goes to recess and comes back and tells me he says, I think we ought to settle this, how you think you settle? "What's the matter, what are you talking about,

Ray Samuels. Anyway -- was it Ray Samuels? What's her name, I can't think of her name. However, I called a friend of mine that I met in Chicago, an usher, and my manager didn't want me to go with an usher, he thought she wasn't up to par. But I thought she was swell.

Anyway I called up to tell her what had happened. I was going to call her to tell her and the detective is coming down the stairs so I can't talk on the phone to tell her. I see the guy coming down so I just got the idea, instead of putting the coin in to phone, I forgot it. And he's coming down, "You don't scare me coming down," "You better not start nothing." "You come down like somebody starting something, I ain't starting nothing." So while he's standing there he's telling me don't you all do so-and-so, don't you do so-and-so, I'm going back upstairs and leave him down there. This is in the basement of the theater, you know.
So I go back upstairs and while upstairs I thought I'd walk around to this place

where this girl is. Her name -- her name -- her name -- oh, I'll think of it. However, I go around to the theater where she was working, which is only a couple of blocks around from where I am or where I was, and I tell her the story, told her why I didn't call, I told her we quit the act and left so-and-so and-so, and I need some money to get back to New York 'cause I didn't have but 25 cents in my pocket. So she goes in her little kitty and gets out $300 for Buck and I to go to New York, give it to me. And we go back to the theater and the manager wanted to keep the trunk. All of our clothes were in the trunk. Street clothes, stage clothes and all in this trunk, you know. So he didn't let us have the trunk. Okay.

We go on to New York. I get to New York, now I've got to scout out the music. I didn't have no music now, got to scout out dancing shoes and costumes to work in and I got to get a date. So I get a date in a

colored theater that we played in in Philadelphia called the Standard Theater, the manager's name was John Gibson, colored man who owns the theater and he decided he would take us in because he knew we would act. See all of us had played there before, all four of us had played there before in an act. But I'm coming back this time with just Buck and I and he booked us. He charged us -- to borrow money now you had to pay 10% of whatever you borrowed. He couldn't advance on salary less than 10%. Okay. So I borrowed a few dollars to get these costumes and things I needed, sweaters and shoes and taps and plates and all. I got the music in New York, I got the music and everything.

We opened up, good success, I got to get another booking. So I booked in Newark. So in Newark he enjoined us in getting on the stage -- enjoined, do you understand me? Put out an injunction against us not appearing in his theater -- against us appearing in the theater. So we couldn't appear according to

this injunction. To enjoin us from working on the stage at the Orpheum Theater in Newark, New Jersey, which happened during Christmas-time. We were unable to do any shopping for Christmas or any food for Christmas or money for food for Christmas. We were in a terrible state for the first time --
You were young boys, too.
Yeah. So my next move -- I can't get no job in New York, I can't get none in Newark, so I won't be able to get a job in the west. So let me get out of New York, okay?

So I go to the William Morris office whom I knew and who knew us and offered them an act with a cut of $350, cut the salary from $750 to $350, understand? To go on any date to Chicago. They're going to give us transportation to Chicago, a couple hundred dollars cash plus the contract to work at the

Orpheum Theater -- no, the Oriental Theater in Chicago with Paul Ash who was The Blue Streak of Vaudeville, another blue streak, he was the King Leader of Bands at that time -- Paul Ash. And we got there for the rehearsal, when we come to the stage door, the stage door man could not believe that we had come there to work. So he calls upstairs to tell them we were downstairs at the door to come to work. When the man come down to see us, he said we got the wrong place -- got the wrong place, I got the contract in my pocket for the Oriental Theater -- look at that one, look at this one. I got the contract in my pocket for the Oriental Theater in Chicago, Illinois, the date to start and all and I'm here at the theater. And the man don't want to receive me because I'm in the wrong place. I said, yeah? He said, "Wait a minute." So he goes back upstairs, gets on the phone and calls up another theater where we had played, all the four of us Nazarro, Buck and Bubbles had played on the west

side of town to tell them about us and ask for a date for us, and got a date for us. Come back and says, you got the wrong theater, the theater is the west side theater, I think he said the Ordean Theater over on the west side. Okay. So they expect you there. That's okay. I go to the theater, rehearse, go on do the show, the same guy that produces the show that Paul Ash is in, he went to see the show, too. He went to catch the show. When he caught the show, he came back to the theater and we got the message that they wanted us over with Paul Ash the following week. Okay. When we come to open the following week, the piana had to be changed from where it was where we saw it, they weren't using it for years, it was on my left of the stage -- on my left, the piano was over here, understand? And the man wants to put the piano on the right. So I can't all of a sudden talk to Buck from my right side. I got to talk to Buck because I've been talking to him, from my

left side, you know. So when Buck was going to rehearse the music that's what they told him about the piano then. He comes upstairs -- I'm unpacking -- he comes upstairs to tell me about it and I says, "Don't cry about it, we're not on the stage, we're not doing nothin' yet. Don't cry about it, I'll go down with ya and we'll see what it is." So he takes me downstairs, "Show me the fella," his name is MacDermott. Okay, I'll take care of it. Soon as I got a chance and there was a lull in what he was doing, I went on the stage and I said, "Mr. MacDermott, my partner was telling me that you want to move the piano from where it is on the left side to the right side. "Yes, I saw your act so-and-so-and-so-and-so. I said, "Yeah, really?" Mh-hm, mh-hm -- and the band is listening all the people on the stage in the show is listening, they're sitting in the audience and the band is in the bandstand. I says, "Yeah, really?" Well, when he finished talking, I says, "Well, I'm sorry, Mr. MacDermott, Buck and Bubbles don't fit your
show and you just count us out until we can fit, okay? And I walked off the stage. Now, I'm finished.

When I get off stage, the stage manager over there says that the reason why he wants to change the piano is because the piano is in the way for them to move this lever for the band to go down forward, move the band down forward and put it back. I said, yeah, when they do that, when they put the band back -- bandstand back, where does Buck and Bubbles go? The band is a success and they put them back. Now we come on in a whole new setting that we know nothing about, and where do we stand? What'll they do for us? Nothing. Don't fit. With the piano over there, we can't go on, that's it. That's the end, we have to leave. So we go on upstairs deciding on we don't fit the show.
Finally the stage manager says they did get their heads together we'll put the piano on the side of the stage where they want it.

We will cut their 14 minutes down to 8 -- down to 9 -- 9 minutes. A 14-minute act, they're going to cut it down to 9 minutes. Now what do we know what to cut out. What do we know what to cut out? We got a 14-minute act, man, that's an act, a perfect act, you know. We don't know what to cut. So I agreed to yes. Buck comes down, Buck tells me the manager wants to cut our act from 14 minutes to 9 minutes. I said, 'Does he?' We don't have to worry about that, we ain't on the stage yet. We'll straighten it out.

So we go down to get ready to go on and I get in the first entrance where they don't want you to be -- don't get in the first entrance on opening day because the stage manager wants to see what the lights are and what the stages are and everything to get his cues. So if you enter on the first entrance you're in the way. But I got in the first entrance purposely for him to say something concerning -- but he never said a word. Come almost time for Buck and

Bubbles, he said to my partner, "Don't forget, I only want 9 minutes." So I answered for Buck, I said, "Sure, we'll do 9, we'll do 2, if you want 2." So we're not on the stage yet, that's my point. When I get on the stage I'm going to do the act regardless -- get me off. This was my point.

When I got on the stage, George, did we do 9 minutes? Man, listen, when we finished our act the same time as we finished it anywhere else, we couldn't get off the stage, do you know what time we got off the stage -- almost 60 minutes. You understand? Paul Ash couldn't get on. That's the band leader, 'cause I had to bid with him to knock him out and knock the rest of the people out, too. 'Cause the bit we did with Nazarro, that was a good bit for anybody, you know, with Buck and I.
What was that?
The bit we do about age. Buck is 18, I'm 19, one one-year difference. He would say, "How old are you?" to

my partner, Buck will say, "I'm 18," and he'd say to me, "How old are you?" I'd say, "I'm twice as dirty." And he'd say, "The little is 18 and the big one is 19 and the difference is a [swallow] sure and a black ear," you know. That's what the band leader is supposed to say. Which was typical, okay? And listen, after that engagement there --
That was the whole routine?

We did this after the dancing and singing is over, man. This is taking a bow, saying the gag after we're finished. This is only a gag after we're finished, you know, come back and take a bow and the guy says -- asks the question, "How old are you?" to Buck. He says, "I'm 18." And he says to me, "How old are you, Bubbles?" "I'm 19." He says "The little one is 18 and the big one is 19, the difference is a (inaudible) a black ear." he says to the audience in Jewish, you know, 'cause he's
a Jewish leader. So however, what did they do for Buck and Bubbles then? What do you think they did for Buck and Bubbles then?
What?

On the Balaban & Katz circuit in Chicago -- a big circuit, theater circuit -- booked us as a show, put a show around us and booked us in all the theaters, all the Balaban & Katz theaters and while we were playing the Balaban & Katz theaters, Nat Nazzaro had sent a -- contacted a lawyer in Chicago to enjoin us in Chicago.
Good friend, that Nat Nazzaro.

Well, he didn't want us to get away from him, 'cause he had nothing else. He was getting too old to understand that voice, so this was his meal ticket. So, however, he contacted a lawyer and the lawyer come to the theater to serve us an injunction that we can't go on the stage and I

smiled at the lawyer, 'cause I said to the lawyer, "You're going to have to wait for him to send you the money, but won't you take $200 a week instead of serving us the summons?" So he agreed and I'm going to give him the money soon as I get paid. So we go to his office and draw up the papers. I give him the money but he didn't serve the summons and I went on the stage. Then when I finished that week out there, then I left town and went to another town. Are you following me?
Didn't pay him.
I paid him, yeah, I paid him, but I went to another town so he can't enjoin me over there. But I paid him for this over here.
What kind of an agreement did you have with Nazarro that he had the ability --
He was a manager, man, he was a manager.
But what agreement did you have with him? Was it a lifetime --

Almost the same thing -- five years, five-year agreement. It was five years and I had to take on top of what Buck did. See, I wasn't going to sign no more with him from the time I told you concerning the case. I was just going to just stall around and not play no more. But he got Buck to sign a contract without me, that he would have Buck on the contract. He might not have me, but where do I go without Buck. I would have nowhere to go without Buck, like Buck would have no place to go without me. We were a team, you know. So that's how you sandwish that up.
Sort of double-crossed you in a certain way.
Yeah. I can't get Buck to understand what he's doing, 'cause he's just like Chuck, he's just like Chuck.
Buck was
easily persuaded.
Yeah. Not only was he persuaded, he was hard to understand.
What made Buck such a good performer?
What made Buck a good performer -- you better tell me that. That's like George Burns said that, who told you you was great? Listen, what made you think that Buck was such a good performer?
From what everybody's told me he was fantastic --

On the piano, man. No performer, because he couldn't do nothing in Porgy & Bess. I got him in Porgy & Bess with me because they couldn't get me without him, because I've got to work when the show ain't going to work and I can work with Buck without the show. Get my point? So I won't go on the show without him. A lot of jobs I wouldn't take without him.
I heard he was
a good comic, too, is that true?

Well, he looked funny, act funny. Yeah, he was good in his way, yeah. Looked funny, talked funny, he had funny lines, they'd give him funny lines. How are you going to be wrong when you get the funny lines? I act like the straight man, he acts like the comedian. There's times when he'd like the straight man and me be the comedian, had to alternate it, you know. What fits one, fits the other. I used to tell a gag that was the supreme gag of the show. I used to tell a gag about goin' bear hunting, you know, which is a terrific gag. "So I was bear huntin', I got tired and sat on a log and don't you know I fell fast asleep and when I woke up there was a bear looking me straight in the face and I was so scared I didn't have time to grab my gun, I just started running back to the house where my buddy was and I ran and I ran, and I dropped my gun and I passed by the house and I says, 'Open the door' to Buck and I run around again and

Buck had the door wide open and I opened the door and side-stepped that bear and the bear run in and I shut the door and I said to my partner, 'Cook that one, there's one for ya, cook that one and I'll go back and get us another one.'"

That was a classy gag, classy gag. And then I said to him, "How did you get out of the house, man, when you opened that door?" "When you shut that front door, I opened the back door," says he. "Yeah, good for you." That's the gag I had -- one gag anyway. We had some gags that was terrific.
Did you act that out as you were doing it?
Yeah.
Was there a set where there was a house and you were running around the house?
No, no.
You were just telling the gag.
That's all. And I told it, too. I told it. You would have laughed if you heard it, you know, if I told it.
Tell me another one. Can you tell me another one?

Now, what could I tell ya now. Let's see, where were we. What did I come out of? The contract was signed for five years and it kind of crippled me, I couldn't do nothing. but how I got out of that, I don't know how I got out of that. I couldn't do nothing. So we went along until we got a date --
You were also saying about Nat Nazarro, wherever you went, he sent out an injunction. So you left Chicago to go somewhere else, right? You were running again like you were back in Kentucky.
Oh, that's when I went -- where did I tell you, where I went
from Chicago -- yeah, from Chicago from the Balaban & Katz theater to --

They paid us.
If they paid you $350 and you had to pay this lawyer $200, you were left with $150.
That was for that one date. I'm gone now with the $150 to some-place else. I think I went to Cleveland. I went to Cleveland.
Seems as if you put yourself in a situation where you were always on the road and always moving, always going -- a fugitive.
I got to keep on going just like -- what's that guy that stole all that money -- what's his name. You act like you don't know the biggest thing -- almost a war
The Shah.

Yeah. Just like he's running, ain't he? Okay. Well, I'm running because of the fact I've got to get jobs. He don't have to get no jobs. I'm running because I can't stand still. What can I do here when a guy's got an injunction on me in Chicago -- can't do nothing. What can I do in New York -- nothing. What can I do in Jersey -- nothing. So I've got to go get jobs. So I'm in Cleveland now.
You must have hated Nat Nazarro.
Don't hate nobody. I didn't hate him. Didn't hate him at all -- uh-uh.
So I get to Cleveland so that's when I decided I would go to -- into cabaret.
How old were you at this point?
26, I think I was, 26.

I'm dancing and I'm doing the act now.

Better.

Everything -- singing, dancing, talking, piano, comedy. What else do you want?

Like?

Then from piano solo go into another song -- medley of songs like "Nobody Knows And Nobody Seems to Care," and then into a little Spanish dance where Buck dances with me and a Spanish duel. Then I do my main dance.

Yeah.

Like in stop-time or what's that song --

Well, you've described your act. I'd like to go a little bit further into your act because you talk about some gags you did. You did tell me the gag about the bear before. And it seems like gags were interdispersed throughout the act. What other kinds of gags were there?
It takes two people to do them, the other gags. Questions and answers. Such as, I say to my partner, he being short, I says and he had big shoes on,

so I says, "Are them skis you got on? Your feet sure is big. How do you get your pants off at night?" "I pull them off over my head," And I says, "Well you pull this off over your head," and I starts playing and he starts dancing.

First I say, "Get out of that hole." "I ain't in no hole." "You sure is a low man, you know." And I start playing for him to dance. He dances and then he comes back to the piano and plays for me to dance.

And I say, "I passed by your house last night. Yeah, I saw you kissing your wife. Now, why didn't you put your window shades down? How come? I saw you kissing your wife. Ha-ha-ha-ha." "What you laughing about, I wasn't even home last night." That's a scorcher, man, that's a scorcher gag. That gag kicks them around like a dog.

Who wrote it?

Yeah.

No, he don't write music. He composed music, though. He composes. What did he compose? Like the "Buck's Boogie," but that ain't no music you can use, you know?
"Buck's Boogie," how does that go?
Can't tell you
how it goes, gotta play it.

Yeah.
Because I heard he was a fabulous pianist.

my hands for them not being in the way. They would always being showing up as part of what I was doing. I would take my hands to emphasize this, my hands to emphasize that in dancing, you know.

No, they weren't doing that.

That's right.

Nobody was
using the heel.
No.

so you could almost tell that's it. You understand what I'm saying?

That's right.

From the sound of the beat
From the taps on my feet

But I didn't get around to it. I guess some day. I

What?

I took all the good steps the audience applauded on and put them together. Do you understand what I'm saying? And took the time step out, there's no breather. I did about five or six steps between that side of the stage to this side. And applause all the way across and I'm going off the stage and the dance is finished. See what I mean?
I'm sure they're wanting more.
That's right. That's right. And I come back and give them more, another style.
The thing that amazes me is that you started tap dancing
at such a late age. You became such an innovater so quickly.
Correct.
But did you have any dancing --

Listen, that wasn't very quick. I had two points ahead of the game, see. See, I'm an actor, I'm a singer, I'm a dancer. Okay? The personality for singing, the personality for acting, the personality for dancing, that's three of them. Now, I've got three talents. Now how am I going to be so far behind? You ain't got but one. Or you ain't got but one. I got three. I sing, dance, talk and act. Now all those have got something to go with 'em. See what I mean? What boosted the dancing was the singing, what boosted the singing was the dancing, what boosted the acting was the personality. That's the way it developed itself. I ain't so far behind, I'm ahead. That's where I beat Fred Astaire, because I had much more to go with than he did. He could
only dance. I could sing and dance and act.
But the thing is you were great at all of that.
I don't know about the great part, just mediocre. Just use mediocre, it's a good word.
Mediocre, okay, mediocre at all of them.

Yeah, it took three of them to be mediocre, it took three of them. What's the difference of being great in all of them and successful in none. I can use the mediocre. So if you're going to give me a dollar and a quarter for a song when the song is worth $10 and $1.15 for a dance and the dance is worth $400, another guy is going to give me $1.25 for acting and acting is worth $450, everything is mediocre, ain't it?
I wouldn't say money is the judge of being an expert or the ultimate in --
Frank Sinatra
couldn't beat me singing, man, what are you going to say that for.
I'm saying that's why you were so great.
Where the money come into it, mediocre, man, mediocre.
Money is a different story --

Okay. Do you understand what a negro has to do to be recognized? You do? All right, then, that's why I use the mediocre term because of the fact that you've got to be twice as great, twice as good. I got to dance four times as good as Fred Astaire to get recognized as a dancer. I can be recognized as a dancer and just dance as good as he can. I can dance up to him, I can dance past him. You know what I mean? I can't sing even with Frank Sinatra, I've got to sing better than him or Al Jolson. See, I sing better than those people. That's what I'm trying to say to you. That's what I'm trying to say to you. I

sing better than those fellas, I dance better than those guys, but I was only mediocre. So what recognition did I get? Look at Frank Sinatra. He's a millionaire now. Look at Sammy Davis, he's a millionaire, too. He's a rich guy, too. 'Cause what -- what -- 'cause what? They want to join in a (unintelligible) situation where they want to carry a couple of thousand dollars in their pocket, yeh, go ahead. I don't carry nothing in my pocket. Just go care of myself. I quit when I want to, go when I want to. Nobody say -- poor Sammy is going down in the stage because he needs more rest than he's getting. He ain't getting enough rest. That's the way he feels.

That's the thing that's necessary. That's more necessary than

There's another song that's terrific. However --

In this country. You were sort of in the center of it -- not only were you in the center of it but you were creating it. What was happening, what was black entertainment like?

I wonder what we should do with them. It was in a wander, man. Black entertainment was in a wander because of the fact that the axe that I guess that they had, were they too much in demand or not enough in demand. And they didn't know what to do with them. Because when they would cut salaries and I refused to work so I laid off for quite a while because I refused to work, they cut the salary to the extent of how will I get it back to where it was and how can I work for $500 if I'm $1000 act. So I'd rather do something else. So I did.

I worked at a tomato place wherethey packed tomatoes. I used

to pick out rotten tomatoes from good tomatoes. I'd pick out good tomatoes from rotten tomatoes at their run, you pick them out and put them in there. New York. New York.

That was in 1948 or '49. I'd say between '47 and '49.

I chose not -- not to be in the entertainment world, right. I was in it but I was out at the same time. I'm

ready for it when it comes up like it should. But as long as they're ain't going to be nothing to it, I ain't going to bother with it. I'm just going to have a paycheck coming in at the end of the month or the end of the week to take care of the expenses.
It was hard times then?
Everything was tough. I had no money. Everything is hard when you ain't got no money.
So it was just a question at that point they weren't paying the amount of money you wanted so you said, well, screw you -- I'm going to go off and do my own thing.
Yeh. Yeh. We had an act in the thing you got now. The song they're singing now, called, 'Shove it, Take Your Job and Shove it.' Did you hear that song. Crazy ain't it. Anyway, I thought I'd put

the theater down, which I did. Then I used to -- we'd take little mountain dates like upstate New York, they called it the "Borsch Circuit," like Grossingers and Apernak -- several different ones -- Concord.

I was by myself.

Buck and Bubbles never did split up, man. Death did it. We never split up.

After death took him then I did it for myself.
And that's when you took those jobs.
We had worked there before. We had worked these other places
But when you took these jobs in the tomato factory -- that's after Buck had died.
Yeah. Mh-hm.

I just told you. January 31st, 1955.

Tell me what you want to know about. Tell me and see if I know it, maybe I don't know it.
Well, you were in cabarets, right? There must have been some --
Cabarets -- what cabarets?

Yeah.

Mh-hm, yeah.

That's right.

But the vaudeville has a bill of variety acts, one after another. Night clubs don't have that. Now, you've been to them. I know you have. It's like going to see a TV show and like going to see a vaudeville show. Now a vaudeville show is different than a TV show but they use the same talent.
Well, the circuits that you were going on, were they in vaudeville or cabaret circuits? You mentioned a number of different circuits.

No that's a cabaret in a cabaret --no circuit. They didn't have a circuit lined up that way. There's just cabaret dates in town, but no circuit. Like the theater, you've got theaters all over town but there's a circuit. 'Cause the owners have a chain of theaters. Orpheum has a chain, Pantages has a chain, Poli had a chain, Loews had a chain.

Mh-hm.

Theater in Philadelphia was a negro theater. That's the TOBA circuit. But who had a contract for the circuit. I didn't have no contract. We didn't have no contract for the circuit. So now what's the other question? Give me another.

nowhere. We were in the Paramount before they ever went there. Before. All the theaters in New York we played. If you follow what I'm trying to say. Bing Crosby, Burns and Allen, Frank Sinatra were nothing compared to Buck and Bubbles when we were on the stage. No don't talk about the performers now. We're talking about being in the business. You wanted to clear up a few points.

I'd love to clear up a few points, especially where we walked out of the theater in Boston, Massachusetts, which was in the year of '23 or '24 and we went on to other engagements that we set up and we got the appointment for the Standard Theater in Philadelphia with John T. Gibson. For the first time we worked by ourselves as a team of Buck and Bubbles and we left John T. Gibson's and booked in Newark, this is in 1923-24, and we booked in Newark. He filed an injunction against us in Newark.
Nat Nazarro.

Nat Nazarro, yeah. And we couldn't go on the stage or work or nothing and we weren't able to draw any money off of the work we already had done and it left us in a bad, precarious position and we had to leave Newark then to further bookings which I
seeked through the William Morris office getting a date in Chicago.
Didn't the William Morris office know that you were being handled by Nazzaro?
Yes.
They took you on anyway.

Kind of a bargain, I could let them have it for $350 on the assumption that they would book us to Chicago. So they did. To get an act that was worth $1000 for $350 was a good bargain. They weren't going to let that go under no circumstances. I didn't think they would. So we went on to Chicago and we opened up there. And while we were there he extended the injunction against us at one of the theaters there. I think it was at the Grenada Theater on the Balaban & Katz.
Well, what did you do back in Boston when you were left with no money. How did you leave, where did you get the money from?

I got it through a friend of mine working in a theater not so far from where we were as a maid to one of the actresses called -- oh, I can't think of her name. But however, she was a maid for one of the acrosses around the corner from the theater we were and she let me have the money, about $300 for Buck and I to go to New York. So we went to New York without the costumes and music that we needed to go and do our act, 'cause we had nothing, they kept our clothes, you know and the trunk and all in the theater in Boston. So we had to get some more material and all to work with. So we did. That's when we got the job with John T. Gibson in Philadelphia.
Can you tell me a little bit about John T. Gibson?
Oh, he was the owner of a theater in Philadelphia. He'd been there for years. All different acts had been playing there for the longest -- even Jack Johnson played there.
He must have been seeing a lot of pretty good acts --

Oh, yeah, yeah, uh-huh. We had quite a lot of comedians, like Sandy Burns, Sam Russell, George Wilkshire, God rest their souls. He had plenty of entertainment coming in that theater. Then he had opposition -- Sam Stiefel had the Pearl Theater over on the other side of Philadelphia that booked a lot of colored acts, too.
What kind of comedy were they doing in these acts?
Comedy like sketches they had, blackouts they had, they did military sketches. It's hard to tell you the comedy acts they had, but it was really terrific comedy.
Was Pig Meat Markham around at that time?
Yeah, Pig Meat Markham was around at that time, he was working in New York at the Apollo.
Can you tell me about some of those acts? Can you remember the kind of acts that they did, the kind of jokes they had?
I can't remember the jokes they had, but they had quite a few good comedy acts, different ones I could say, and naturally they had acts that you can't explain their material at all.
Well, what kind of subject matter, what were they dealing with, what did the humor deal with?

They were dealing like one guy is sick and he's in the hospital and got to get an operation and they're going to drill and one of the soldiers next to another soldier says, "Major, make (so-and-so) put his wing down." He would have his arm up and the guy would make him put his arm down because it didn't sound so good when he had his arm up. That was some of the things they did -- but it's hard to explain it to you.
Was it -- this was during World War I?
Yeah.
So there was a lot of entertainment gearing itself around the war, too.
Yeah, sure.
Were you, in your own act, were you doing stuff that was geared towards the war?
No, I was just doing the act. No do no stuff towards the war. Just doing the act.
You didn't add any different additional routines?
No.
Soldiers -- did you enlist?
No. I couldn't enlist.
Why's that?
I was too young.
How old were you?
The first World War?
Yeh.
I was 15.
So basically the kind of comedy that they were doing, this now during the 20's, some of them were still doing war.

Well, the gag that they used on little bits concerning the army. It wasn't going out doing an act concerning the army, the war or nothing like that. They'd do bits of the army that you wouldn't ordinarily do just dry long so. You got to build it like you build a sketch of anything. They do the hospital bit now but in the act it's just a bit they do from the hospital. This is the kind of thing they did.
Were there any specific people at that time that were
playing an important role in your own develop- ment as an entertainer?

No. Just that there were entertainers, I'm not the only entertainer -- Buck and I weren't the only entertainers. There were plenty of entertainers. They had a variety act of maybe 8 or 9 acts on the bill, 6 or 7 acts, something like that.
How would you normally travel from place to place?

By train. That's in the early times we started by train, pullman. Then we'd get onto where we could drive, and started traveling by cars. We would drive to different towns. See in the year of 1926 and '25 and '23, we were traveling betwixt and between. We would travel sometimes by train and sometimes by car. Over the little sucker we traveled by car to some of the places, too, that are in the city, we could travel by car. We would go from New York to Chicago by car many times. And from Chicago to California by
It must have been sort of difficult traveling on the road all the time.

'Cause it was a pleasure. See the scenery, too. It was nice.

Yeah, in New York. I had a family in New York, took time to get them there but from where they came, where I brought them from. Can we get back to when I was working in Chicago. That little place I want to clear up for you in Chicago. It was in the year 1926 from the Pathe' studio in California in the year of 1921 and '22 was good, but after that we went into New York and
after New York we went to Canada and from Canada we went again to the Loews circuit throughout New York. Then we had the difficulty with the contract in the year of 1926 and '25.

They weren't brothers. He hired this little fella as an act to work with him on the stage. That's who he had working with him.

Nothing. We did
our act. We did our act on the stage where he was. Do you see that, or do you?

That's right.

say nothing the way we were concerned. The kid is just going to be along doing the act with him.

Yes. Yeah. Yeah.
Who else?

Oh, many of them. He had a lot. In fact his office was the only office that had more than one negro act, because I'm the one that let them have the other negro acts because I wanted the other negroes to get jobs. But Bill Robinson and Ethel Waters, they were too individual and selfish to allow their agent to have any more negro acts. They thought they ought to have them by themselves. But I didn't have that kind of a brain, I guess. See, what harm I was doing myself, or Buck and I. They didn't have more than one negro act because I didn't know he was going to play one against the
other.
Who were some of the other acts that he got?
Oh, he got the (inaudible), he got George Jackson, he got Arbie Andrews (phonetic spelling) and her husband and we got Jigsaw Jackson and we got --
What did these people do?
They're entertainers, they're entertainers -- versatile, versatile -- that's all, versatile. Versatile entertainers, that's all.
They didn't have any novelties --

They're versatile that will take care of that. Versatility takes care of all of that. They were versatile, they could do anything more or less. They could do the best that they could do. Versatile in acrobats, versatile in dancing, versatile in singing. You get my point?
How would he play one off of another?

Well, this happened concerning -- for instance, take Chuck for instance, you want to use Chuck. But George don't know a thing about Chuck. But you know him and you're going to book him. But they want John Bubbles. You book John Bubbles, too. Now you tell the people that want John Bubbles that John Bubbles is busy and you give Chuck the job. Do you understand that? Now you tell the people that Chuck is just as good as John Bubbles, although you had never seen Chuck before. Then they buy Chuck because you said he was as good as John Bubbles was. They never saw John Bubbles before, they only heard about him. Never saw Chuck before, but you're going to make them know about him. You're going to get him a job at maybe $250 to $300, it might take him four years to get that kind of money. Through the name of Buck and Bubbles. You see what I mean? That's what you call playing one against the
middle. That's what he did. That was his job, Nazarro. So what can I say about it, I didn't know it until after it was over.
Well, was he managing other groups, other than yourself initially?
Yeah. Yeah.
When you first went with him.
No.
You were the first act for him to manage you?
That's right. He just had this boy work with him as an understander.
What sort of guy was he?
Who?
Nazarro. How would you describe him?
Russian Jew, he was a Russian Jew. That was him. But he

appears to have a heart of gold, but a mind of Hitler. Do you understand what I'm saying? He wouldn't let up off on nothing. He wouldn't let up off on nothing. So I can only say that's all I can say about him, and God rest his soul he'll pay for his. He's dead and gone now. Oh, I know that. That's without a doubt. Sure. Sure, man. No ifs, ands or buts about it. He was afraid that we would get too big and he would lose us. That was the idea, I'm sure. See what I mean? 'Cause

many people wanted us to leave him. Many people. We didn't have brains enough. We were too grateful and too loyal to do that. We thought the fella brought us up -- he took us over when we got to New York from this other guy that was so sad and we thought we were still paying the respect. But we didn't know at the same time this was a trick of his that he'd been doing. No, I didn't know that. But that's the way life went.

The whole thing, that's right.
What was Buck doing this whole time?
Nothin', what's he going to do.
Did he have any idea what was happening? Did he care, did he get --

No, he didn't have that kind of mind. He was satisfied as he was. Just like Chuck would be satisfied as he is if nobody enlightened him on anything, he'd be stay put. And that's the same way Buck was. I had to get him out of Kentucky. I had to teach him how to be and act in public. I was just like a father to him. So anyway, he --
What do you mean you had to get him out of Kentucky?
He would still be in Kentucky if it weren't for me. Why would he go? Why would he go?
What first attracted you to him?

His piana playing, his piana playing, that attracted me. Then I wanted to sing while he played piano. And that developed the act, it developed a whole lot of things. No use to leave him behind if I have to bring my own music with me, no use leaving him behind. I wanted to take him to the
carnival. I wanted to take him with the carnival, but he was too young.
Were you very close friends?
Yeah.

Oh, yes, that's the biggest mistake he made when he first got married. He got married while we was at the Sunset in Chicago in the year of 1926. I thought that was silly. I said, he doesn't have enough money to get married. That's right. That's exactly right.
But Buck obviously didn't take your advice.
In what way?
On getting married, he chose to get married.
That's right. His wife wouldn't take my advice either. I advised her, too. I advised them both. Told her why I'm speaking about him not getting

married and she didn't believe me, she thought I was jealous and I wasn't jealous at all. However, they found out. Trying to keep him up to the par of the public. In dressing, appearing, and his jokes -- he used to tell jokes. He'd tell a dirty joke in front of anybody and I had to break him of that habit.

During that time, during that period.

Miller and Lyles?
No, no -- there was another act, but I can't think of the name of it.
Eubie Blake?

No, no -- who were they -- what's the name of that act -- it's a team, I can't think of the name of it. dirty gags on no doggone stage. A negro couldn't get in the theater to tell -- couldn't get on the stage. (Inaudible) I just told you that.

So I'm in that era, before your time so you can't pull this time back to that time, what they're doing today. 'Cause they're doing more today against everything than anything I've ever seen and you ain't never seen it either. When did you ever see a 2¢ stamp go up to 15¢? Did you know Bert Williams?
Yeah. I met him after I went to New York. I knew Jack Johnson, too.
Was Bert Williams -- he was performing on the stage prior to you.
Oh, he was before me, sure he was. Sure he was. So was Johnson. There were quite a few on before I was but they

weren't in the business. I hope you can get the understanding that these people were on the stage before me but where were they on the stage? Where were they? If you're talking about a theater, you're not in any theater in the united world unless you are at the Palace or the Paladium as of today and as of 20 years ago. So where were they if they were on the stage? Where were they? You got the minstrels -- you got Huntington's Mighty Minstrels, you got Al G. Fields Minstrels. You got so many minstrels that's going on and plantation shows that went on in years gone by that the theaters weren't taking such acts -- negro acts especially. So the negro acts was like a godsend to that world the same as television was to the picture world. Television was an amplification on pictures. You don't know what it is, but there's going to be something
else.
What about Bill Robinson? Was he around prior to the time that you were dancing?
Yeah, but where?
Where was he?

That's the point. Where? That's what I'm trying to say. He was around, but where? All these acts you may talk about -- Bert Williams, he was in the Ziegfeld Follies. Bill Robinson wasn't in the Ziegfeld Follies. Bill Robinson wasn't at the Palace Theater. Bill Robinson wasn't in any big time movies. It took time for him to get in there but he'd been on the stage before me as a performer in different shows some places. But who knew? The people who knew today is like people who knew before you were here that I was on the stage.
Now my point to bring to your attention is that these dirty gags don't be told in the theater, man, because -- today they

tell 'em. Look at what they tell ya, saying the Lord's name in vain on television now. They're saying everything on television now. They're almost making love on television. What are you talkin' about. They didn't do that before. Where's the censors today? Where are they? You tell me so I know. The censors are gone, I don't know where they're gone.
So the kind of humor that was being done in those days was just clean humor?

All the way through, man. All the way through. They've got more gags in pictures now that we didn't have in years gone by. There's so much, people want excitement and all that, so they thought they could sell more of that than they could anything else so that's what they're doing with it.
What kind of things did Bert Williams do?
Comedy. Like

the Dark Town Poker Club, play cards, poker and do it by himself on the stage, play poker, let you see him in a poker game which is immense. Then he had a partner -- the team was Williams and Walker before it become Bert Williams. Bert Williams become the comedian and got in this show. But Williams and Walker was a team just like Buck and Bubbles is a team and I go in another show and Buck ain't here. Bert Williams did the same thing. His wife, Bert Williams' wife -- walker's wife, she used to dress like nobody's business, you know. And they did an act that was out of this world, yet and still, Bert Williams could make more money with them Ziegfeld Follies than he could with his partner.

Prize fight arena?
Yeah. We did the prize fight, you know. That was good, too.
This was all part of the show, all contained in the show.

And in that other play they had a racetrack treadmill right on the stage where the horses ran on the stage on a mill. You'd see one horse passing the other horse. I didn't get to that part, couldn't think of it. And we'd do 'Carmen Jones' in 1931 --

Oh, a long time before that.

Entertaining. That's all, entertaining, it's a club.

We had Leonard Reid. Had Clarence Robinson.

Yeah, they'd stage the shows.

Yeah.

Oh, yeah, oh, yeah. They had the other club called Connie's

No. No, no. No they come in the part where we go -- we got to go -- I've got to go to England and come back now.

He set it up but he messed it up after that, so we had to go on our own. So we went to England to the Palladium, splitting headlines with Gracie Fields, Gracie Fields was an English comedienne. And all the variety shows there. We played the Cafe de Paris. We played all the variety theaters there.
