Mr. Bubbles, you've talked to me before about how you were able to feel an audience out and you had a natural ability to sell your performance to an audience and you were just mentioning about the English audience that you had to feel them out. How were they different and did you change your act? Did you do anything different for them?
No, they're the same, but we had to change it around to make it meet with their sense of viewing. Because what was humorous to America wasn't humorous to English.
Can you give me an example?

For instance, the gag I used to pull, 'I passed by your house last night. I seen you kissing your wife. Why didn't you pull your window shades down? Ha-ha-ha. What you're laughing about, I wasn't even home last night.' That humor is different in

England. You would say it in a different way. I'm still trying to learn it -- so I didn't learn it, so you better leave and come back to America. Because the gags ain't going over like this, you know. But we were successful otherwise, all other bits we'd do, like get out of that hole, you little old man -- that was going over all right. "What's that I see walking down your neck?" "That's a mole, man" -- No, "What's that on your neck?" "That's a mole," He's walking." "If you had $5.00 in your pocket, what would you thing?" "I think I had on somebody else's pants." And "Who's that lady I saw you with on the Freeway last night." "That was no lady, that was my wife." These were all different for England, you know.
They liked that.
That was all different humor, you know. Things don't go as good over there as they do over here in that category. So you had to change it around. And

what you change it to, you'll find out, you can't wait forever to find out you have to come back directly to find out, it seemed like. 'Cause by the time you try to get the gags to fit the personalities, you could starve to death.

We had a good stay, westayed at the Palladium two weeks and come back. I had a beautiful time over there. The funniest thing about it, while we were over there we made the first broadcast of television for BBC. That's in 1930. We're now in 1930. And BBC made the first broadcast on television, BBC. Right. And then we made a couple of records with Eddie Condon over Columbia Records -- and what else did we do?
You made the records in England or --
Yeah, Columbia Records Company in England.
This was during the two weeks that you were there?
Yeah.
You did a lot
in two weeks.
Yeah.
This was your first time on television?

Yeah, this was the first time we was on television -- no this was the first broadcast television -- I think it was in 1936, not 1930. '30 we went on the radio -- we did a television broadcast in 1936. You understand? And it was their first broadcast of television, in '36. And we went out with Dudley Coates, Lady Montbatton, to Ascot Park, they took us out there to entertain the Duke and the Duchess and they took us out in a Rolls Royce, they brought us back in a Rolls Royce and they was racing all the way. I said, Oh, if I died, wouldn't that be something? All this royal blood we were mixed up in, you know. I said, what could be sweeter. However, we do the show, do the show entertain them. And it was so cool the way we entertained over ther -- great big

old fireplace in the middle of the room, baby grand on the one end in the room, and the fireplace in the center of the room and you entertained, they sitting by the fire, drinking, and you entertained at the piano, and when you finished a song, they don't know you finished, then they ask you to do another song, you do another song in the same style and they're still getting warm, drinking. It's just like a dead -- I don't know to mention it. It's so nonchalant, I got sick of the idea so I had to leave there. So when they brought us back to England I'm going to come back to America. So Dudley Coates want us to stay over another week longer and they would give a party for us. Mr. Coates, I said, I'm sorry, but I want to know how long it will be, only a fortnight. She said to a friend who was with her, they are only going to be a fortnight. "We want to give a party for you -- so and so and so --" Here's my card in case you change your mind give me a ring." I says, "Okay." Never did ring her. Come on back to America. But you see,

before we got to America at that time -- the manager, Nazarro, had sent a telegram for us to come back because he had a picture for us, picture contract for us -- no, it couldn't have been in 1930. It wasn't that, he didn't have it in 1930 -- come on back to America. But he didn't have no picture for us then, it was in '36 he had the picture.

So we come back to America after we did that and we opened up the Loews Circuit, Loews Theater in New York. Loews State Theater in New York. We played there. And while we were playing at Loews State Theater --
He sent you a telegram to come back?
No, not that one. Later on he did that. Later on he sent the message. It was in '36 he sent the message.
It was on your own motivation to go back, you were tired of it.
Yeah, it was only a two weeks' contract anyway. I was ready to go back anyway. And I paid for the transpor-

tation because we paid for the transportation to come out of our salary. So I didn't have any money left. I just paid for the tickets to come on back. And we started over in those Loews Theaters in New York when we got back and it was in 1931 when we went into Ziegfeld Follies. And to get in the Follies there was a show there that everybody wanted to play in, they would go on for nothing. Everybody wanted to go in the Ziegfeld Follies then, you know.

And we were picked -- the first colored act after Bert Williams. Bert Williams was the first negro that played in the Ziegfeld Follies and Buck and Bubbles was the second negros to play in the Follies. And we -- I took -- that's another job. Billy Rose for the Ziegfeld Follies. How that happened, we were playing at Loews State Theater in New York and I went to this show for the first time to see this show before we appeared. And the Ritz Brothers were playing and they were headlining the show. Ritz Brothers on the marquee,

Ritz Brothers in a banner and I wanted to catch this show and man, did they die. They died the death of a dog. So after the show I go downstairs to see the manager. So I saw the usher and told the usher to tell the manager that John Bubbles wanted to see him of Buck and Bubbles. So he says, okay, he'd go tell the manager to come out. So I could tell he was a manager because he came out in a tuxedo. He knew about Buck and Bubbles because Buck and Bubbles were going to be in his show next week. So he knew me. He wanted to know what I wanted. I said, I wanted to let you know I was here and saw that you had a wonderful show. Yeah, a rotten show. I told him it was wonderful. But I wanted to let him know I was there. I didn't want him to know that I wasn't in there to see his show and see how the headliner was flopping, had to steal a bow, and didn't give but one bow. And then I left the theater. I asked the manager what time was the rehearsal tomorrow -- he said 8 o'clock. I said, I'll

see you tomorrow, said I to he. So I leave and all the way home I'm thinking -- Ritz Brothers headlining that show. Couldn't take a bow. Imagine that. But I let the manager know I was there, didn't I? I wouldn't work in that theater any more. If we're not headlining that theater tomorrow I'm going to quit show business. That's what I'm going to do.
So I go on home and I don't sleep that night. If we don't headline that theater tomorrow, I'm going to quit show business. That's what I'm going to do.

And so I go on home and I don't sleep that night, I stay up all night that night, trying to solve how I'm going to solve how I'm going to quit the show, 'cause I'm just figuring aint going to headline it -- all night long. The next morning I get myself together to get ready to go down to rehearsal and would you believe that I go down to rehearsal and there's a jald (?) in the road at 47th Street and 7th Avenue and Broadway, there's a

jaded in the street that you get so far and you can see the theater, the front of the theater, of the Loews State Theater, the block between 43rd and 44th, and the big banner out there says "Buck and Bubbles," around the marque in lights, it says "Buck and Bubbles." This what had happened overnight. I'm saying to myself, who could have told them, -- do they care whether I quit or not. Who could have told them that I was going to quit. Nobody. Because I didn't tell a soul. My manager didn't know and my partner didn't know that it was in my mind that I was going to quit vaudeville and all the theater business. I was going to quit if the name wasn't headlined in that theater that day. And Lo and Behold --
Could you say that again.
My manager didn't know and my partner didn't know that I had it in my mind not to go on the stage any more and I was going to quit show business if

Buck and Bubbles won't be headlining that theater tomorrow. He didn't know that. So as I near the theater in the cab and saw this marquee with Buck and Bubbles in a banner over the marquee, Buck and Bubbles in lights around the marquee and even under the marquee they had Buck and Bubbles across on a banner. Well, I said to myself, who could have told them. What do they care? And I went to the theater, went backstage and the stage manager says -- come on in, Mr. Bubbles -- the first he said Mr. Bubbles since I've been coming to the theater over five years and played the theater two or three times every year. However, they give us the star dressing room with a phone in the room -- the first time we had a phone in the dressing room and Buck would rehearse the music and got the rehearsal over, he comes down for the show -- we went on to the first show and the audience didn't know what to think of Buck and Bubbles because it was the first time in any act that

they brought a headline that had anything to offer. They'd bring in movie stars out there and just headlines, they weren't doing nothing. Walk on the stage and this is Miss so-and-so-and-so. And that was it. But when Buck and Bubbles got on and give them an act that everybody enjoyed, we couldn't get off the stage. We stopped the show cold.

And from what I had said it would have no effect in my mind unless somebody was told, and who could I have told, I didn't tell anybody. And I had the coffee and the tears was rolling down my cheeks at the same time thinking this over, so I come back to the theater and when I come back to the theater -- the stage door is on the sidewalk, you go off the sidewalk to the stage door and

there's a vestibule inside and there's a phone on the wall at the end of the vestibule, right next to the staircase going back stage. And as I opened the door to go back stage, Buck was on the phone and saying to whoever was on the line, "Oh, here comes my partner now," with his hand over the mouthpiece, telling them, here comes my partner, just a moment. Then he puts his hand over the mouthpiece and says to me, "It's the Ziegfeld office calling." This is after the first show now. I says, "Really? Give it to me. I take the phone. I says, "Hello." "Mr. Ziegfeld wants to know when you can have an audition." Well, before we use any jokes we have to pass through the manager and the telephone number is Bryant 9-2335. Yeah, Nat Nazarro, yeah. "Okay. All right. Good-bye." I go upstairs and tell Buck, I don't know who it was but they got the gag, I give them the gag.

For a whole act -- you and Buck $1,000 altogether?
Mh-hm.
Or $500 each.
$500 each.

However, we could go to Nazarro and get a hundred dollars any time. And by that time I walked back to the piano and I said to Buck, 'We're going to do so-and-so-and-so for

" I heard him. I said, "What did you say?" He said, "Mr. Ziegfeld can only
afford to pay you boys $500 a week and I'm asking for seven -- no, $750." He's asking for $750, he is. Ziggie can only pay $500. Okay.

I could have said thousand just as easy as I said eight. But I already heard what the show -- who wants to do the show, and what I'll do the show for and so-and-so-and-so. And he made me so angry trying to get over there to do the rehearsal.

This is for special service now, this is. That's all the agents were booking over there, special service. That's what this was and that's what this guy, Lee Bouveau was booking, Special Service. However, I said no. So I showed them my pictures. Somebody got on the phone and I'm ready to go now, so when she got on the phone I'm ready to go. So she hollered to and says, "Don't you want to leave one of your pictures?" And to me I just said, just another picture left, that's all. I'll just give her another picture, it won't hurt me. Just give her the picture. I left it there, walked out. Understand.

Now I go down by the Bonnhoff as I told ya and I find that this guy that was going to give me a job for $20 a show, something like that and I couldn't take it. I couldn't take it. I told him what I wanted, they couldn't pay it. I didn't work. But I did a number for 'em. Okay?
So now I ain't got no job,

ain't got no nothing. I got to do the best I can. So what I do I go to the Bonnhoff -- now I'm only across the street from the Bonnhoff, so I go across to the Bonnhoff and I'm just going in to watch the people coming and going. I don't know what told me to go, but I went. And who should be going to get on a train that I could see about 150 feet from me -- the back of him, and I call him "Hey, Norman," and he turned around and came back and he saw me and he said, "Watcha doin' here, Bubbles?" I said, "Man, I was over here on a fast one." He said, "Where are you going now?" "Going back to America. I ain't got the first ticket." He says, "Yeah, you can't go home, you can make money over here." I said, "What do you mean make money over here?" "All they want to pay you is $15 a show, man." "They don't know who you are." I says, "I done try to explain who I was." And it was his office that he works out of that I was in that gave me $15. He says, "You stay here, don't you go. You wait until I come back," and "How you fixed for

money?" Man, I didn't know how to answer that, man. Old friend of mine. I says, "I'm all right. He took a card out of his pocket and wrote on his card to give me 100 marks, you understand, deduct it from him because he's earned his money. See, the Service pays off the agent and the agent pays the act. So they send all the money he makes for the shows he does, it's so much a show, they send all that to the office. He may have four or five hundred dollars worth of shows, they send that in to the office, to the agent and the agent pays him.
Well, when he give me the card, I still got the card somewhere, I didn't throw that card away, I never give it to the office, it says 'give bearer 100 marks' --
Who was this?
Norman Thomas of the Norman Thomas Quintet, played right here in America, old team I knew and the boy who played drums for him is in Switzerland now.

He's dead now, Norman is, God rest his soul. So I don't take the card to the office now. I just go on to the hotel, this is in the evening, I just left the office, I just go on to the hotel -- where this guy got me a room, it weren't no hotel, it was a private house. Like the roomers stay? I went to this place and time to go to bed almost. I don't want to go nowhere so I go to bed. The phone call ringing is what woke me up the next morning. It was the office that this guy was out of. I forget her name, but out of this fella's office, they was handling the acts, they was handling him. They asked me, 'Why aren't you on your way to Kaiserslautern? (phonetic spelling).' I said I didn't know nothing about it. I said 'How am I going to get to Kaiserslautern, how am I going to pay the people the rent here?' She says, 'Put the lady on the phone.' I put her on the phone, she could talk German -- I ain't going to take a thing unless it's paid for, I ain't going to take a thing out
of there. Keep it all there. But she told the woman over the phone that it would be taken care of, let him take the clothes and all, he's got to make a date and so-and-so-and-so. That was straight.

So I come out of there to make the date but I tell her on the phone though, I ain't got no money to get no ticket to go to Kaiserslautern. I ain't got no more money. She told me, can I get to the office and make the train. That's the only way I can go. She says, well you come on.

So I get a cab and asked the cab could he go to such and such a place and get me back to Bonnhoff to catch such and such a train. He said, yeh, we'll try it, come on, get in. He cabbed me out of there.

When I go into the office -- now remember this is the woman who couldn't give me but $15 a show. Anyhow she had booked it up to $35 a show plus hands me a 50 mark note to pay my transportation. I can't pay the cab, and

get the train and all that. So I tell her -- how can I pay the cab off and pay the transportation all out of this 50 mark note. So she gave me another 20 marks. So that means 20 marks for the cab, 50 marks for the train. So I go down, get the cab, make the train and I pay the cab and get on the train.

George, the tears rolled down my cheeks when the guy gave me the card to get the money from the office. I had to cry on that one, you know. When I got on the train, in the vestibule -- one car and the other -- I'm between the cars, and I got a cry there on my way to Kaiserslautern, man. Couldn't believe it! Couldn't believe it! I'm going to Kaiserslautern!

Getting to Kaiserslautern, I can't believe what I run into when I get to Kaiserslautern, 'cause a woman there she knew me. She's the woman who brought the / fellow here to write my life story. She's out of the services now at this time and she knew me. Then here comes another guy that works in the

"South Pacific" the play, a dancer, he knew me and he was there in Kaiserslauternand he had to boost me up to her concerning what they had charged me against that I was not the fault of. The club was prejudiced, seemingly, because they wouldn't keep quiet when I come out to M.C. the show and I was M.C.-ing the show he was with that I had and the show was built around me, you know.

So I'm M.C.-ing the show and when I got on the floor to speak, everybody was noisy, and it's a mixed club now, mixed club, Officer's Club, too. They got white and black in there, you know. I'm standing out on the floor to use the mike to introduce the show, who we got on the show and all, I got Mr. and Mrs. Valente, Katerina Valente's mother and father and her husband is on this show that I'm on in Kaiserslautern, and would you believe that when I went on the floor, intending to introduce the show, I got it all assembled and everything and everybody keeps quiet, but I stand there, and

they must have been thinking, "What's he standing there for?" They all kept quiet to see what I was going to say. Just like say, "Let's see what he's going to say." Look like they all got together and did that. Quiet. And I just said two words "You're prejudiced. Don't jibe me with nothin', you're prejudiced." That was my thought and I walked off. What did I say that for?

When I got upstairs, there's a balcony here -- when I come up to my dressing room, one guy tried to stop me. I go in the dressing room, get my bag and my briefcase and I'm going to cut out and go back and get on the bus and come back to Kaiserslautern, you know. Back to the city. I'm out in the outskirts. I'm out in -- what's the name of this airport -- it ain't -- it's kind of a bad reputation anyway.
But when I go get in the bus, while the rest of the show goes on, you going to do it, but I'll be in the thing waiting for you.
Were you the
only black in the performance?

I'm the only American entertainer. I'm the only black in the show, in this show, this revue. For entertainment I'm the only black and the only American-speaking person in the crowd, too, there. You know, they all were German.
In the audience.

And the audience is mixed, you know. So I go to get back on the bus, waiting for them to come out after the show is over and the guy's got the bus surrounded -- when I'm putting the things in the bus, in the back of the bus -- while I'm doing that some guys, soldiers, surround me, make a semi-circle around me and one guy says, 'You shouldn't have said that.' I said, I shouldn't have said it, I done said it. It still goes, I done said it. It still goes." I done say it still goes, I just said I done said it.
This was an American who said this to you?

He was an American. So by that time the bus driver comes out for the bus and the security guards that were inside that brought me out, they came out. They had to bring me out to the bus and they came out, when the bus driver came out, they came out, the security guards, and they saw these guys and these guys left. I get on the bus.

Now do you know what all the people in the show had in mind, I was drunk. I wasn't drunk, never was so sober in my life. But I don't know they was going to say this when they get back to the office to Mrs. Reddy, that was the lieutenant's name, Lt. Reddy. I didn't think they were going to tell her this, 'cause I wasn't drunk. But they told her I was drunk.
So the piano player, he could understand English, but he was German, he didn't say a word about nothin' he kept neutral, okay. I told her she could verify it by him. He didn't

verify it. But when this fellow called Red Knight was there and heard her tell him about what had happened with John Bubbles -- he stood her down because they were her guests, this Red Knight was her guest there and when they got through telling her about me and she went and told all the rest of them, 'Look, if I hear anything about John Bubbles again, I'm going to cancel the entire show and I'm going to get you off the bases, you're not going to play the base no more.'
So, man, they were scared to breathe where I was concerned the next time I went out on the show.

I went back to that same club again and I sat in the car while they did the show, 'cause they don't want to see me in there no more, and I don't want no more myself. But those in there don't know I'm in the car. They think the whole show is in there. They're in there to see the show they wouldn't be seeing me nohow.
So they all come out and somebody had thrown a glass and hit Mrs. Valente in the face with a glass. Then they knew that was a bad club.

When they got on the bus after the show, they got on the bus and told me about this. I asked them, was she drunk? No, she don't drink, old lady -- daughter, Katerina Valente, husband, her son -- oh, no, she don't drink.

However, George, they got the bus back to headquarters and they had to report what had happened with her about getting hit. So, therefore, something must have been wrong with that club according to me if they did that to her. So Red Knight had already told her about me, so she knew that I was right. Then they wanted me to stop with them to get themselves a drink on the way back or get a sandwich or something and I wouldn't get out and get with 'em. I got out of the bus and went over to the bus driver and I sat down at his table.
I didn't sit with the actors, I sat with the bus driver and had a sandwich and a cup of coffee, but I didn't bother the actors, no more to do with it.

You know what this woman did? She took a tape just like you got there and recorded my act -- I'll never forget this as long as I live -- recorded my act and sent my act into Wiesbaden where the headquarters for the Special Service was and let the man over at headquarters hear it and that man from then on I was in the driver's seat. You understand? When he heard me entertain he must have contacted America and told America about me, 'cause as soon -- I don't get back right then, I'm there yet scruffing up money for my fare to come back to America. What got me back was Lou Irwin. Lou got a part for me to do in a picture, the Bill Robinson Story, I was number one on the dancing list for the Bill Robinson Story because I could sing, dance and talk and move and act, 'cause I'd been in everything. You understand?
So I get back here, leaving

Germany, I left Wiesbaden, Germany, and went by way of London to come to New York and I got back into New York, I wasn't here no time before Bob Hope was asking for me to go with the show. Now you know that was really moving, wasn't it?

Now remember, Buck passed away while I was there. I'm there five years now, I had to stay five years to get back -- five years it took me to get back. You understand? Look how long I stayed there to get back here. All the time I was trying to build up the thing for Buck and Bubbles over there. If I could get on the ground floor over there, I could get Buck over there and we could start out from over there, because we are a good act, you know. But he died before I could get back here. And I got a card that he passed from my wife who said, "Buck passed and his wife wouldn't tell her where this or where that or nothing, and man, I cried when I got that card. Did I cry! Oh, dear! It hurt me to think I just come

over there for those 10 days and I was going to try to make up a foundation over there for Buck and Bubbles and send him his fare to come on over there instead of trying to break out on that low-paying salary trying to get Buck and Bubbles on in America. And I'd start over there for nothing. I'd be better off, that was my thought. You know?

So, I ain't got no one to work with and Buck starts to work with Timmy Rogers and his band. I got a clipping out of the paper and I got another clipping where Buck said that he was planning on doing an act without me before I'd even thought about it.
Well, what happened is, when I go with Bob Hope, man, that did it. Bob Hope himself had to congratulate me from what he thought about negroes to what he found out in me.
Now that's the kind of pace I set for the negro world, man. Now you know I've been through the mill. You understand?

And nobody's gone through that but me. I know that. I ain't worried about that. I'm just thinking about what fields I have covered in my way of doing and I'm so proud of them and so pleased. I got trophies from way back. You see one up on the wall up there. From way back that one up there. And I've got some in the family room back there. And I've got different things I got from Special Service.

Now at this time I am married for the second time. I'm married the second time now and when I come back this first wife has already served a prison term that I knew nothing about until afterwards, after she had gotten prosecuted for it. But I tried to buy it out, but I couldn't buy it out. Judge told me to send her a letter. I went through that.

Then I meet a girl when I go over with Transatlantic Rhythm, I meet a girl -- was that it? No -- no, the wife that I had then is the one I gave up on account of her getting in this trouble. Then I bumped into--
What trouble?

The trouble I had to get back to America. The trouble that she had in the incident that happened concerning the Guild, she was executive of a Guild -- Negro Actors Guild. She was executive of that Guild at the time and some funds got misappropriated and she was found to be guilty of it and I know it was a set up because one of the guys, his safe was busted and he had to get a safe man to unlock the safe and he fixed it so she wouldn't be able to get the safe open and he took some things -- fixed it so she couldn't get the safe open and he took some things that she would be accused of out of the safe so she wouldn't get to open it until she got the safe man to open the safe, and at the same time she was going to take a vacation and come to California with me, joining the theater with Paul Small and Finklehoff, Ella Logan's husband and an agent friend of his in "Curtain Time" and "Laugh Time" at the Current Theater in San Francisco.

So she came and I asked her, did she have everything straight, she said yes. She hadn't been in San Francisco one week before the news was out and they were looking for her. So when I got the wind of it, I talked her into going back to New York -- don't let them pick her up here. Go back to New York, it's better for you.

So I sent her back to New York and when she left the club to go back to New York that's when the detectives came to the club to find her with me, but she had gone. But I still don't believe at that time that she's guilty of nothing.

However, that went down and she got back to New York, then this fella, he's alive yet, the guy that said everything was going to be all right, he was going to help her and take care of her. He was the one that held her like, I got the crook here, I got the thief here, instead of telling her what best to do. And he's an old-timer.
But anyhow, that did that.
So she serves her time and after she finishes -- I waited, kept the apartment so she'd have some place to come to and stood by her. Her daughter was going to be a mother, she had the child.
Anyway her daughter came....

When I said to the Principal of the school it would be much better for us to go to New York with his hands being such a genius on the piano than it would for him to go to school 'cause he'd never learn enough to accumulate enough money as he would make with his hands. When I said that at 13, here's a guy that went to school and finished and everything and found that out, and I did this when I was a kid, the difference between that and he had to live it to learn it. I learned it by accident, to show you what I mean. But I chose the theatrical profession because there was more money in it than it was in jobs, labor jobs. Any time you can go on first (prize) with $50, now you're making a lot of money in less than 10 minutes because at that time my father was getting $18 a week. Do you understand? And I didn't want none of that $50, I gave it all to my mother but a quarter. Just give me a

quarter, that's all. I don't want nothing.
See, if I could just teach
the people -- if I could only write a book --
I'm going to try to write a book, I'm trying
to finish mine first but I'm going to write
another book on life -- like something on
life concerning marriage and children, because
that should be something for the people to
learn about the children -- the law is bad
against the children, too, because the law
says you can get married at 18. But that's
all. But look, if you have to learn the left
turn and the right turn and straight ahead,
the stop sign, and to slow down, not too fast,
if you had to learn that in life instead of
learning it by an automobile, the world would
be much better off because the children would
be born knowing what to do instead of waiting
to get to be 18 so they can get married.
Because after you get 18 and get married, here's
what else you've got to do, here's what else
you've got to -- what else -- see what I mean?

But now let's clean up what we dirtied up. We dirtied up mama and papa's life because they had to take care of us until we got big enough. So let's put back in what they had to take out. That should be the children today and of yesterday and the children of tomorrow should have the same idea, because it's set up so bad, so bad.

Look at a boy trying to take care of a wife and his poor mother done scuffled herself to the bone to take care of him to raise him big enough to get married. Now he's going to take care of the wife and in this world her people have done the same thing for her. But she can't stay to help mama get through the things, all the things she got to do, she got to go take care of the things the husband wants to be done.
So look at how all that's separated. It's all mixed up in my book. It don't come out right. I think there should be a law against all the things they got that

there ain't a law against. You get married at 18, but look at what you got to do after you get married. Look, you've got to have money to go to school, you've got to have money after you get out of school, you've got to have money to get a job to set yourself up in any business. Who's going to do that? The government should furnish that for you, too. The government should do that.

When you raise a child to a certain age the government should take over and find a position if necessary for him to get into to manipulate his education or utilize it for him, you know? But it's all so backwards.
How come you chose not to have children?

That ain't my choice. I was too busy, man. I was too busy. If there was any children the person that would be guilty didn't know they would be, so they didn't take no time out and I didn't take no time out so I just let it go. It just wasn't

my formula, I guess. But today I'm glad in one way and sorry in another, because I wisht I had had a brother instead of a friend I meet to take his word for it and don't know what side of the street he's on. Had to take a chance. Just like a nurse, looked like my sister's child. She come here to help me and he was worse than a stranger. But that's the way life goes, I guess. Your relatives are more harmful than strangers, some of them.
Did you feel that Buck was like a brother?

Yeah. Yeah. He was closer than a brother to me. I felt he was closer. We could understand each other. We had a whistle that we crossed to each other, know the whistle, you know. It was good. We would call each other Mike. He never called me Bubbles. I never called him Buck. I called him Mike. Oh, we were two, we were two -- I don't think there's any other two negroes in the world like Buck and Bubbles -- no other two, uh-uh,

impossible. Because, first of all, we were so gullible on helpin', helpin' people and doing and loved to do benefits -- hospitals and urban league and all those things -- we loved to do that and we did that along with Bill Robinson. He likes to do benefits, too, he was King Benefit Man. King Benefit of the theatrical profession, he was, Bill Robinson. And I think somebody else -- I think Georgie Jessel was the other one. We handed down, man, when you think about it -- m-m-m. I'm going to do something, I don't know what it's going to be, but I'm going to do something.

I want to change the National Anthem. I want to change that song and I want to change NAACP. I want to change that. I want to change the AARP, they ain't doin' nothin' -- all people aged 65 and over should get all their information concerning their condition in any form or fashion from the AARP, that's where it should come, not from Social Security. Anything you want to find out about old age, you've got

to call Social Security. Now what's it going to do about old age, they don't know nothin'. 'Cause I've called them to find out. They don't know half the things they should be doin' for people this age. You know what I mean? And there should be government insurance for old age, too, but there ain't. There should be insurance for the United States, but there ain't. And we had insurance before, ain't got no insurance now. You know what I mean?
Since they started this tax, the tax should be paid in insurance instead of us trying to pay taxes and insurance, too. That should be your money like Social Security is.
Do you think if Buck were still alive you would be more active in entertainment, do you think you would be doing things together today?
If he was alive?
Yes.
Oh, yeah, because I'd be able now, since I've gotten out of the

mind that I had concerning these old friends of his that he used to hang out with and the character because they have almost legalized what they prosecuted him for. That's almost a legalization thing now. And it's disgraceful when you think people had to go and serve time in jail and all for that and the days going to be free for nothing. That's a disgrace.
And look what they did to Louis Armstrong. That's the first one they caught doing that and they sure persecuted him.
What happened with him?

Well, he's the first one out here in California that they caught with the marijuana and they found him plus he was obligated to Joe Glaser for getting him out of the difficulty and Joe Glaser greased that one a bit to get him out when everything would have been hushed over.* That's how they got out.
He was
*Glaser's involvement comes later.
obligated to Joe Glaser --

Naturally, if you do me a favor I'm obligated to you. If you do me a favor I'm obligated. That was a terrible thing then, smoking marijuana. And at that time they made it bad -- so bad that they don't want you doing nothing but serve time for doing it. So if Joe Glaser can keep him out of jail and squash it down I think I'd be indebted to him, too. Why wouldn't you? Well, that's what will happen. But Louis Armstrong paid the price for that. Then comes Charlie Barnet, then comes the rest of them. Benny Goodman is the only one I think they didn't catch. You know? Caught quite a lot of them. But they paid for it.

They got Count Basie, they got some of his men out of his band, quite a few they got -- marijuana and it's now almost a legalized drug. Just shows to go ya, what the world turns out to be. It's terrible, the world is in a bad state.

Do you feel when Buck was gone and you were then performing as a soloist, did you feel that a certain part of you that maybe lacked the strength to go on and perform in the same capacity that you had with Buck and Bubbles, or did you feel as confident alone as you did in a group?

I feel as confident because everything I got to do is all made to order for me. I made it to order for me -- singing my songs and my dance. I got everything set up like I told you, the dances I picked. I picked the songs the same way and the dance the same. I fixed that up so that I had a definitely understanding when I went on the stage that this is me, I'm not short of anything. I didn't need the partnership to go on stage because I had that before I went on the stage. See, I had this partnership of my sister's before I went on with Buck. We did an act in Indianapolis, my little sister and I,

called, "Walkin' the Dog," then we could 'walk the dog" to the extent that they threatened to put my mother in jail if she didn't keep us off the stage. But we stayed on the stage and those were the days, I'm tellin' ya.

Getting back to a point I'd like you to know about is that when Buck was a little fella he was all right, but when he got to New York he got to foolin' around with the people in Harlem and he got uncontrollable and I couldn't do much with him. I'd leave him go one way and I'd go another.

We got in a big fight uptown in a club for the first time we got into a big fight. His wife, my wife and him and I all went to Small's Paradise on New Year's night, that was it. Then going in the club -- and I had already been going to another club owned by this same man, Ed Small, over at 5th Avenue and 135th Street, down in a hole, called Small's. But now Small's Paradise, he made a nightclub and I used to come over to the nightclub and watch the

entertainment on the strength of being in the hole with him when he first started, but never asked for nothin'. But I'd do this for nothin', sing, dance for him and when he got this -- the first New Year's party we went out to in his nightclub, Small's Paradise, he wanted to charge us -- it cost $20 a person to get in. Then they didn't charge the price, then he wanted to raise the ginger ale and Coca Cola stuff and ice. I think he sat a bowl of ice on the table when we got in in the amount of two and a half for the bowl of ice and a dollar and a quarter for a pint of ginger ale or two and a half for a pint of ginger ale, something like that.

However, I thought it was too much so we're going to leave there, we're not going to stay there. So -- just take it back. So he took it back and when he got it back he went and told -- I had to tell Ed Small that we broke the ice bowl. Now, George, if I broke an ice bowl it only cost a dollar and a half for a bowl. When I said I didn't break the

bowl -- wouldn't I say I broke the bowl for a dollar and -- how much is it. If it was two dollars, wouldn't I say what I (inaudible)? My name is Bubbles. Why would I worry about a dollar and a half bowl for. Do you know what I mean. I wouldn't have no kind of ruckus about no kind of bowl. Do you know one of the waiters told Ed Small and as we're going out, Ed Small stopped us at the door and says, "Did you pay for the bowl?" I said, "What bowl?" "The boss says you broke a bowl. I said I wasn't breaking no bowl. "Oh, yes you did." Why would you say that? My wife got made because I said "I didn't break it" and Ed Small says that I did. Now that made my wife mad. This is my first wife now. So my wife steps in front of me and says to Ed Small, "He didn't break the bowl." He says, "I'm not talking to you." She says, "But you're talking to my husband," she says. He says, "I don't care if I was talking to your mother," says he to her. Now I can't say nothin' 'cause

I'm very quick tempered. I just got to go through everything and get it out the way. So what did I do? I just said -- when he went to push her away from me, push her back out of the way 'cause he's talking to me, I just lift my hand out and help him push her back. And when I got my hand back far enough I come and I hit him right up side of the head with my hand, knocked him down, knocked him out, 'cause I had to drag him out of there. Okay?

Now, when they dragged him out then all the waiters they're goin' to jump on me because they all carried knives and everything. They were tough bunch and they would fight for Ed Small. So they're going to jump on me. So my partner was at the door trying to tell the waiters that I didn't do it. "He didn't do it." "He didn't do it." So the first waiter that got by my partner came to me, I had my hand alongside of me and said, "No, I didn't do that." "I didn't break the bowl."
Now he ain't satisfied when I

said that. He said, 'Oh, yes, you did.' And I hit him. Down he went. Now you wouldn't think that I could hit two -- don't tell me. And Jesus was with me, too. I had God on my side, too, 'cause I was right. 'Cause God was helping me hit him. Anyway, that was that. Now, the public got in it. They saw the whole thing, what people were near it saw it. They come out and joined it. They started fighting, waiters was fighting, everybody was fighting on account of me and Buck. And they were trying to stop the thing and while they were fighting and all crowded on me, I just saw so many pictures, just like I told you about that thing in Naptown, when I come out behind that box. Listen, I'll just say one thing -- let me get out of here. And I ducked down on the floor and it looked like everybody was piling on top of me and I go out between the legs of somebody and come out over there, they

think I'm down there. The ones on top thinks I'm under there and I'm over here behind them, you know? And I look at the bunch and I go upstairs, right there, I go up the stairs. I get to the top of the stairs and I wonder why Buck don't come on out. No, Buck don't come out right then. So I waited a couple of minutes at the top of the stairs and here comes Buck and a policeman has got Buck by the arm, by his right arm. And the policeman has got the club in his right hand, hitting Buck with the club. Understand?

When they get up to the top of the stairs there's a sidewalk then because it goes from the sidewalk down in the hole, you know. When get get up on the sidewalk -- now I'm saying to the policeman, "He's with me." Why did I say that for? The police drew back the club to hit me and I scooted out from under it, scooted away from him -- you know how you scoot back -- I scooted back from the club so he missed me and when he straightened up, he

straightened up with a right because I hit him up the side of his head and down he went, knocked him out -- now, I'm not hitting just with me, I've got everything hitting with me. I got all the right to hit him and I've got the right hitting him and the power of the right. So when I knocked him out, understand, up comes the policeman on the beat -- comes up and he comes running with a gun in his hand and Buck runs up to the policeman, says, "Don't shoot him. Don't shoot him." Now I take Buck and the policeman and back them against the wall of the building. I get them against the wall of the building, this policeman is trying to get up and I'm going over to the policeman to keep him from getting up, that's when the other cop -- see now this cop that hit on the sidewalk with his club getting more help and when this cop decides to get up and I go to the cop, the other cop comes up the street with a gun in his hand. Understand? When I grabbed the cop that came

up the street with a gun in his hand and the cop that was trying to get me off him, I pulled both against the wall with Buck in the middle of 'em. And somethin' says "leave." Just like that and I was the mast on picking up on any kind of clue I got. I pick up on the stage the same way. I get a cue on something, pick it up.
Somethin' say to me "leave."

I'm about as far from the corner as I am to the front door -- that's 35th Street, I'm on 7th Avenue in front of this place here and I'm on the corner here and 'round the corner there to go down. Now, I've got to pass a police station right around the corner here 'cause the police station is between 7th Avenue and 8th Avenue on 135th Street. I got to pass there. Well I knew how bad they were in there. So I ain't going around there. They got me in there on that. So I go on past the police station and I'm zig-zagging in and around cars so they can't shoot. I get all the way to 8th Avenue which is a block --you know how long them blocks

are in New York. I get to 8th Avenue and the elevated is still on 8th Avenue, the elevated and there's a cab going downtown and I run under the elevated and hail a cab that's going downtown, got in the cab and said to the driver, "Straight ahead," and by the time I said to the driver "straight ahead" the cop comes around to the car and opens the door before the cab could pull out and tells me to get out. And I'm saying "Shoot! Shoot! Go ahead, shoot!" He don't shoot like they do out here right away. No, he waited.

So somethin' said "get out." Somethin' told me. So I get out. Now I'm going by all intuitions, anything that comes in my head I'm going to execute. I don't care what it is. So I get out of the car -- the cab, meanwhile the cab opens forward like that, that way, hinges are back here. When you get out of the cab, you get out in front. So I get out of the cab here and just as I get out of the cab here, a cop comes from over here and he hits me

with the club. He going to hit me side of the head with the club. But before the club got to me, somethin' said to me -- I don't see him now -- somethin' said to me "duck." And just as I'm lookin' at you, I don't see the cop. It said "duck," I ducked. Bamm! I heard this club hit against the door of the cab. He broke the glass out of the cab, then I get this policeman that's here in front that told me to get out of the cab. I get him and the other cop, I said somebody is going to hell this morning. And I was determined. I didn't care what happened.

And by that time they subsided to the extent of taking me down, and instead of taking me to the 135th Street police station right at the block, they took me to 53rd Street police station between Amsterdam and St. Nicholas and that's where they booked me from.
Now, I done hit the cop -- understand -- I did all this mess. Now what's left is to get out of this. How am I going to

get out of it. Not Nazarro got me out of it. He came up to see what was the matter and he took out his money, a wad of bills and started pressing down, "Did they hurt you that much? Did they hurt you that much?" I said, "No, it's all right." He gave them a $50 bill and went to court, beat the case. That ended that.
What happened to Buck and your wife and his wife?

Look, Buck has gone home, his wife has gone home. They don't go with me. They go on home. 'Cause they don't know where I went. I was running, you know. I get the cab that goes straight ahead. They don't know where I'm going. So they go home.
I contacted them the next day.
Your wife?
Yeh, I contacted her the next day, 'cause I was where, 'cause I know they're going to look for me home, 'cause I don't go there, you know. But I got out of

that, Thank God. But I scaled some close quarters in life. But I made it. But I got out of that and everything, because I wasn't the kind of guy to get in anything. That's how I got out. I had a good reputation on everything I went in. A good reputation when I got in there -- before I got in, you know. So that's what helped me to get out.

"What did he ever do?" "How long has he been there?" What school did he go to," all that. "He's been on Broadway" so-and-so, so-and-so. That's what did it, you know. So I wasn't displeased about nothing but one thing. I was displeased about the management and displeased about the money received for the interest put in plus the efforts extended in this profession. I've been always unhappy about that. Thought it was disgraceful. I should be a rich man, but how can I be rich when I ain't got no money. Can't be rich that way, m-m. And I've been underpaid so much
it ain't even funny. Never mind. I don't mind that because I figure I'd get it on the next job.

Lou Irwin did one for me, he booked me on a show with Jerome Kern who put on a show with all the songs he had written in Hollywood and I was one of the performers that was in it with Louis Prima and Dick Powell and Robert Montgomery and Fred Astaire, with all these people in this show. He books me in there and would you believe that the man that puts on the shows, it's like the aged father show that you put on -- he was the one that got me to my agent, but my agent don't know that I'm going to bump into this man -- I guess he knew that he was going to bump into me but when he saw me and my associates that knew me so well, this is the agent that I was telling you about that Lou Irwin had booked me through for this show. But when he saw me hanging out with these people that knew me so well and we looked like we're such a family, he came to me and says, 'You need

to get another agent. I says, "Why?" He says, "You could have got more money than what you did. You could have got better than $750 (I think it was) for this show. He just didn't fight enough for it." I says, "Really?" I says, "That's all right. I'm getting more now than what I'm doing -- for more than what I'm doing now. I'll make it up some other time to clear my point of it." But I never did tell Lou about that. I just made it from that point on that I'll set a salary for him to go by instead of him setting one. I used to let him set the salary just like I let Nat set the salary. Then he'd ask me did I want to go for it. If I don't go for it then if I need ten or fifteen or twenty dollars or a hundred dollars, he's not going to turn down it down that day. See what I'm saying?
So that was the only thing that I went along with that I changed after this incident happened.
So now when you speak about

salary, that's why I go and let this girl book me in this show because she didn't know enough about the salary. She don't know what California is, she don't know about agencies neither. So I didn't want her to mess with this idea of booking me in that show. So I said do it through whats'name because he knows, because she worked for Lou Irwin and Lou Irwin knew what to do where I was concerned and I figured she knows the same thing. She's a good agent. She's a good agent. Very good.

Well, I guess you never took a very active role in the business part of your career. You always let somebody else handle that and very often you didn't find out the details. You pretty much just went along with the business as it was presented to you.
Mh-hm.
And you're saying now if you had learned more about the business you would have been further -- as far

I went to the bottom. That's all right -- top and bottom, okay? Now, you see, I would rather have finished school and learned what was needed more so than I wound up in this. I wisht I hadda finished school because I would have had more brains on the world than I have, in all these crises, I'd have been one of them guys up there on that there calendar,man. I would have been one of them guys, you know that? Because I know I've got the mind -- those are the presidents. And to think what education you have to have. Of course you don't need no education to be a thief and a liar. You don't need that for that. And that's what we've turned out to have. Men finish school and turn out to be thieves and liars. That's all they turned out to be. A bunch of crooks. And why they do that, I don't know. That's what it's

turned out to be.
And how they could have
reached down south to get a man for President
and leave a person that's more deserving of
being in a position for . . .

During the time I was in Indianapolis when I was selling papers like the Indianapolis Star and the baseball extras, I used to have to go to the newspaper office to get my papers. So I'd get to the paper office to get my papers, quite a few of the boys -- me being the only negro boy seemed like was there picking up papers -- thought they'd want to have a little fisticuff with me. So they picked up the best one they thought could fight me and they got some gloves and put the gloves on us and everything, but I don't want to, I just had hurt my thumb sliding down a pole and got cut on the barbed wire fence and tore my thumb wide open. However, they didn't pay no attention they wanted me to put on these gloves and fight this boy and I had to do it. So I did. So we boxed and we boxed until they found out I was no slouch, you know. 'Cause I could fight a
while, you know, which I loved and I loved to fight, how I loved that. But I hate to get into an argument, 'cause I know he's going to make a fight out of it.

So anyway, I quieted him down on the idea of us boxing or anybody fighting in this group, after they saw me fight, they saw I was too good for this boy. So I got my papers daily with all impunity, nobody said anything against my getting them or nothing. So we all got along fine. Then I went to get into this Indianapolis contest to win a bicycle, you know, the first prize is a bicycle and so forth and I get that all right.

And then I played all the biggest theaters in Indianapolis from the New Royal, which is the biggest theater, and we got to Indianapolis, you know, I got a trio together. See it was only Buck and Bubbles at the time and then I got a little boy called Sugar Babe and we put him in the act and made a trio and we were the first Ink Spots, you

know. Buck and Bubbles and Sugar Babe were the first Ink Spots out of Indianapolis, Indiana, where Deek Watson who is one of the Ink Spots now, took the name and started the Ink Spots with Bill Kenny 'cause he's from Indianapolis -- Deek.

However, the Lyric Theater in Indianapolis is where we did the act called the three Ink Spots. It was sensational. We played in the Royal Theater which is the biggest theater in Indianapolis and I played the Two Johns and I played the Senate Theater and played every theater they had that was more or less worth our playing.
And I also worked in the five and ten cents store, J.J. McCrory, I think it is. I was a janitor in the five and ten cents store.
Can you describe a little bit about who the Ink Spots were and what they became?
They became

famous by the name of the Ink Spots. Deek Watts was from Indianapolis and I don't know where the other boys were from. But they had Deek Watson, they had Bill Kenny and two other boys from time to time, they'd take one out and put one in. However, they made a big name out of the Ink Spots, you know. But we started it. Buck and Bubbles started that and we were the first three Ink Spots and that was about the year of 1914 -'15 -- '14 I think it was, 1914, something like that. It could have been a little later. But it seems like those were the years.

I 'scared to leave you
'Cause my heart would break
I don't want you to break
'Cause you can't (inaudible)
Oh, oh, oh, you beautiful doll."
That was a lovely song.

called -- oh, Lord, I can't remember all the
songs, it was so far back, goes way back, that's
over 50 years back. It's hard for me to
remember the songs we sang.

This is where I got to the
place where I just sit down and start to,
you know, meditating over things I've done,
then I can go into what the songs were.

Then we did "Somebody Loves
Me," and we did -- only thing at that time my

for the Ink Spots. I would have written a song
for the Ink Spots, if you understand what I'm

And that's Indianapolis I was

telling you about and in Indianapolis is where I played these theaters and where I started in a theater called the Pioneer Theater. I first started with this guy that had the Pioneer Theater right near the fire department on the other side of the railroad. When they first started they had the olio screen for the moving picture and they had a little platform, you had to stand in front of the screen to sing, 'cause I wasn't dancing then, just singing. But I could sing a while, you know. And I was singing like "Georgia Rose" and "Curse of an Aching Heart," "Brothers and Sisters (inaudible) Pray for the Lights to Go Out."
Oh, I had a ball in those days, didn't I have a ball.
Can you sing any of these songs?
I don't remember the words, don't remember the lyrics.
Just for the information of the person who's reading these

transcripts or whatever, we're going to go back a little bit in time again -- in fact to the beginning where it all started. You're talking about when you were very young, these songs you were singing when you were in your early 'teens?
Yeah, early 'teens.
When you first formed the ink spots, how old were you?
About 13, I think.
I don't quite understand how you came up with the name of Ink Spots.

Because that's what they give us at the theater. See, there weren't no negroes playing on the stage in that time in these white theaters and they wanted to put a name out there that everybody would kind of feel good about and they couldn't get people that had a big name to play that because they didn't have no negroes playing in that theater.

So they took like what we call little kids, you know, and they put the idea of the Ink Spots which would draw attraction, they'd take three spots of ink, understand,and put it on a piece of paper and you'd see the ink spots, that was the idea and they put Buck and Bubbles pictures on the thing, Buck and Sugar Babe and myself.
What happened to Sugar Babe?

When we got to Chicago, a fellow that we used to work for, they had us there, called William Poe, P-O-E. William Poe and he was a meat man, he handled meat and he took us to Chicago from Indianapolis and when we got to Chicago that's when we played the O'Clean Theater and he ran off with the money and we are all stranded there and the fella that was our tutor putting us on the stage in Louisville, he had his wife along with him and he was taking care of us. His name was Billy Maxey. He was a comedian, Billy Maxey was. That's the

fella, the manager of the theater in Louisville, had to dress us all, we first went on as urchins in the theater and I was just with his sister before she died. She was in Chicago and he went to New York and I saw him in New York since I've been grown and I met his sister and I only learned about her when he passed, 'cause she got in touch with me to let me know he passed and so forth and I found out when I got in touch with her she moved to Chicago from New York and in Chicago I went to see her. I got pictures of her I think and a postcard of her and I got it down to put it in my book, my story, you know. I got some data on her for my story. She liked to travel all the time. She was a warden for the women's prison in Chicago. She's got a daughter that's still in Chicago, I think.
We were stranded in Chicago with the Ink Spots doing the act at the Olean Theater — I forgot the name of the show or the people we was working with. The guy for who

we did the show and finished that engagement there and were expecting to get paid off, the man run away with the money, left us all in Chicago stranded. That's Billy Maxey, his wife, Buck, Sugar Babe and myself and at that time the weather was cold, too, and you know how the coal men drive by and put a pile of coal in front of your door, or in front of your gate, you know, on the sidewalk and the people have to get somebody to put it in. So I hauled coal into people's houses to get money enough to buy food for us and I took what little money that there was and bought us some potatas and made us a stew and everything, for Buck and I, and we had a good meal with little or nothing. And I give Maxey some money to buy food for him and his wife.
And then when we got back to Indianapolis Sugar Babe's mother wouldn't let him go any farther with us because of that incident. So we lost the three Ink Spots.
What was
Tenor singer.
So you two just did harmony with one another.
All three of us. Buck and I only did a duo. No, he wasn't a tenor, he was a baritone -- baritone or a soprano -- Sugar Babe was. I had the tenor voice and Buck had the baritone voice.
Were there other singing groups like that at that time that you had heard that you tried to pattern a bit?
No -uh-uh.
You just came up with the idea of having a --
That's right, that's right, that's exactly right.
Did they ever record the Ink Spots?
No, we didn't make no recording. We didn't but they did.
There is something that exists then.
Yeah, but not of Buck and Sugar Babe and myself, nothing as to that but what I'm telling ya.
Well, when you went off with Buck and Bubbles and the other Ink Spots, how was it taken over by another group?
Well, he was from Indianapolis and he could just use the name because you can't copyright the name, we couldn't copyright that name, at least we didn't.
How long were you together.
Oh, about six weeks. Six weeks as Inks, that's all.
Did the subsequent Ink Spots sing in a similar style as you?
They were different altogether, they were grown people
singing? We were kids singing.
But the name was --

The name is what they had. They had a big reputation. The Ink Spots? I know you've heard of them. So that's what they made out of that. But they weren't the beginners of it. We were the beginners of it, you know.

And I want to get you back to where this carnival that I was with had traveled to Nashville, Tennessee, and that's when the big epidemic of the flu was around and the show was quarantined in Nashville and we were lucky to get out of Nashville over the quarantine -- a hundred however got out and I went back home to Louisville. When I got into Louisville I found my mother had been sick and a fella on the show that I was with on the carnival, I've forgotten his name, doggone it, can't think of his name. However, he says what I could get -- he showed me what he used for

people getting colds in his mother's age and it was good and he said the soldiers use it and it was rock candy, glycerine and whiskey. So I went back to Louisville and my mother was in bed and been in bed for two weeks and I didn't know it. So I made a fire in the stove, we were using coal then, you know, and I went to the liquor store, I got half a pint of whiskey, went to the drug store and got a bottle of glycerine and some rock candy and I brought that back home and gave it to my mother. She got a big dose of that, like a wine glass, I get about three of them and the next day my mother was up and out, you know. I never forgot about that as long as I live. I said the Good Lord brought me back there with my mother then -- instead of me going off with the show then, I went on with the government building highways.
How old were you then?
15, about 15.
This carnival
which you had referred to earlier, you were with a black group of performers, right, there was one group -- troupe of black performers that were a part of the carnival; is that right?
Yeah, yeah.
And when the carnival performed, what role did you all play in it?
I was playing by myself.
I know, but the whole group of black performers --
They did mostly like a minstrel thing -- you have an end man and an interlocuter.
What's that?

That's the straight man that asks all the questions. He's called the interlocuter. And two end men, interlocuter and they have the rest of the people fill in like a chorus, you know, we all sang together, we all had jokes together.
Do you remember any of the jokes, the songs from that time?

Yeah, I remember a couple of the jokes. One of the jokes that says -- one fella says to the other fella, he says, "You know, Henry, I saw you go down the road there you had a cow on the end of your rope. Where were you going with that cow. Is that your cow?" "I had him, didn't I?" "Yeah, that ain't nothing, I heard about you, so what did you do?" "What did you hear about me?" "I heard that you was in a jewelry store and you stole a watch." "Who told you that?" "Oh, you know so-and-so, he told me." "Did he?" "Yeah, ole cowie, old watchie." So the guy who stole the watch says to the guy who has the cow, he says, "What time is it?" He says, "It's milking time." The way he had the line it was funny. Sure was funny. I laughed, I thought it was a funny gag. Course today it isn't as funny as it was then. Time marches on, you know.
What is it about today that wouldn't make that joke work today?

The two people to deliver it. Ain't any two people that could deliver it as the two people who did it. Just like you Moran and Mack, Amos 'n Andy, two people. One person can't do what two people do. Intonation is one thing, characterization is another, you know. That's what makes gags. Like I tell the gag to my partner and say, "Man why don't you pull your window shades down. I saw you kissing your wife." And the characterization of that is how you laugh. "Whatcha laughing about, I wasn't even home last night." That's the funniest gag I ever heard in my life. That guy's gotta be awfully dumb to just take a gag like that, you know. The audience used to roll at that joke. And I just loved to say it all the time. That's the way life goes. Let's get back to (whats'name.)

I told you about the mule with the light when I was working for the government. I had to strike a match to find my mule at 3 o'clock in the morning. I told you about that. And I told you about how the cart would pick up dirt and I got dumped on the dirt with a truck and all. And I told you about leaving there and going back to Louisville and I used to imagine all these years going and I ain't found a sweetheart. All these years gone by and I haven't found a sweetheart. I go back to school, you know, when I went back to Louisville, I started looking from nowhere and found one of the girls in the school, I'll never forget her, her name is Mary Lucy. She was a pretty girl. And I ain't tend my mind on no girls at all. I wasn't thinking about that. All this time I was working on how to make some money. How to make some money and I couldn't be worried about no girls when I'm looking to make some money, man. I got to do something. And that's what I'm busy doin'.

Oh, then I did this what's the name, in Louisville, I worked for what they call the Midtown Grocery Store. I used to deliver groceries from that grocery store. I'd drive a horse and wagon and my father used to work in Louisville Trust Company, firing boilers. He was an engineer-like, huh. That's in Louisville. And in Nashville when my father got the job there when I was going to school there before we were transferred to the 24th School in Indianapolis, my father worked for the Nashville Saddlery Company, you know. He died at the age of 47 -- 46 or 47.

And I had a good life. My family was good. I just loved my family. My mother was good to me. My father was good. My sisters were good. Had eight children, and out of eight children there was seven girls and one boy and I'm the only boy. So you can imagine how lucky I was, huh? 'Cause I was one they didn't want. But they couldn't get rid of me. That's the only thing about it.

Just to think Nazarro got to the point where he thought he was going to break up the team of Buck and Bubbles because I didn't want to sign no more contracts because my mother told me not to sign for a couple of days and he was trying to beg me to sign before the contract runs out. I said no, mama says that I should take a little rest. So while I'm taking a little rest, that's when I missed that I didn't have the-Buck's contract, the partnership, and he took Buck and told him a story to the extent of what his father told him. His father told him that Buck was half a shade lighter than me, you know. He would say to Buck, you know, my father told me a colored fella with your complexion is honest but a fella with your partner's complexion, he dishonest and he put all the bad marks on me. He tell my partner this. He's going to separate Buck and Bubbles, you know. But I was determined he wasn't going to do it, but I didn't tell him this, you know.
So I said to Buck one day -- so

he told me, he said to me, his father told him that a fella my color was honest and a fella Buck's color was dishonest, understand? So Buck had it one side and I had the other side. So one day I said to Buck, I said, "Buck, did Nazarro ever tell you that a fella your color was dishonest and a fella my color was honest?" Just the opposite, just the opposite. You get my point? I can't tell him the truth of it or he won't tell me his story, 'cause he knows the man told him that he was good and I was bad and I'm telling him the man says he was bad and I was good. I'm telling him about this so he says, yeah, but I know he's telling me wrong because he told me just the opposite way. You know? Now ain't that something. Now my partner don't trust me because his father told-- this fella's father told him what I was and what he was. And I let him do that. That's what this guy was doing. Now how would I detect that. Think about that. How would I detect that. Get my point? Ain't that somethin' for a guy to do?

As much money as he has made off of Buck and Bubbles. If I was that man -- oh, he must be turning over, wherever he is. He gotta be turning over. He can't lay in one spot. Too hard. You know what I mean? But that's life for ya, and he died three days and nobody knew he was dead. He was dead for three days. Had to break into his apartment in order to find that he was in there.

Just died. All the breath went out of his body. (Chuckles) I don't know what kind of disease he had, he just din't breathe no more. I don't know whether that's a disease or not. up.
